noticias.titulo: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79
noticias.resumen: Odochie rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.
noticias.texto:
Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79
- Published
Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.
Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.
In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.
Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.
His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.
The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.
Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.
"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.
Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers.
"Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said.
The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.
Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.
He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

noticias.titulo: Two children among six dead after plane crash off Mississippi coast
noticias.resumen: Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, the US Coast Guard said.
noticias.texto:
Two children among six dead after plane crash off Mississippi coast
- Published
Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard says.
The Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said.
Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.
Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said.
Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, said: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

noticias.titulo: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
noticias.resumen: The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
noticias.texto:
South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
- Published
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.
In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (Â£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.
Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.
The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".
In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make".
"It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said.
The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.
Political analyst Khanyi Magubane said the court ruling was a victory for Ramaphosa as it gave him "political and constitutional credibility".
She made it clear that the ruling was not a criminal finding on possible improper conduct at the farm but rather an indictment at the independent panel's report.
"[So] he does get significant reprieve ... but there will always be the shadow of the Phala Phala report," Magubane said.
The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.
The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.
Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.
The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.
Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.
Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.
The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".
It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".
Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.
He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.
It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.
In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".
The Western Cape High Court's ruling could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.
If they do, and the appeal is successful, the parliamentary committee would be able to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.
If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.
Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.
He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.
Legal expert Professor Richard Calland told the BBC he had expected the court ruling, given what he termed as "fault lines" in the independent panel's report.
Calland said the court's findings now meant that the impeachment process was "dead in the water [and] cannot continue".
He said that any political party that wanted to revive it "would have to come up with a whole new basis" for this.
Calland said political parties who want to hold Ramaphosa accountable would likely seek to appeal the ruling but it was unlikely parliament would also do so.
"So, the president's political career is now free of the cloud of impeachment," he said.

noticias.titulo: Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty
noticias.resumen: Solomon Islands leader Matthew Wale said his country would no longer be a point of regional uncertainty.
noticias.texto:
Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty
- Published
The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.
At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".
In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing.
There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.
On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.
Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.
He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".
"Those days are done, gone," Wale said.
Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.
"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity."
"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions."
On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.
"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said.
The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.
It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.
Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.
"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.
William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".
Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.
Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.
The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.
Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (Â£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.
Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China.

noticias.titulo: Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date
noticias.resumen: The son of Zimbabwe's late former President Robert Mugabe has faced multiple legal troubles in the recent past.
noticias.texto:
Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date
- Published
A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.
Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.
The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.
They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.
Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.
The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.
Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.
Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.
His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.
Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.
In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.
In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.
He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.

noticias.titulo: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
noticias.resumen: The US president's intercession to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang has inextricably linked their fates.
noticias.texto:
Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
- Published
After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.
"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.
Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised fist clenching a red bra.
The post was classic Trump â potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.
Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal â one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy â the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?
Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?
At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.
And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.
While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.
"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".
Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.
They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.
State governments could also launch their own investigations.
Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing â and, by association, Trump himself.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.
"Congress has much to investigate," he said.
- Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away 
  - Published21 hours ago
- What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump 
  - Published1 day ago
- US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation 
  - Published12 hours ago
While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.
Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.
Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.
In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.
"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.
The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.
The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.
Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.
Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.
The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.
Trump's decision to help save Huang â noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" â could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.
"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.
"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."
For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.
Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.
He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).
And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.
Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.
He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI â which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" â will control the fate of the world.
If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.
In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.
Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.
US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.
The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble â like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 â that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.
Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.
On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.
Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.
And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.
- US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal 
  - Published1 day ago

noticias.titulo: Senegal deny Morocco’s allegations of ‘contact’ with CAS amid AFCON row
noticias.resumen: The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.
noticias.texto:
Senegal deny Morocco’s allegations of ‘contact’ with CAS amid AFCON row
The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.
The president of the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF), Abdoulaye Fall, has denied Moroccan allegations that he had “contact” with a Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) arbitrator who ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.
The Moroccan federation (FRMF) alleged after Tuesday’s ruling there had been “contact” between Fall and German arbitrator Ulrich Haas, one of the three CAS panel members, 48 hours before they decided “unanimously” to award the trophy to Senegal.
“That is absolutely false. I have never had any exchange with any member of CAS,” said Fall on private television channel TFM on Wednesday.
“It surprised and astonished me that such accusations could even be made. I have never been in contact with anyone in connection with this procedure.”
In January, Senegal won a chaotic final 1-0 after extra-time.
But two months later, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) sensationally overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory, and the title, after many Senegalese players walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty given to the hosts with the game still goalless.
The CAF Appeals Committee had justified its decision to overturn the result and declare Morocco champions based on Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations.
Those state that if a team “refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee, it shall be considered [loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition”.
However, the Senegal players eventually returned to the pitch and the final carried on.
The three-person CAS panel therefore considered the referee’s decision to restart the final showed “the conditions for resuming the match had been met”, and that articles 82 and 84 were therefore “not applicable in this case”.
The Moroccan federation has the option of lodging an appeal with the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, which does not rule on the merits of the case, but intervenes in procedural matters.

noticias.titulo: South Africa court repeals ‘farmgate’ impeachment threat against Ramaphosa
noticias.resumen: The ruling hands the president ​a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment.
noticias.texto:
South Africa court repeals ‘farmgate’ impeachment threat against Ramaphosa
The ruling hands the president a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a court bid challenging an independent panel’s report that had paved the way for his possible impeachment over misconduct allegations linked to a burglary-turned-political scandal called “Farmgate”.
The Western Cape High Court on Wednesday declared unlawful the 2022 findings of an independent parliamentary panel that accused Ramaphosa of a conflict of interest over the origin of large amounts of cash stolen from a sofa at his ranch in 2020.
The ruling hands Ramaphosa a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment at a vulnerable moment for him and his African National Congress (ANC) party.
“The court found that the panel fundamentally misconstrued its functions,” Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said, reading the court’s unanimous decision.
“The ‌panel went beyond its lawful remit, asked itself wrong questions and made several material errors of law.”
Ramaphosa “notes” and “will study” the court’s judgement relating to his Phala Phala game farm, the president’s office said in a statement.
“In seeking the judicial review, President Ramaphosa exercised a constitutional right,” the statement read. “In line with his respect for the rule of law including judicial independence, President Ramaphosa will study the decision of the court.”
The theft came to light after a former intelligence boss reported to the police that Ramaphosa had allegedly sought to cover up a theft of millions of US dollars in cash at his farm, initially claiming it was about $4m.
Ramaphosa has always denied wrongdoing and said the $580,000 stolen at his farm was money from the sale of buffaloes.
But the episode raised questions about why he had so much cash stuffed in furniture.
The 2022 report said the president failed to report the theft through proper channels, violated the constitution regarding paid work from his farm and directed presidential security to do police work.
The African Transformation Movement party, which is in favour of Ramaphosa’s impeachment, criticised the ruling.
Embarrassing saga
The matter has been embarrassing for a leader who came to power promising to fight corruption and clean up the image of the former liberation movement.
The ANC won about 31 percent of the vote in this month’s local elections, its worst-ever such result, extending a decline that saw it lose its national parliamentary majority in 2024 for the first time since the end of apartheid and beginning of democracy.
The Constitutional Court revived impeachment proceedings against the president in May.
It found that a 2022 parliamentary vote to stop the process was invalid and parliament should set up an impeachment inquiry.
The Western Cape High Court in July temporarily halted the inquiry pending the outcome of Wednesday’s ruling.
Ramaphosa, 74, has been head of state since 2018, and his second presidential ‌term ‌is to end in 2029. The ANC is due to elect its next leader next year when Ramaphosa will step down after two five-year terms as party leader.

noticias.titulo: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, wrongfully deported from US, arrives in Spain
noticias.resumen: The Salvadoran national's lawyer said in a statement that it was 'a temporary departure'.
noticias.texto:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, wrongfully deported from US, arrives in Spain
The Salvadoran national’s lawyer said in a statement that it was ‘a temporary departure’.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia relieved to not be arrested after US court hearing
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador drew sharp criticism of United States President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has arrived in Spain.
Abrego Garcia did not speak to reporters as he arrived at Madrid’s main international airport on Wednesday, but raised a fist as he climbed into a van.
He voluntarily departed the US a day earlier after months of legal opposition to a second deportation, this time to one of various African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials. A judge had told him to self-deport by Tuesday, The Associated Press news agency reported, citing a source familiar with the matter.
In a post on X, the DHS said: “It’s not surprising this criminal illegal alien would choose to go to Spain, a country that earlier this year was invaded by tens of thousands of illegal aliens … Good riddance.”
Abrego Garcia’s lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, described the move as “a temporary departure”.
“Mr Abrego Garcia has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child. We don’t expect that to happen under this administration,” he said in a statement.
Sandoval-Moshenberg noted the US government had sought to deport Garcia “in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia”.
US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, the state where Abrego Garcia lived with his family for around a decade before being deported, said the Trump administration “was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will.”
The departure of Abrego Garcia, 31, brings an end to a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US Supreme Court.
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Abrego Garcia in Baltimore in March 2025. He was then transferred to a megaprison in El Salvador despite a prior court order barring him from being sent to the country because of the risk of persecution.
A US official later called the transfer an “administrative error”.
After the Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate Garcia’s return, prosecutors secured a criminal indictment charging him with human smuggling in a case stemming from an earlier incident. The Trump administration then brought him back to the US in June 2025. It later tried to deport him to Liberia after a US judge dismissed the human smuggling charge.

noticias.titulo: US Army detonates toxic lead explosives in Iowa amid health concerns
noticias.resumen: The US Army destroys nearly 4,500kg of lead azide amid fears of toxic fallout affecting residents, farms and livestock.
noticias.texto:
US Army detonates toxic lead explosives in Iowa amid health concerns
The US Army destroys nearly 4,500kg of lead azide amid fears of toxic fallout affecting residents, farms and livestock.
Five tonnes of explosives set to blow up in Iowa
A large stockpile of lead-rich explosives in the Midwestern state of Iowa has been destroyed in controlled detonations by the United States Army, ending a brief legal battle spurred by concerns that toxic dust from the fallout would endanger residents, livestock and farmland.
Video showed that the nearly 4,500kg (10,000lb) of lead azide – a highly volatile, lead-based explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I – was detonated in two successive open-air detonations on Wednesday at around 9am (15:00 GMT).
Environmental groups have raised concerns that the explosions would release particles that could eventually land on homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site, potentially travelling more than 160km (100 miles).
Before the detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, outgoing Republican Governor Kim Reynolds declared a disaster emergency across three counties in southeastern Iowa – Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren – activating state and county emergency response plans.
Shortly before the controlled detonations, Assistant Secretary of the Army Jordan Gillis appeared in a video on X, discussing the decision behind the detonation and explaining how the Army is attempting to mitigate the particles released. “The choice that we faced here was between a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation of dangerous material or a controlled detonation where we could choose the time and place to optimize the conditions to deliver the best result – not just for our operation but for the safety of the public,” Gillis said.
Revised wind projections released by the Army on Tuesday showed that airborne lead particles would shift southwest into northeast Missouri, prompting health officials there to advise residents 8km to 32km (5 to 20 miles) southwest of the plant to shelter indoors with windows and doors shut until an all-clear is issued.
A looming hazard for communities under strain
Amid a groundswell of concern over the prospect of toxic lead fallout, some residents have warned of the added burden the operation could place on communities already contending with chronic economic pressures, including a shortage of affordable housing, rising food costs and stretched local services.
The detonation’s impact will be felt across Des Moines County, which covers the city of Burlington and the rural community of Middletown, immediately adjacent to the ammunition plant.
Home to about 38,000 Iowans, the county had 38 percent of its households below the Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed (ALICE) threshold in 2024, according to the latest figures published by United for ALICE, a national research initiative.
“We shouldn’t have to experience an environmental disaster to become worthy of national attention or investment,” Megan Brincks, chairwoman of the Burlington Homelessness Task Force, told Al Jazeera.
Brincks, a Burlington resident who previously worked in the ammunition plant’s chemistry laboratory, stressed that the Army’s shelter-in-place orders cannot suspend the daily obligations of those whose work keeps the community running.
“Our food-insecure families will still need food tomorrow,” Brincks said, adding: “People experiencing homelessness will still need shelter. Individuals will still need transportation to medical appointments.”
“Unfortunately, the world doesn’t stop spinning because this is happening in our back yard.”
‘Land is their currency’
The blasts rocked one of southeastern Iowa’s most heavily cultivated stretches of land in a state that ranks second only to California in agricultural output value.
According to the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), Iowa is a leading producer of corn and soya beans and ranks first in the country in commercial red meat and egg production.
Across Des Moines County, about 648 farms span nearly 60,300 hectares (149,000 acres), including more than 49,775 hectares (123,000 acres) of cropland.
On Tuesday, Richard Fordyce, an undersecretary at the USDA, said the agency and the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship estimated that about 350 farms across Iowa and Missouri could lie within the projected plume area.
The prospect has stoked alarm over the risk of lead leaching into soil and groundwater, compromising crops and livestock and jeopardising the livelihoods of the farmers whose land underpins a vital part of the country’s food supply.
Will Sander, an associate professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said much of Iowa’s corn and soya bean harvest has already been completed, reducing the likelihood of acute exposure to this season’s crops.
Cattle producers, he said, should cover feed and water supplies where possible to limit animals’ ingestion of lead dust even if they cannot bring their herds under shelter.
“The acute exposure is the biggest risk in this situation, … that lead will not have dispersed and diluted into the environment,” Sander told Al Jazeera.
“For [these] farmers, land is their currency,” Eri Saikawa, a professor of environmental sciences at Emory University, said. “It is not acceptable that their livelihood is impacted this way. It also impacts all of us who rely on these farmers and their crops.”

noticias.titulo: Trump announces new trade tariffs: Which countries will they target?
noticias.resumen: The US is planning tariffs on 14 economies it accuses of using subsidies to help their industries overproduce.
noticias.texto:
Trump announces new trade tariffs: Which countries are affected?
The US is aiming tariffs at 14 economies it accuses of using subsidies to help their factories overproduce.
The Trump administration has announced plans to impose new trade tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods. China faces the highest rates.
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the duties on Wednesday following an eight-month investigation into what Washington calls “structural excess capacity”.
A senior US official told Reuters that USTR defines this as countries “promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles”, including through subsidies and other industrial policies.
The tariffs are the latest attempt to rebuild Trump’s sweeping import taxes that the US Supreme Court struck down in February.
Here is what we know so far.
What new tariffs are being announced?
The latest tariffs are being imposed under Section 301, part of a 1974 US trade law, which allows Washington to penalise countries it determines are treating US businesses unfairly. Trump used it to place large tariffs on Chinese goods during his first term, and those tariffs survived challenges in court.
The new tariffs are Trump’s latest attempt to bring back the “Liberation Day” tariffs he announced in April 2025 shortly after he began his second term in the White House. He imposed those under an emergency powers law but, in February this year, the Supreme Court ruled that the law did not allow him to impose trade tariffs.
“It’s supposed to be for international economic emergencies,” Dmitry Grozoubinski, a trade policy expert, said of the emergency law. “Tariffs are like taxes. You can’t really fight emergencies with mild taxes.”
The administration then used another law to put temporary 10 percent tariffs on trading partners in place, which ran out in July. It then replaced those with tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies, which together supply almost everything the US imports. This time it used Section 301, arguing that those countries do not do enough to keep out goods made with forced labour.
Grozoubinski said Section 301 was designed to allow a president to hit back quickly at one country over one industry, not to tax almost every import. “The legislation is supposed to be a scalpel, and they used it like a flamethrower,” he said. “It is not meant to set the US tariff code, which is what this effectively did.”
The recent investigation into the “structural excess capacity” of trading partners began in March and covered industries from steel and cars to computer chips and solar panels. It examined government subsidies, wages suppressed by the state and the operations of state-owned companies.
Washington argues that this support enables foreign factories to sell their goods more cheaply around the world, undercutting American manufacturers and discouraging investment in the US. The senior official told Reuters that the new duties would not be added on top of the forced labour tariffs.
Which countries have been targeted
The investigation covered 16 economies, and tariffs have been proposed for 14 of them: China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. For now, Mexico and Norway, which were also investigated, have been spared.
The Trump administration views China as the biggest offender, pointing to its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries. Beijing rejects the accusation and says its exports are simply competitive. Washington also accuses Chinese companies of investing in Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia to bypass earlier US tariffs.
For the other economies, Washington pointed to the large trade surpluses of Germany and Ireland as evidence against the EU. It also singled out the car industries of China and Japan, Singapore’s computer chips and Norway’s fuel and seafood exports for criticism.
What will the new tariff rates be?
The senior official cited by Reuters did not provide rates for most countries ahead of their publication in the Federal Register. However, China will face the highest charges. The official said its proposed 20 percent excess capacity tariff would come on top of the roughly 25 percent in tariffs set during Trump’s first term. That keeps China above Vietnam, which also faces a proposed rate of 20 percent.
The official said the new duties would not break the tariff limits in trade deals the Trump administration has negotiated. According to earlier Reuters reporting, those include caps of 15 percent for the EU, Japan and South Korea, and 19 percent for Malaysia.
For China, the limit is 20 percent on tariffs imposed during Trump’s second term, under a trade truce with Beijing that expires on January 10.
India has no signed trade deal with the US. The two sides agreed the outline of one in February, but it was never finalised, and talks have dragged on for months. On November 14, Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar said a deal could be sealed soon.
Why is Trump doing this now?
Grozoubinski said the timing is significant. The proposal comes just weeks after midterm elections in which Trump’s Republican Party suffered unprecedented electoral losses, in which the cost of living and trade tariffs were major issues. A Reuters/Ipsos poll after the vote indicated that 62 percent of respondents would support efforts to scrap trade tariffs.
“One interpretation is, like, OK, they’re going to chill out on these tariffs, because basically every time they say the word tariffs, people remember that their costs are really high and get angrier,” Grozoubinski said. “This shows that at least on some level, they are still prepared despite the headwinds, to go ahead and push that button.”
Hisham Wahby, an independent political analyst, said the key question after the vote was whether Trump would “double down or pull back”. Days after the midterms, Trump named his longtime adviser, the hardline anti-immigration activist Stephen Miller, as White House chief of staff. Wahby said that “was a clear indicator he is going to double down”.
US importers are currently challenging the forced labour tariffs at the US Court of International Trade, and Grozoubinski called the reasoning behind them “incredibly dubious”. Accusations about subsidies, he said, will be easier to defend.
“One theory is maybe they’re going to impose these little tariffs now, but if their big tariffs on everybody on forced labour get cancelled, they can fall back and say, we’ve already done the investigation,” he said. In that case, he added, the new tariffs would “replace the tariffs that replaced the tariffs that replaced the tariffs that replaced the Liberation Day tariffs”.
The announcement also comes weeks before the US-China trade truce, agreed between President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jingping last year, runs out, while trade talks with India remain unfinished.
Wahby said the decision is hard to explain in economic terms. “He lost the midterms because of the cost of living, because of the price of goods. Small businesses were suffering,” he said. “Households are suffering, small businesses are suffering, and you double down on it.”
Could the new tariffs be struck down?
Grozoubinski said the new tariffs will certainly be challenged in court. However, he said they were likely to stay in place while the cases went on, because lower court rulings are usually appealed and put on hold. The emergency tariffs, he noted, stayed in force for months after the trade court first ruled against them, until the Supreme Court struck them down.
He added that these latest tariffs stand a better chance of surviving than earlier ones, because foreign subsidies are a more believable complaint than forced labour.
“There’s probably something there,” he said. If the investigation genuinely found unfair practices, he said, the Supreme Court may decide that Trump is within his rights and that it is up to Congress to stop him.
“Of the tariffs he has imposed so far, these, at least from the outside and without having any of the details, are probably the most legally robust,” he said.
Will Trump’s tariffs restore manufacturing in the US?
The Trump administration argues that tariffs will push companies to build factories in the US to avoid paying import duties.
Grozoubinski said tariffs could help American companies that compete with imports, but will hurt those that rely on them. A US carmaker gains when foreign cars cost more, he said, but loses when the imported steel, engines and parts it needs also cost more.
The bigger problem, he said, is that nobody knows how long the tariffs will last. A new factory can take a decade or more to pay for itself, while Trump raises and lowers tariffs as negotiations shift. Congress could also limit his power to impose them, and a future president could scrap them altogether.
A company weighing a new US factory would worry about that, he said: “I can’t guarantee those tariffs will still be around for all the 10 years I need them.”
“If I wanted to use the US tariff code to encourage people to build factories in the US, I would not do it this way,” he said.
What is the likely fallout?
The most immediate cost is likely to fall on US companies and households that depend on imports. “If you make components from somewhere else more expensive, then, really simplistically, the people who buy them in your country lose out, and the people who make them in your country win,” Grozoubinski said.
Wahby said small businesses would be among the hardest hit. “How is that going to increase jobs if small businesses can’t manage to buy what they need from China?” he asked.
Markets were already uneasy, and US stocks came under pressure on Tuesday as reports of the plan emerged.
Abroad, the tariffs risk straining the US-China truce, which expires in January, and could complicate trade talks with India. They are also likely to anger US allies who already accuse Washington of breaching existing trade agreements. “This is not a free market economy when you’re putting tariffs on everybody,” Wahby said.
At home, the move sets up a clash with Democrats, who take control of both chambers of Congress in January. Wahby said they would push back, but their power is limited because Trump can veto legislation. “They will stand up to him, but we don’t know how effectively,” he said.
