noticias.titulo: US court convicts Huawei of theft: A history of Chinese firm’s global woes
noticias.resumen: Chinese tech giant has faced legal problems from Europe to Asia, and its products have been banned in trade war with US.
noticias.texto:
US court convicts Huawei of theft: A history of Chinese firm’s global woes
Chinese tech giant has also faced legal problems from Europe to Asia while its products have been banned during trade war with the US.
A United States jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei and three of its subsidiaries guilty of serious violations, including defrauding banks and conspiracy to steal trade secrets from US firms.
The verdict on Tuesday was handed down in a New York federal court and came after a lengthy trial of the Chinese electronics and tech giant.
Huawei faced multiple allegations, including accusations of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. But the company’s troubles extend as well to a number of other countries, including Canada and Australia.
“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft and deception,” said Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva of the Criminal Division of the US Department of Justice.
“Huawei’s crimes threatened the US financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market and undermined our national security.”
Here’s what we know:
What was Huawei convicted of?
Huawei was convicted on 10 of 11 counts along with its Chinese subsidiary Huawei Device Co Ltd and US subsidiaries Futurewei Technologies Inc and Huawei Device USA Inc.
The jury found them guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), substantive violations of IEEPA and money laundering conspiracy.
In a statement, the US Justice Department revealed specific instances of alleged misconduct.
A Huawei employee stole information about Tappy, a robot developed by T-Mobile, although both firms had signed a nondisclosure agreement, the department alleged.
In another instance, Huawei engineers were accused of copying the source code of Cisco routers.
Another employee allegedly disguised as someone else went to work for the US tech company CNEX even though the firm had earlier indicated it did not want to work directly with Huawei.
The convictions also related to allegations that Huawei operated in Iran and North Korea, countries under US sanctions, and made false statements to US officials and banks to hide that fact.
Huawei, however, was acquitted of the most serious charge: engaging in criminal racketeering conspiracy.
Criminal charges were first brought against the company in 2019. Its lawyers said investigators used isolated cases of wrongdoing by a few employees to paint a grand conspiracy.
Sentencing is set for September although Huawei’s lawyers said the company will appeal.
Huawei is expected to pay huge sums in penalties.
Is this part of the US-China tech tussle?
Yes. Washington and Beijing are in a race to command technological advancements, particularly artificial intelligence.
Beijing has condemned the verdict as an attempt by Washington aimed at “containing and suppressing” Chinese firms.
“The Chinese government firmly opposes movies by the US side aimed at containing and suppressing Chinese enterprises, and firmly supports Chinese enterprises’ lawful rights,” the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Wednesday.
The verdict was announced as the Nvidia scandal has been rocking Silicon Valley. Jensen Huang, the cofounder and CEO of the advanced chips company, is under US investigation for potentially leaking critical information to China after it was revealed a woman he had a romantic relationship with could have been a Chinese spy.
Beijing has denied involvement.
Nvidia’s chips power AI products, and Washington has restricted the company from selling its most advanced semiconductors to China. Nvidia is the world’s second most valuable company after only Apple with a market capitalisation of more than $4.4 trillion.
What issues does Huawei face elsewhere?
For years, the company has been blacklisted in the US, where it is restricted from selling equipment to telecommunications carriers without special approval because of security concerns.
Other US allies have flagged it over concerns that the company is too close to Chinese authorities:
- Australia and New Zealand – joined the US in banning the firm from supplying 5G equipment and services in 2018.
- Britain – banned telecom providers from buying new Huawei 5G equipment after 2020 and set a deadline of 2027 to remove all existing Huawei gear from networks.
- Canada – barred Huawei from supplying equipment for 4G and 5G networks in 2022. In 2018, Canadian authorities arrested Meng Wanzhou, the chief financial officer and daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei. She was extradited to the US, where she faced allegations of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran. Charges were later dropped, and Meng returned to China in a prisoner swap.
- Europe – In 2024, major German providers like Deutsche Telekom agreed to remove Chinese-made telecom equipment from 5G networks, including those from Huawei and ZTE, another Chinese manufacturer, before a 2029 deadline. Germany is also preparing sweeping bans on Chinese mobile network equipment that essentially could bar Huawei and ZTE. Other countries – including Estonia, Denmark, France, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Portugal, Romania and Sweden – have outright banned or restricted Huawei and other Chinese manufacturers.
- Japan, Taiwan and India – have also either completely excluded or restricted the company.

noticias.titulo: ‘Second home’: Why Israel is celebrating Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia
noticias.resumen: Israel's tech sector and economy have strong ties to chip giant Nvidia, which invests billions of dollars.
noticias.texto:
‘Second home’: Why Israel is celebrating Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia
Israel’s tech sector and economy have strong ties to chip giant Nvidia, which invests billions of dollars.
When Jensen Huang returned to lead the chip giant Nvidia this week after a scandal over his extramarital affairs, US President Donald Trump was not the only head of government to welcome his second coming.
Thousands of kilometres away, Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was celebrating too.
Huang once called Israel Nvidia’s “second home”, and Netanyahu reflected that feeling as he wrote on X: “Nvidia’s partnership with Israel’s tech sector has created enormous value for the company and for Israel’s innovation economy.”
“Continuity in Nvidia’s leadership is good news for that partnership and for the global AI industry,” Netanyahu added, referring to Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president on Monday.
Global headlines have focused on Huang’s affairs, including with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset; his resignation’s implications for the AI industry; and the larger technology race between Washington and Beijing. His reinstatement at the company he cofounded has gone a long way to settle market jitters. Nvidia’s share price rocketed up by 30 percent on Monday.
But Huang’s return has also calmed nerves in Israel – arguably the country most impacted by Nvidia’s performance outside the United States as it hosts the US-based company’s largest overseas operations.
Here’s what we know:
Why is Nvidia important for Israel?
California-based Nvidia, the world’s most valuable semiconductor company with a market capitalisation of about $4 trillion, holds the key to the modern artificial intelligence revolution. Huang’s company holds an extraordinary near-90 percent share of the global market for GPUs – graphics processing units, which are specialised AI processors used in AI data centres.
Nvidia’s operations in Israel are its largest in research and development outside the US. It has doubled employees there in the past three years to 6,000 people across seven research and development centres in Yokne’am, Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Ra’anana and Beersheba. It also has plans to build a major research and development campus in Kiryat Tivon near Haifa to accommodate up to 10,000 employees.
The Bank of Israel has estimated that Nvidia’s work in the country alone will add 2.2 percentage points of growth to Israel’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026, bringing it to 5.6 percent. Without Nvidia, that would be 3.4 percent growth, or 40 percent lower.
Next year, Nvidia is expected to add a further 2.4 percentage points to its GDP growth.
Nvidia paid about $1.29bn in taxes to Israel in its financial year that ended in January, according to its annual report. The company is projected to account for nearly 3 percent of Israel’s total state tax revenues in 2026, according to some estimates.
How did Israel react to Huang’s exit?
Huang’s resignation on November 12 initially rattled investors on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange (TASE) with the benchmark indices sliding after the announcement.
But by the end of the day, they had recovered. The TA-35 index finished 0.22 per cent higher at the close of the day while the broader TA-125 gained 0.07 per cent. The BlueTech Global Index, which tracks technology companies, fell 0.15 per cent.
The Haaretz newspaper reported, however, that officials at Israel’s Ministry of Finance were concerned about the potential consequences for the Israeli economy of turmoil – and particularly Huang’s exit – at Nvidia.
On Monday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog congratulated Huang on his return, noting “his deep appreciation to Huang for his continued support for Israel and for his commitment to strengthening the connection between Nvidia and Israel”.
Herzog’s office said Huang told the president that he was “moved by the message and that he intends to make the most of the second chance he has been given”.
How important is Israel for Nvidia?
Nvidia is helping fuel Israel’s economic machine during its genocidal war on Gaza, pogroms by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and the occupation of southern Lebanon.
But Israel is also returning strong numbers for the company.
The root of the tech giant’s relationship with the country can be traced back to Nvidia’s acquisition of Mellanox, an Israeli company that supplies computer networking products, in April 2020 for nearly $7bn. That acquisition was central to Nvidia’s success.
Nvidia was already able to make powerful engines that process AI workloads, but a single GPU cannot handle that workload and needs to exchange information with other GPUs.
Mellanox made the networking infrastructure that allows those engines to work together at a fast pace, creating the foundational structure of a data centre.
Nvidia’s networking business, built around Mellanox, generated more than $21bn in revenues in the third quarter of 2026. That’s about 18 percent of Nvidia’s total quarterly revenue.
At the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January, Huang spoke about Israel’s role in the development of key Nvidia chips.
“Nvidia’s BlueField-4 DPU and three networking components – the ConnectX-9 SuperNIC, NVLink 6 Switch and Spectrum-6 Ethernet Switch – all came out of Israel. So four out of six chips came out of Israel,” he said, praising the employees in Israel.
“Pretty amazing and maybe next time, six out of six chips,” Huang added.
What is Nvidia’s role in Gaza?
A review by the American Friends Service Committee, a group that won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947 partly for its work rescuing and providing relief to Jews during the Holocaust, has found that the Israeli military uses multiple Nvidia products.
Several purchases of Nvidia products were disclosed by the Israeli Ministry of Defence during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, a report by the group last year noted.
“They include products that are designed for AI applications, like Jetson cards and DGX,” it said, adding that since the public database only records unclassified contracts, “this likely represents only part of the full scale of the military’s usage of Nvidia products and services.”
Israel has made extensive use of AI systems in the Gaza war – including those known as The Gospel, Lavender and Where’s Daddy? – to track and target Palestinians at an unprecedented scale, the group said, adding that Nvidia “could therefore be potentially implicated in these war crimes”.
The Nvidia Jetson TX2 AI processor is also reportedly integrated into Elbit Systems’ Lanius drones, which Israel has used to kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

noticias.titulo: Solomon Islands signs security deal with Australia
noticias.resumen: Solomon Islands will have to consult Canberra before making new security or infrastructure deals under new pact.
noticias.texto:
Solomon Islands signs security deal with Australia
Solomon Islands will have to consult Canberra before making new security or infrastructure deals under new pact.
Solomon Islands and Australia have signed a sweeping treaty affirming that the small Pacific country will allow no foreign military bases on its territory.
The deal, signed on Wednesday, is seen as a blow to the regional ambitions of China, which had been moving closer to the Solomon Islands for years.
“Solomon Islands has been for a number of years a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region. Those days are gone,” Prime Minister Matthew Wale told journalists alongside his Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese.
The treaty establishes Australia as the island nation’s “primary security partner” and will see Canberra provide 740 million Australian dollars ($490m) over the next 10 years to fund free education and other programmes in Solomon Islands. Solomon Islands has a gross domestic product (GDP) of $1.75bn, according to the World Bank.
In exchange, Solomon Islands will allow no foreign military or security bases on its soil, and the country’s “sensitive” infrastructure will “remain free from militarisation, foreign interference and unauthorised access”.
That includes ports, airports, energy and telecommunications, as well as road and bridge construction – areas China has dominated in the islands through its Belt and Road Initiative. The deal will not apply retroactively.
Solomon Islands will also have to consult Australia before making deals involving its critical infrastructure or security cooperation unless it is with members of the Pacific Islands Forum regional bloc, Albanese said.
China relationship changing
Since being elected in May, Wale has upended Solomon Islands’ diplomatic moves towards China and realigned with Australia and the United States.
Asked about reports he had ended a secretive security pact with Beijing, Wale told journalists that discussions with China were “ongoing”.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not confirm whether the deal had been scrapped, but warned that the new agreement with Australia “should not target any third party”.
This is the latest in a string of similar deals Australia has struck with Pacific states, including Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and Fiji.

noticias.titulo: Trump to meet Abdul El-Sayed: Will he agree to a renamed Medicare-for-all?
noticias.resumen: Weeks after a bitter Senate race in Michigan, US president calls Democratic victor ‘a smart guy’.
noticias.texto:
Trump to meet Abdul El-Sayed: Will he agree to a renamed Medicare-for-all?
After offer to rename policy ‘TrumpCare’, US president calls Democratic victor ‘a smart guy’ weeks after a bitter Senate race in Michigan.
United States President Donald Trump says he will meet Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss the Democrat’s push for a single, low-cost government health insurance programme, which El-Sayed has suggested renaming “Trumpcare”.
One month ago, Trump was using anti-Muslim rhetoric against El-Sayed during his race against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan.
But on Tuesday, the US president appeared to have changed his tune. During a 45-minute interview in the Oval Office, he told the New York Post, “He’s a smart guy,” as he answered questions about El-Sayed’s offer to rename “Medicare for All” as “Trumpcare”.
“He did a good job. He actually did a very good job,” the president said.
“I know I’ll be meeting with him,” he added. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.” He did not give a date for the meeting.
Since the Republicans’ crushing defeat in the November 3 midterm elections, in which they lost their majorities in the US Senate and the House of Representatives, Trump has already indicated that he plans to make liberal use of his presidential veto to block “insane” Democratic policies.
However, he has also suggested that he may be open to negotiations, telling Fox News that he would “veto, veto, veto” but the Democrats would eventually call him hoping to do a deal.
“Congratulations to the Democrats. They did a good job,” Trump said. “I congratulate them and look forward to working with them for the good of our country.”
Here is what we know:
What has El-Sayed proposed, and how has Trump responded?
In the New York Post interview, Trump praised El-Sayed’s idea of putting his name on the healthcare programme as “very smart”. He also said he and Democrats could work together on healthcare but “Obamacare hasn’t worked”.
Obamacare was an overhaul of the individual health insurance market under former President Barack Obama that had slowed increases in insurance costs and halved the number of uninsured Americans.
Trump added: “I’m just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point, I think they’re going to want to negotiate.”
El-Sayed first floated the idea of renaming the proposed healthcare plan on November 6 in an interview with Zeteo editor-in-chief Mehdi Hasan. “If he wants to pass Trumpcare for all, I’m OK with it. He seems to like to put his name on things,” El-Sayed said.
On November 12, he posted a mock-up of a gold “TrumpCare” insurance card bearing the president’s signature on X. “Donald, this is on the table,” he wrote. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”
In a video posted on November 17, El-Sayed addressed the president as “habibi”, an Arabic term of affection. “Trumpcare for all. It’s really popular. People really want healthcare,” he said. “You can put your name all over it.”
The White House was initially dismissive. Spokesperson Allison Schuster called the proposal “Medicare for none” and described it as a socialist government takeover of healthcare.
But on Saturday, Trump reshared El-Sayed’s post on his Truth Social platform without comment. NBC News later reported that Vice President JD Vance’s office had contacted El-Sayed’s team to set up a meeting.
On the NBC TV network’s Meet the Press programme the next day, El-Sayed called the plan “the ultimate Trump card”. He said he did not care what it was called as long as universal healthcare coverage passed. In a post on Monday, he wrote: “The point of winning elections is to do something good with the seat.”
What did Trump previously say about El-Sayed?
The warmth displayed by the president is a reversal of his previous approach to El-Sayed.
During the election campaign, Trump repeatedly questioned El-Sayed’s loyalty to the US and tried to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood.
At an October 25 rally in Port Huron, Michigan, Trump said he was there “to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator”. There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the group, and he has denied any. Democrats denounced the attacks as targeting El-Sayed’s faith and his Egyptian heritage.
Vance told a rally in August that there was “something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil”.
El-Sayed, a physician and former head of Detroit’s Health Department, hit back throughout the campaign and at one point called Trump an “unserious fool”. He defeated Rogers to become the first Muslim member of the US Senate.
How is healthcare paid for in the US?
While most other wealthy countries have built universal health systems paid for from taxes, the US has relied largely on voluntary private insurance, leaving a substantial share of the population without coverage.
Despite decades of calls for national public insurance, it was not until 1965 that Washington created its two main public programmes: Medicare for people aged 65 and older, and Medicaid for people on low incomes.
Medicare, which also covers some younger people with disabilities, now serves nearly 70 million people.
Most Americans under 65 with health insurance rely on a patchwork of employer-provided insurance; private plans bought through the Obamacare, or Affordable Care Act, marketplaces; and Medicaid.
According to the US Census Bureau, 26.7 million people, or 7.9 percent of the population, were uninsured for all of 2025.
The Affordable Care Act, passed in 2010, made almost all lawfully present residents eligible for more affordable coverage than they had before. But taking it up remains largely voluntary, and millions still go without insurance, often citing cost as the barrier.
The US insurance model has proved expensive for the nation as a whole. The US spends more on healthcare than any other country in the world, and the gaps in coverage have deepened over five decades. In 1970, it spent about 7 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) on healthcare, roughly in line with comparably wealthy countries, which averaged about 5 percent. By 2024, the latest government data available, that figure had risen to 18 percent of GDP.
Per person, the US spent an average of $14,775 on healthcare in 2024, compared to an average of $7,860 in comparably wealthy countries, according to Peterson-KFF.
What is Medicare for All?
Medicare for All is a policy proposal that would extend government insurance to every resident, not just those over 65, with disabilities or with low incomes.
The main bill on the table is Senator Bernie Sanders’s Medicare for All Act. It would replace most private insurance with a single public plan with no premiums, deductibles or copayments.
Sanders has called on Democrats to start by reducing the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55.
Polling has traditionally been mixed but may now be rising. Pre-election polling by KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research organisation, suggested support for Medicare for All was 66 percent. Mollyann Brodie, who leads KFF’s polling, called it “the highest level of support … we’ve ever found”.
What does El-Sayed want?
El-Sayed wants one public plan to cover every American “from cradle to grave”. In a book he cowrote, he described this as “an enhanced version of the traditional Medicare program that tens of millions of seniors rely on today”.
Doctor visits, prescription drugs and emergency care would be covered, and patients could see any participating provider without out-of-network charges.
Coverage would also no longer depend on a job or family circumstances. “Turn 26, get a job, lose a job, get married, get divorced: None of these would cost you your health insurance under Medicare for All,” he said in testimony to the Senate in 2022.
Why are Democrats like El-Sayed making overtures to Trump?
It comes down to the presidential veto.
In the November 3 midterms, Democrats flipped nine Republican-held Senate seats and won a 56-44 majority, including two independents who caucus with them. They also won a majority in the House – raising the number of their seats from 214 to 258. When the new Congress meets in January, it will be able to pass legislation without having to find Republican votes in the House and, on some measures, in the Senate.
But Trump may veto any bill. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers: 67 senators and, with all seats filled, 290 House members. Democrats are 11 votes short in the Senate alone, so an override would need a significant number of Republicans to break with the president, which is unlikely to happen.
Trump has signalled he will use the veto freely. A day before the midterms, he pledged to become “Mr Veto” if Democrats took control of Congress.
The easier route then is for Trump not to veto legislation. That is the bet El-Sayed is making: that Trump, ever the politician, might sign a popular bill if he gets the credit for it.
Will Trump agree to Medicare for All?
Analysts doubt the talks will deliver the system El-Sayed wants, but they see room for a deal of some kind.
“I do not think it will lead to anything like the single payer system El-Sayed favours,” Ian Lesser, a senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, told Al Jazeera. “But as with Mayor [Zohran] Mamdani in New York, they may have a strangely positive relationship.”
In November last year, Trump heaped praise on then-mayor-elect Mamdani after the two held surprisingly cordial talks in the White House. That too was an about-turn from Trump, who, during the mayoral election campaign, had caricatured Mamdani as an anti-Semitic communist and threatened to strip him of his US citizenship while Mamdani called Trump a “despot” in his election victory speech.
Lesser said the El-Sayed exchange followed “very much the same pattern we saw with Mayor Mamdani: curiosity and the president’s focus on personalities above all”.
“The president could be inclined toward some new health reforms if he can put his own stamp on them,” Lesser added.
Why has Trump changed his tune?
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute at University College Dublin, said a meeting with El-Sayed would be part of an effort by Trump to salvage his legacy after the midterms defeat.
“He wants the good photo ops,” Lucas told Al Jazeera. “He’s going to have to try to do some photo ops that aren’t just simply his standard insult, trashing people, … because clearly voters rejected that type of politics earlier this month.”
Lucas said El-Sayed’s victory had also forced a rethink. “They threw everything at him – not just the state Republicans in Michigan but the national Republicans in the Trump camp – and he still won,” he said. “Trump or those around him have to realise that the proposal to do something about healthcare resonated with voters.”
Trump, 80, enters the last two years of his presidency after elections that are widely seen as a rebuke of his administration and Republican Party. His second term has been marked by an unpopular war with Iran, rising living costs and cuts to public health coverage.
“I think what has happened now with the midterms is that that was shown up abroad because they couldn’t win in Iran. They couldn’t win in Greenland. They did win in Venezuela. But he’s been shown up as a bit of a paper tiger beyond that, and now he’s being shown up as a bit of a paper tiger at home,” Lucas said.
A major healthcare law with his name on it could give Trump a signature domestic achievement.
However, his record points the other way. In 2018, he dismissed the idea as “Medicare for none”, and as recently as August, he said Medicare for All “doesn’t work”.
Lucas said he does not expect Trump to sign off on El-Sayed’s plan “at this point”. “Trump doesn’t understand the details,” he said. The real question, he said, was whether officials around the president and Republicans who will be in the minority from January would make it a priority.
For now, he said, the gesture “doesn’t cost Trump anything” because Medicare for All would first have to win over Democrats. The US healthcare system is “extremely complex, it’s extremely tangled” and replacing it with universal national health insurance is “not simple at all”.
Lucas said a better test of whether Trump is serious would be whether Republicans agree to restore the expired Affordable Care Act subsidies “before you get to Medicare for all”. Democrats, he said, should “hold their feet to the fire” on that.
The subsidies, introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic, provided lower health insurance costs for eligible individuals and families. Since they expired at the end of 2025, prices have returned to higher levels.
“If no Republican senators are speaking out for it, that tells you they’re just going to be hanging back,” he said. “It’s a show.”
But it is a show that also benefits El-Sayed, Lucas added. “The guy who was going to be the danger, the ‘extremist’, the ‘radical’, … the ‘jihadist’ is now having a meeting with the president.”

noticias.titulo: Trinity Rodman out of USWNT’s World Cup qualifier due to shoulder injury
noticias.resumen: Star forward Trinity Rodman sustained a minor shoulder injury during Washington Spirit's 2-1 loss to Kansas City.
noticias.texto:
Trinity Rodman out of USWNT’s World Cup qualifier due to shoulder injury
Star forward Trinity Rodman sustained a minor shoulder injury during Washington Spirit’s 2-1 loss to Kansas City.
Trinity Rodman has not been included in the United States women’s national team squad for a qualifying tournament for the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2027 because of a minor shoulder injury.
Rodman, 24, was injured on Saturday early in the Washington Spirit’s 2-1 loss to the Kansas City Current in the NWSL Championship Game — the Spirit’s third consecutive setback in the title match.
She was challenging for a ball when Current defender Laney Rouse collided with her midair and sent Rodman hard to the ground. Rodman left the playing field for several minutes and met with trainers before returning to the game.
Gotham FC midfielder Jaedyn Shaw has replaced Rodman on the 23-player roster for the CONCACAF W Championship tournament, which is a qualifier for the Women’s World Cup next summer in Brazil.
The USA squad opens the tournament on Friday against El Salvador in the quarterfinals in Mansfield, Texas. Eight teams are competing, with the four quarterfinal winners clinching the confederation’s four direct World Cup spots. Jamaica opens with Costa Rica, Canada plays Panama, and Mexico faces Haiti this weekend.
A victory for the Americans would send them to the semifinals on December 1, also at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium. The championship is slated for December 5 in Houston. The tournament also determines the region’s squads for the 2028 Olympics.
Rodman recorded 15 goals and 10 assists in a total of 33 games for the Spirit this season.
Shaw, who turned 22 on Friday, helped Gotham FC capture the NWSL Shield as the league’s regular-season champion. She scored 11 regular-season goals.

noticias.titulo: Bayern Munich’s Musiala checked for neurological symptoms in April 2025
noticias.resumen: Musiala was examined by the German club for neurological dysfunction after the initial onset of symptoms in 2025.
noticias.texto:
Bayern Munich’s Musiala checked for neurological symptoms in April 2025
Musiala was examined by the German club for neurological dysfunction after the initial onset of symptoms in 2025.
Bayern Munich midfielder Jamal Musiala was first examined for neurological symptoms in April 2025, more than 16 months before the official announcement of the diagnosis by the player, the club has said.
Bayern said they held talks with Musiala’s management team on Tuesday amid speculation about his contract situation following comments by senior club officials over his future and whether he could ever perform again at the highest level.
The comments from honorary president Uli Hoeness and board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, among others, were strongly criticised by the German players’ union.
Musiala, who signed a contract extension to 2030 in February 2025, was diagnosed with a neurological disorder in August after he collapsed in two games and had to be taken off.
“A constructive discussion took place yesterday, Tuesday, between FC Bayern Munich and Jamal Musiala’s management,” the club said in a statement.
“For both parties, the player’s health is the absolute priority. Jamal Musiala will receive full support throughout his recovery process.”
“In light of various rumours circulating over the past few days, FC Bayern and 11WINS — the agency representing Jamal — wish to clarify the following: Jamal Musiala was first examined for absence-like symptoms on April 22, 2025,” Bayern said.
“This examination took place in consultation with FC Bayern and the club’s medical department, immediately following the initial onset of these neurological symptoms.”
Musiala said in August that he had been diagnosed with “temporary, brief, but easily treatable absences caused by a neurological dysfunction”.
Musiala missed much of last season after breaking his leg during the 2025 Club World Cup. In September, he was sidelined with a hamstring injury, returning to action last week in a 1-1 draw with Cologne in the Bundesliga.

noticias.titulo: Catalan separatist Puigdemont to return to Spain on December 12
noticias.resumen: Former regional leader says he will unveil his proposal for a renewed Catalan independence push on December 17.
noticias.texto:
Catalan separatist Puigdemont to return to Spain on December 12
Former regional leader says he will unveil his proposal for a renewed Catalan independence push on December 17.
Catalan separatist and former regional leader Carles Puigdemont has said he will return to Spain on December 12, ending nearly a decade of self-imposed exile.
Speaking at a televised news conference from Brussels on Wednesday, Puigdemont said he would unveil his proposal for a renewed Catalan independence push on December 17.
Puigdemont’s return to Spain comes after the Supreme Court applied an amnesty law and shelved the criminal case against him.
“I left as president of the government of Catalonia, and I will return to the place where Catalan democracy elects or dismisses its presidents: the Parliament of Catalonia,” the former leader said.
He added: “I will do so on Saturday, 12 December, at midday, and that very night I will be able to sleep at home, with my family,” Puigdemont told the Brussels news conference.
In exile since 2017
Puigdemont fled to Belgium in October 2017 after organising an independence referendum that Spanish courts deemed illegal.
The vote triggered Spain’s worst political crisis in decades and deepened tensions between Madrid and Catalonia, a wealthy northeastern region with its own language, culture and a strong separatist movement.
Puigdemont briefly returned to Spain in August 2024, delivering a defiant speech in Catalan capital Barcelona, advocating for Catalonia’s right to self-determination before disappearing and prompting a police operation.
The amnesty, approved by parliament in 2024, was part of a deal between Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s Socialist Party and Catalan separatist groups, including Puigdemont’s Junts party, after an inconclusive election in 2023.
Spain’s conservative opposition unsuccessfully challenged the measure in the courts and parliament.
Puigdemont will return to Spain after this Sunday’s snap general election. Opinion polls suggest a potential coalition of the conservative People’s Party ‌and far-right Vox – both strong supporters of a unified Spain – winning an absolute majority of parliamentary seats.

noticias.titulo: Russian strikes on Ukraine kill five, cause power outages in five regions
noticias.resumen: A Ukrainian official says attacks on Zaporizhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions damaged a number of energy sites.
noticias.texto:
Russian strikes on Ukraine kill five, cause power outages in five regions
Ukrainian official says attacks on Zaporizhia, Dnipropetrovsk regions damaged a significant number of energy sites.
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least five people, wounded dozens of others and caused power outages in five regions, local authorities said.
Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said on Wednesday that the regions of Dnipropetrovsk, ‌Donetsk, Zaporizhia, Odesa and Kharkiv were affected.
He said the situation was difficult in Zaporizhia and Dnipropetrovsk, where the attacks damaged a significant number of energy facilities essential to electricity supply.
The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant lost external power after shelling and switched to diesel generators, he said, noting that it was the unit’s 17th ‌loss of external power this year.
“Repair and restoration work is ongoing in all affected regions. At the same time, repeated enemy attacks and constant air raid alerts are significantly complicating these operations and delaying the restoration of electricity supply,” the Ministry of Energy said in a statement relayed by the Interfax news agency.
The outages come after Russian strikes killed two people and injured three others, including a child, in Ukraine’s Black Sea region of Odesa, hitting cars and private and industrial buildings, Governor Oleh Kiper said on Telegram late on Tuesday.
In northern Ukraine, Russian forces struck enterprises in the Chernihiv region late on Tuesday, killing one person, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SES) reported late on Tuesday.
In eastern Ukraine, Russian forces shelled settlements in the Donetsk region seven times over the past day, killing one person in Kramatorsk, the head of Donetsk Regional Military Administration, Vadym Filashkin, said on Wednesday.
Russian forces also attacked Kharkiv city and six settlements in the region over the past day. One person was killed and 14 others were injured in the attacks, the head of Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, Oleh Syniehubov, said, according to Interfax.
Russian forces also attacked the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, with drones overnight, triggering a fire in a multistorey apartment building and injuring two people, the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said.
Meanwhile, in Russia, a Ukrainian drone attack killed one person and triggered power cuts in the Samara region, a major oil refining hub for the state oil company ‌‌Rosneft, Russian news agencies quoted Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev as saying on Wednesday.

noticias.titulo: Sudan’s RSF kills at least 19 in drone attacks on Blue Nile state
noticias.resumen: The attacks on Blue Nile state also wounded at least 20 people – in a drone war that is quickly escalating.
noticias.texto:
Sudan’s RSF kills at least 19 in drone attacks on Blue Nile state
The attacks on Blue Nile state also wounded at least 20 people – the latest casualties in a drone war that is quickly escalating.
At least 19 people have been killed in drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan’s Blue Nile state, according to a rights group.
A Sudanese military source told Al Jazeera that the RSF, which has been fighting Sudan’s army since 2023, targeted the city of Damazin in a series of attacks late on Tuesday that also wounded at least 20 people.
The attacks targeted multiple sites across Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile, and the neighbouring town of Roseires.
Three families were killed in the bombing of a residential area in Damazin, the military source said.
According to Emergency Lawyers, a rights group based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, drone attacks also targeted electricity facilities in Damazin and a big dam in Roseires.
Emergency Lawyers said six women were among the dead.
Sudan is currently in the grip of a large-scale civil war between the Khartoum-based Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF.
The southeastern Blue Nile state is strategically significant because it neighbours some of Sudan’s most unstable regions and is home to some of the SAF’s most experienced fighters, Al Jazeera’s Almigdad Alruhaid explained.
Reporting from Khartoum’s twin-city of Omdurman, Alruhaid said, “The attacks come amid a sharp escalation in the use of drone attacks between the RSF and the SAF in the last days.”
On November 22, drone attacks in Sudan’s capital area around Khartoum and Omdurman killed at least four people and damaged a United Nations building while staff were inside.
Between January and June this year, at least 1,390 civilians were killed in Sudan – 80 percent of them by drones. In the following four months, another 840 civilians were killed, including about 520 in drone attacks.
“Civilians right now are paying the price. There is no safe zone for civilians, whether in Damazin or in Khartoum,” Alruhaid said.
Three years of war
Civil war broke out in Sudan in mid-April 2023 after a power-sharing agreement between two rival camps fell apart following the protest-led ousting of then-President Omar al-Bashir in 2019.
Two rival military leaders emerged in al-Bashir’s wake: Sudan’s de facto ruler Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, who now heads the SAF, and his deputy-turned-rival Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, also known as “Hemedti”, who heads the RSF.
Each accuses the other of attacking first and starting the war that is now in its fourth year.
Reports say the war in Sudan has killed at least 59,000 people, displaced about 13 million and pushed parts of the country into famine.

noticias.titulo: Ex-England star Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving
noticias.resumen: Raheem Sterling admitted inhaling 'laughing ⁠gas' and driving erratically before ​crashing his car.
noticias.texto:
Ex-England star Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving
Raheem Sterling admitted inhaling ‘laughing gas’ and driving erratically before crashing his car.
Former England winger Raheem Sterling has been spared an immediate jail sentence after he admitted dangerous driving by inhaling “laughing gas” while behind the wheel before crashing his Lamborghini.
Sterling, 31, was reported driving erratically on the M25 and M3 motorways in southern England during the morning rush hour on May 28, with witnesses saying ‌he was inhaling from a balloon and weaving between lanes.
Police later found Sterling sitting in the passenger seat of his crashed car holding two canisters of nitrous oxide. No other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.
Sterling, who most recently played for Dutch side Feyenoord, pleaded guilty in September to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide and failing to provide a blood specimen.
He appeared for sentencing on Wednesday at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court, where Judge Kirsty Allman said Sterling had acted with “conscious disregard for the safety of other ‌road users”.
But, she added, Sterling had substantial personal mitigation, including his charitable work and his engagement with addiction services since the incident.
She sentenced Sterling to 12 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, and ‌ordered ‌him to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.
Sterling won 82 England caps, the last of which came at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.
The winger, currently without a club, made his senior debut at Liverpool before joining City in 2015, winning four Premier League titles.
He left for Chelsea in 2022 but subsequently fell out of favour and spent the 2024-25 season on loan at Arsenal.
Sterling joined Feyenoord on a short-term deal in February, playing eight times in the Eredivisie, but left at the end of the season.

noticias.titulo: Sinner uncertain for Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery
noticias.resumen: The five-time Grand Slam champion has not played a match since winning Wimbledon in July.
noticias.texto:
Sinner uncertain for Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery
The five-time Grand Slam champion has not played a match since winning Wimbledon in July.
Jannik Sinner risks missing the Australian Open in January after confirming that he has undergone surgery on his troublesome right knee.
The five-time Grand Slam champion has not played a match since winning Wimbledon for the second time in July, with less than two months until the start of the first major tournament of the season in Melbourne.
“Over the past few months, together with my team we’ve tried everything to treat my injury without surgery,” Sinner said in a statement on Tuesday.
“After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn’t respond as we had all hoped, that’s why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band.”
The procedure, which had been reported earlier in the day by broadcasters RAI and Sky Sport, and sports daily La Gazzetta dello Sport, was performed by knee injury specialist Lasse Lempainen at a clinic in Finland.
Another knee specialist, Fabrizio Terrone at the Isokinetic centre in Turin, told Sky Sport that Sinner’s absence could last “at least three to four months”.
That means the earliest Sinner might be back on court with a racket in hand would be during the American hard-court swing, at Indian Wells and Miami Masters.
The 25-year-old admitted recently that the worst injury of his career left him barely able to move.
“The worst part for me about this injury is that I cannot compete, I cannot play tennis,” said Sinner in a recent video.
“Also, my life outside of tennis is a bit more limited because of a simple fact that I cannot do things that I really like, because I want to protect my knee.”
Sinner, a two-time champion at the Australian Open which begins on January 17, recently said that he will make his comeback at the “Six Kings Slam” tournament in Saudi Arabia, which has been rescheduled for late December due to the conflict with Yemen’s Houthis.
But that now looks impossible and a difficult start to 2027 seems in store for the man who has in recent years risen to be, alongside Spanish star Carlos Alcaraz, the pre-eminent force in men’s tennis.
Sinner was having a brilliant campaign before being stopped by his knee problem, with five Masters 1000 titles going alongside his triumph at Wimbledon.
The Italian’s 94 percent winning record in 2026 is the best of his career, even beating his figures from the previous two seasons in each of which he won two Grand Slams and the ATP Finals.
He suffered a major disappointment at the French Open when, leading Argentina’s Juan Manuel Cerundolo by two sets and 5-1 ahead in the third, he succumbed to heatstroke and was eliminated in the second round.
Sinner recently lost top spot in the men’s world rankings to losing Wimbledon finalist Alexander Zverev, who has taken advantage of injury problems for both Sinner and Alcaraz to win Roland Garros and the US Open.

noticias.titulo: After Brexit, is Britain heading back to the EU?
noticias.resumen: A decade after the Brexit vote, a new deal brings Britain and the EU closer, with economic gains for both sides.
noticias.texto:
Counting the Cost
After Brexit, is Britain heading back to the EU?
Ten years after Britain voted to leave the European Union, London and Brussels have struck a deal to bring their economies closer.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Brexit “has not worked” and would like to see Britain rejoin in his lifetime.
But not in this parliament, and he is sticking to the Labour Party’s red lines on the single market, the customs union and free movement.
Critics say he has no mandate to reopen the debate. Burnham says it is up to voters.
United States President Donald Trump welcomed the Brexit vote. Now his tariffs are one reason Britain and the EU see more to gain together.
Published On 25 Nov 2026

noticias.titulo: Zidane was much better than me: Bellingham after Real Madrid wonder goal
noticias.resumen: Jude Bellingham admits he had 'no idea' what he'd done after scoring a goal that drew comparisons with Zinedine Zidane.
noticias.texto:
Zidane was much better than me: Bellingham after Real Madrid wonder goal
Jude Bellingham admits he had ‘no idea’ what he’d done after scoring a goal that drew comparisons with Zinadine Zidane.
Real Madrid star Jude Bellingham has brushed aside comparisons with football great Zinedine Zidane following his sensational goal against PSV in the Champions League.
The England international came on at half-time with Los Blancos trailing and inspired a sensational second-half display, including a magnificent effort from distance, at the Santiago Bernabeu on Tuesday.
Bellingham said he “did not know” how he scored his brilliant goal, flicking the ball up on the edge of the box and slicing a stunning effort inside the far post.
Having seen an acrobatic volley blocked minutes earlier, the England midfielder controlled Kylian Mbappe’s pass with two touches in the air and curled a superb shot into the far corner from well outside the area.
“I have no idea what I did,” Bellingham told RMTV. “I had the ball in a good position and thought about shooting.”
The 23-year-old, upon joining Real Madrid, took Zidane’s number five shirt in “homage” to the Frenchman, whom he admired, and some have compared his goal to a Zidane-style strike.
“I do things that you guys think are similar to Zidane, but he was much better than me,” Bellingham told reporters.
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho hailed Bellingham’s game-changing display as the midfielder gave Mourinho credit for helping him find arguably the best form he has enjoyed at Madrid in recent weeks, with Los Blancos winning a 10th straight match, but the coach said the midfielder only had himself to thank.
“I think the main figure responsible for what Jude is today is Jude, and his teammates. I try to help a little,” said the Portuguese coach.
“He’s an absolutely extraordinary player who has everything – he has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything and today, obviously not by himself, but he changed the direction of the match.”
“He’s an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world,” Mourinho said.
Madrid’s victory over the Dutch champions maintained their 100 percent start to the league phase, in which they are provisional leaders.
Mourinho reiterated his view that it was a “scandal” that Bellingham was not ranked in the top 10 players in the world at this year’s Ballon d’Or ceremony.
Mbappe netted twice to put Real out of sight before Vinicius Jr got in on the act with a late goal, having struck the post twice earlier in the game.

noticias.titulo: Israeli strike in Gaza kills senior Hamas official, his wife and children
noticias.resumen: Gaza's internal security director and his family are among seven Palestinians killed in one day by Israeli forces.
noticias.texto:
Israeli strike in Gaza kills senior Hamas official, his wife and children
Air strike hits their Gaza apartment amid escalated Israeli attacks, Gaza’s Interior Ministry says.
Israeli attacks on Gaza have killed at least seven Palestinians, including a senior security official, according to medical sources and local officials.
In a statement on Wednesday, Gaza’s Interior Ministry said Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf, director of the Internal Security Service in northern Gaza, was killed in an attack on Shati refugee camp. Al-Awf’s wife and two daughters, aged 13 and 15, were also killed, it added.
The ministry described the killings as a “horrific massacre perpetrated by the Israeli occupation forces when they bombed [the family’s] residence in the Shati refugee camp” in Gaza City.
The attack is part of “ongoing attempts to undermine the security apparatus in the Gaza Strip in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society”, it added.
A source at al-Shifa Hospital confirmed to Al Jazeera that four people from the same family were killed and several were wounded in an Israeli attack on an apartment in the refugee camp.
The attack came less than 24 hours after the killing of the Internal Security Service’s director general, Brigadier-General Naim Abu Nahal.
Other Israeli attacks
In another deadly incident, two Palestinians were killed in a drone attack on the al-Karama neighbourhood in Gaza City while a seventh Palestinian man was killed when an Israeli attack hit a tent sheltering displaced people in Jabalia al-Balad in northern Gaza.
Medical sources at the Nasser Medical Complex reported that a Palestinian girl was injured when she was shot by Israeli forces in areas outside their control in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip.
Near-daily Israeli violations of a “ceasefire” in Gaza have been recorded since it began in October 2025. Israeli air attacks regularly hit the enclave, and at least 1,680 people have been killed during the “ceasefire” and more than 6,000 injured as Israel’s genocidal war continues.
Hamas called on the guarantor states of the “ceasefire” to intervene immediately “to rein in the occupation, impose a halt to its crimes and obligate it to adhere to the agreement’s path”.

noticias.titulo: US Army detonates unstable lead-based explosives in Iowa
noticias.resumen: The US Army says a controlled blast is the safest way to deal with explosive chemicals that began crystallizing in storage. US President Donald Trump said "mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations."
noticias.texto:
US Army detonates unstable lead-based explosives in Iowa
November 25, 2026
The United States Army detonated nearly 5 tons of aging lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant on Wednesday, saying the explosive chemical has become too unstable to store.
The controlled blast occurred a little after 9 a.m. local time (1500 GMT) at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, and will destroy the country's entire stockpile of the chemical. Plumes of smoke were seen on camera in video footage after the controlled blast in Middletown.
The US Army has said residents of a small town and other nearby areas should leave "out of an abundance of caution."
"We don't believe that the public should be in a panic," said acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle. "Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling."
"Early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations," US President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
What do we know?
The material was moved to Iowa for storage from bases around the country in 2009.
But a March inspection found that it had partly crystallized, which makes it sensitive to friction and cold and could set off a spontaneous explosion.
"Inaction is no longer an option," said Major General Eric Shirley, who leads the operation.
Rob Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, told reporters: "It's not a matter of if, it's a matter of when, and that would not be a great place for us to be in."
Is it safe to detonate the chemical?
To limit toxic lead dust, the Army has built barriers around the bunkers holding the material and will use foam and water to trap particles.
Reuters reported that Army projections show dust could settle up to 40 miles (64 km) southwest, reaching northern Missouri.
Officials expect the wind to carry the plume away from Burlington, a city of nearly 25,000 people.
While residents within 5 miles (8 kilometers) were encouraged to evacuate, the Federal Emergency Management Agency has also advised people 5 to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed.
How have people reacted?
The date of the detonation changed three times after public backlash over its impact on the environment and public health. A federal appeals court cleared the plan on Monday after environmental groups sued.
Farmer Jill Holler, who organized a protest, told Reuters: "I'm not opposed if this is the only safe option."
"What I'm saying is that it's been so mishandled that people are confused and don't trust anything they're saying," she added.

noticias.titulo: EU must set out a new timeline for cage-free farming, court rules
noticias.resumen: European General Court ruled that the European Commission has failed to set out a timeline after pledging to end caged farming by the end of 2023.
noticias.texto:
EU must set out a new timeline for cage-free farming, court rules
November 25, 2026
A European Union (EU) court told the bloc on Wednesday to draw a new timeline for plans to ban cages for farm animals.
Judges at the European General Court ruled that the EU has failed to follow through on a pledge to ban the practice.
In 2021, the European Commission set out the goal to pass a legislation by the end of 2023 to stop farmers from cooping hens, rabbits, sows and other animals in cages. The move came after 1,4 million people signed a petition.
But it failed to follow up on the pledge. This resulted in the campaigners requesting a new timeline and eventually led to a court case when that was also not happening.
The Luxembourg-based General Court, the European Union's second-highest, on Wednesday ruled in favor of the animal rights campaigners.
"The Commission is under an obligation — which is not limited in time — to set out a timeline for all the measures which it intends to take in response to such an initiative," the court said.
According to the "European citizens' initiative" system, the Commission has to receive the petitions that gather over one million signatures across at least seven bloc countries. However, it is not obligated to meet the demands.
The court noted that if the Commission decides to take action, it has to keep the public and the European Parliament posted on a timeline in accordance with the principle of "good administration."
About 143 million chickens are kept in cages in EU
The Commission said it was analyzing the ruling before making a decision. It can still appeal the ruling.
It has previously stated an intention to put forward a proposal for the phased elimination of cage systems for chickens by the end of this year, as well as a separate proposal to transition from farrowing crates to pen-based systems for pigs by 2027.
According to the Albert Schweitzer Foundation, no timetable has been set for calves, rabbits, ducks, geese and quail.
In the EU, about 143 million egg-laying chickens are kept in cages while the majority of female pigs spend at least part of their lives caged.
The use of cage systems in agricultural production accredited as "organic" is already prohibited in the EU.

noticias.titulo: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
noticias.resumen: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?
noticias.texto:
Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
November 25, 2026
Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.
The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).
Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.
The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.
Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria
Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.
To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.
However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.
These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.
Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior
Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."
"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.
At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.
"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.
Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI
Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."
He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.
"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.
Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.
He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.
Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech
Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.
Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.
Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.
However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.
Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine: Poland to set up no-fly zone near Ukraine border, urges others to follow after Russian airspace incursions
noticias.resumen: Poland urged NATO allies to be vigilant at their borders after repeated Russian airspace incursions. Allies have also offered different opinions on Kyiv attacking Russian ships in Libya. Follow DW for the latest.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine: Poland to create no-fly zone near Ukraine border
Published November 25, 2026last updated November 25, 2026
What you need to know
- Poland hopes to establish a no-fly zone near its border with Ukraine by the end of the year
- Russia attacks have halted output at Ukrainian gas facilities as well as a thermal power plant
- Ukraine says it attacked Russian oil facilities in the Samara region
- France's foreign minister defended Ukraine's attacks on Russian shadow fleet ships off the Libyan coast, though Italy's called the attack 'a mistake'
- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned against ending Ukraine support, saying 'Russia wants more than Ukraine'
Keep reading for the latest news in Russia's war in Ukraine on Wednesday, November 25:
Poland to create no-fly zone at Ukraine border, urges others to do same
Poland's Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk told reporters that Warsaw will set up a no-fly zone inside its border with Ukraine and suggested other regional allies do the same in the wake of repeated Russian incursions into NATO airspace as part of Moscow's war of aggression.
"An ordinance is already being prepared by the government and should enter into force at the end of December or the beginning of January," said Tomczyk.
"We will also urge our allies — the entire NATO alliance — to establish such a principle along the eastern flank," he continued, "Poland was a pioneer in this regard, ‌and the Baltic states have since followed our lead."
Poland strictly limits air traffic at its border already.
On Wednesday, Tomczyk said the proposed no-fly zone will cover several dozen kilometers of territory from the border and provide added support for Poland's armed forces.
Merz defends Ukraine aid, says those opposed are lost or have other aims
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended his government's expenditures on Ukraine aid during a budget debate in the Bundestag on Wednesday.
Merz tackled criticism from opposition parties on the left and right head on, saying "Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine."
"Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea. Russia is escalating ‌in space. And Russia is now escalating massively here, in our own country, too, even at the risk of loss of life," he added.
Merz said, "anyone who doesn't see that, doesn't understand the world around them, or they are pursuing entirely different aims."
The Left Party and Alternative for Germany (AfD) have both called for an end to Ukraine aid and better relations with Moscow.
Among other things, Germany blames Russia for an explosive drone incident at Leipzig airport this summer as well as cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace incursions across the EU and NATO.
Merz said on Wednesday that by supporting Ukraine, Germany is protecting itself.
"We are learning from Ukraine," said Merz, "technologically for civilian use but of course also in defense technology."
Moscow, Kyiv exchange overnight attacks on energy infrastructure
Kyiv and Moscow both assessed damage to energy infrastructure on Wednesday morning as both sides continued to inflict damage on one another amid Russia's over four-and-a-half-year attempted invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Russia again focused its attacks on Ukraine's energy structure in an attempt to break the will of the country's civilian population as the bitter cold of winter sets in.
Moscow's troops attacked a thermal energy power plant, shutting it down; as well as targeting a gas production facility in Poltawa, where ensuing fires also shut down operations.
Ukraine's acting energy minister said that power outages were reported in five regions as a result of the Russian attacks.
In Russia's Samara region, Ukrainian drones hit at least two oil refineries, killing one person, sparking large fires and and causing energy blackouts.
France, Italy offer different takes on Ukraine's actions in Libya
Kyiv's attacks on Russian ships in and off the coast of Libya over the past couple of days have ruffled feathers among Ukraine's allies, with France and Italy, for instance, coming down on entirely different sides of the issue.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Kyiv was justified in its actions because it has an "absolute right to self-defense." Libya on Wednesday announced that two of its soldiers had died from injuries sustained during a weekend drone attack that sank a Russian warship.
Speaking with French broadcaster TF1, Barrot said, "For nearly five years now, [Russian President] Vladimir Putin has not only been bombing Ukraine, but has also been constantly engaging in acts of aggression and harassing Europeans in an attempt to undermine our unity."
Barrot said Russia alone is to blame for the war and its expansion, and then asked, "What would we do if we were being bombarded day and night by an enemy — an invader?"
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Wednesday criticized Kyiv's actions, saying, "It was a mistake to violate Libya's sovereignty" and warned against further similar activities in other regions.
Speaking with Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper ‌on Wednesday, Tajani said, "Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv's intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port."
Tajani said he had spoken with Ukraine Foreign Minister Andrii Sybihato and conveyed Italy's concern over the matter, adding that Rome would continue its staunch support for Ukraine and its sovereignty while at the same time seeking to keep the conflict from spreading.
Welcome to our coverage
As Russia's invasion of Ukraine creeps toward its fifth year, both sides continue to blast each other's infrastructure.
Overnight attacks targeted gas, oil and thermal energy facilities on both sides of the conflict's front lines.
While Moscow chided former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson's calls for a contingent of Western soldiers to be stationed in Ukraine, France's foreign minister defended Kyiv's recent attacks on Russian maritime vessels in far away Libya — something Italy's foreign minister criticized.
In Berlin, Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended German support for Ukraine as opposition parties with sympathies for Moscow complain it's too expensive.
Merz called out those wanting to curtail support as either "failing to grasp" the fact that "Russia wants more than Ukraine" or "pursuing entirely different aims with regard to our country's freedom, openness and liberalism."
Lastly, Poland's defense minister on Wednesday expressed astonishment over the fact that the US has not yet condemned or even reacted to repeated Russian drone and missile incursions into Polish airspace in recent days.
Stay tuned to DW for these stories and all the latest news on the conflict in Ukraine….

noticias.titulo: US plans new tariffs on EU, China and 12 others
noticias.resumen: The Trump administration is planning new import duties of up to 20% to counter excessive manufacturing abroad. The measures could put further pressure on US consumers already struggling with high living costs.
noticias.texto:
US plans new tariffs on EU, China and 12 other economies
Published November 25, 2026last updated November 25, 2026
The United States on Wednesday proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on imports from 14 economies, including the European Union and China.
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) unveiled the proposed duties after completing an eight-month investigation into alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners.
Washington accuses the targeted economies of promoting excessive industrial production, allowing cheaper goods to undercut American manufacturers.
The proposed tariffs largely stick to rates set under existing trade agreements, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Wednesday. However, he added that some rates could be "topped up" by a few percentage points.
The duties will be subject to a public comment period and a hearing before taking effect, possibly in January at the earliest.
Which countries would face new US tariffs?
China would face an additional tariff of 20%, the joint-highest rate among the targeted economies.
The proposed duties would respect the 15% tariff cap agreed with the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, as well as the 19% cap agreed with Malaysia, a senior US administration official said.
Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam would also be affected.
Mexico and Norway are currently excluded from the proposed measures. Greer said talks with Mexico were continuing as Washington's investigation into its trade practices remained ongoing.
In a separate announcement, the USTR also proposed higher tariffs on Brazilian raw and refined sugar and a new 10% duty on aircraft, which would affect Brazilian manufacturer Embraer.
How would the new US tariffs work?
The senior US official said the proposed duties would not exceed tariff limits negotiated under existing trade agreements.
However, the new tariffs on China would be added to duties of around 25% imposed during Trump's first term, bringing the combined rate for some Chinese goods to 45%.
Around $30 billion worth of Chinese imports that Washington is considering for tariff reductions would be exempt from the new measures.
The proposed duties would not be added to existing sector-specific tariffs on products such as automobiles, steel and aluminum.
Nor would they be combined with tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% imposed in July against 60 trading partners over alleged insufficient action against forced labor. Where both measures apply, the higher rate would prevail.
How have the EU and China responded to the US tariffs?
The European Union said on Wednesday it would examine the proposed US tariffs but rejected Washington's allegations of excessive industrial production.
"We strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity," the EU said, adding that it expected Washington to honor the trade agreement reached with Brussels last year.
Beijing also rejected Washington's allegations of excessive industrial production and reiterated its opposition to trade wars, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.
"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Washington has accused Beijing of flooding global markets with cheap exports, ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.
Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping last week in Shenzhen and is due to host him at the G20 summit in Miami in December.
An existing trade truce between Washington and Beijing is set to expire on January 10. Access to rare earth minerals and Chinese purchases of US agricultural products could feature in further negotiations.
Why is Trump introducing new tariffs?
The measures are intended in part to replace revenues lost after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping global tariffs in February.
The court ruled that Trump lacked the authority to impose the duties by declaring an economic emergency and bypassing Congress.
The new measures instead rely on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to investigate and retaliate against unfair or discriminatory foreign trade practices.
Trump has repeatedly promised that tariffs will bring manufacturing jobs back to the US and reduce the federal deficit.
Could Trump's new tariffs fuel US inflation?
The proposed duties could put further pressure on American businesses, which may pass additional costs on to consumers.
US consumer inflation reached 3.7% year-on-year in September, close to a three-year high. Earlier tariffs, the effects of Trump's war on Iran and a boom in artificial intelligence investment have contributed to rising prices.
High living costs were a key issue in November's midterm elections, which saw Trump's Republican Party lose control of both chambers of Congress.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the elections found that 62% of respondents supported efforts to repeal Trump's tariffs.

noticias.titulo: German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets
noticias.resumen: German businesses are optimistic about Africa, but Berlin's cautious approach to risk is holding them back from cashing in on the opportunities that their competitors from countries like the UAE and Turkey are seizing.
noticias.texto:
German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets
November 25, 2026
"Africa is a land of opportunity." "The German-African relationship is a win-win." "The continent is the market of the future."
That's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the sixth edition of the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana. While these descriptions aren't new, there's a palpable sense of urgency and seriousness this time.
German firms are increasingly viewing Africa as an attractive destination as they scramble to find new markets amid wars in Ukraine and Iran, high energy prices, punishing US tariffs and slowing growth in traditional markets like China.
"For a long time, many German companies had a secure source of revenue from the major export markets in North America and China, but the geopolitical ruptures of our time have undermined this certainty," German President Frank-Walter Steimeier said during the event.
"One could also say that it is time for new horizons, time to take a closer look at economic opportunities still waiting for us."
Why Africa matters?
Africa is home to some of the fastest growing economies in the world like Ethiopia and Rwanda. Even as European and other advanced economies contend with declining working-age populations, Africa is expected to add hundreds of millions of workers in the next decades, emerging as a key source of future labor.
Germany has already signed a migration pact with Kenya and is working on one with Ghana as it seeks to attract skilled workers to help ease acute labor shortages in certain sectors at home.
Even as Africa remains one of the poorest regions in the world, economic growth in parts of the continent has created a larger and more affluent consumer class over the past three decades. This group is aspirational and a growing source of demand for many of the goods that German firms want to sell, from cars to cosmetics.
The continent, with its mineral wealth and renewable energy potential, is central to European Union efforts to diversify its sources of critical raw materials and reduce reliance on China-dominated supply chains.
It is also playing an increasingly important role in strengthening the EU's energy security after the bloc phased out most energy imports from Russia.
German firms have committed to invest billions of euros in green hydrogen projects in countries such as Mauritania and Namibia.
"We don't have the capital to develop them [natural resources]. So foreign investors are coming to help us develop those resources.
