Whilst we are getting jobs and industrialization is taking place, they are also making profits," said Amin Amidu Sulemani, energy and infrastructure commissioner at the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).
"It's not a relationship where we send raw materials outside of Africa every time, when we can actually process them here," he told DW.
What is wrong with Germany's Africa strategy?
Despite Africa's growing economic appeal, many obstacles to investment remain, including corruption and governance concerns, unreliable energy supplies, foreign exchange risk and poor infrastructure.
African leaders say they are working to address these challenges and improve the ease of doing business.
Yet while German companies have largely remained on the sidelines, competitors from countries such as the UAE, Turkey and India have made significant inroads across the continent.
German firms enjoy a strong reputation in Africa because of their engineering expertise, vocational training programs and long-term industrial investments, which are more likely to create stable jobs than investments in extractive industries.
However, they have struggled to translate that goodwill into a larger commercial presence. Africa, for instance, accounts for less than 2% of the total foreign investment made by German firms over the past several decades.
Business leaders complain that German firms lack adequate financing and risk protection for projects in Africa. They also criticize excessive bureaucracy and the absence of a coherent German strategy, with engagement fragmented across ministries and agencies.
Industry bodies say German institutions and firms often perceive risks too broadly, treating diverse African markets as if they pose the same level of risk.
"German companies can be a bit more bold and maybe also innovative in the way they approach the continent," Khadi Camara, deputy CEO of the German-African Business Association, told DW. "We see that in the companies that are successful, they don't do business as usual. Every country has its nuances that companies keep in mind and say, okay, this model works here, that model works there."
The 2026 World Investment Report by UN trade body UNCTAD showed that investors from the Gulf and Asia are becoming important sources of investment in Africa, especially in energy, logistics, real estate and infrastructure.
The UAE has been a major investor in greenfield megaprojects in recent years, including the $34 billion (€31 billion) Infinity Power renewable energy project in Mauritania, the $24 billion Ras El Hikma real estate development project in Egypt and the $6 billion H2 Global Energy hydrogen project in Tunisia.
How can German firms seize the African opportunity?
Business leaders are calling for better financing and guarantees and more risk-sharing and easing of bureaucratic hurdles.
Meanwhile, others, including the German president, are urging German businesses to take on more risk and seize opportunities in Africa. Otherwise, they risk being edged out by foreign rivals.
"Be curious, take risks and invest in our common future," Steinmeier said.

noticias.titulo: EU plans €50 billion sovereign tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
noticias.resumen: The European Commission proposed a tech fund with a target size of €50 billion to boost quantum computing efforts. The bloc aims to keep up with the US and China in the global race.
noticias.texto:
EU plans €50 billion tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
November 25, 2026
The European Commission proposed a €50 billion ($54.73 billion) equity financing fund on Wednesday to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe.
The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete in a race against the United States and China.
"Quantum technologies will shape the future ‌of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a ‌profound impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now €50 billion," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point."
Virkkunen introduced the officially named "Sovereign Tech Equity Fund" while presenting new rules to support Europe's quantum technology sector.
The new rules will push public authorities to favor European companies when giving public contracts and funding.
The European Union (EU) also wants to reduce its dependence on third countries amid concerns that US companies could use so-called "kill switches” to disable their products in Europe.
Why is quantum computing important?
Quantum computing technology is still at the early stages of development, with both the US and China competing to achieve dominance in the field.
While classical computers process data using bits — which are either 0 or 1 — quantum computers use qubits (quantum bits), which can exist in a blend of both states at once.
By using qubits, these machines could eventually solve complex problems much faster than today's supercomputers.
The EU expects the quantum computing to lead to breakthroughs in several areas, including drug development, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries and even AI development.
Although quantum technology offers significant potential, it also poses cybersecurity risks, as it could undermine encryption and other safeguards for digital data at a time when governments are battling AI-driven cyberattacks.
Europe is home to one-third of the world's quantum companies
Around one-third of the world's quantum companies are based in the European Union, according to the Commission. Last year, public funding for quantum technologies reached €8.6 billion in the bloc, compared with €5.3 billion in the United States and €13.6 billion in China.
However, European quantum start-ups have attracted €1.1 billion in private funding so far, compared with €7 billion in the United States.
The EU launched its "quantum Europe" strategy in July 2025, aiming to be a global leader in quantum technologies by 2030.
The bloc is already a global leader in quantum research but it falls short when it comes to transforming this into viable commercial opportunities.
The draft legislation must be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament in the upcoming months before it can be law.

noticias.titulo: Ice hockey prospect Max Calce follows Leon Draisaitl's path, leaving Mannheim for Canada
noticias.resumen: The player widely seen as Germany's biggest ice hockey talent to come along in years is leaving the country's top professional league for Canada – changing tracks in his bid to make it to the NHL.
noticias.texto:
German ice hockey prospect Max Calce leaves Mannheim for Canada
November 25, 2026
Max Calce made the surprise announcement that he would be moving to the Brantford Bulldogs of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) in a statement issued on the website of his German Ice Hockey League (DEL) team, Adler Mannheim late on Tuesday.
"I have long had three goals," he said. "To play for the Adler, in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL), and in the NHL. Today is a difficult and emotional day for me, as I say goodbye to my home."
Having started the season in Mannheim, many thought the 17-year-old would finish the season in the DEL.
The announcement came after Calce, who had been a regular in Mannheim's lineup this season, had been left off the team sheet for Tuesday night's game in Straubing.
This comes less than a month after he became the youngest-ever player to score a goal for the German men's national team – against Slovakia in Germany's final game of the annual Deutschland Cup invitational.
Mature decision-making on the ice
"It was only a matter of time; he's an incredible player," said former NHL player Tobias Rieder, who frequently played on a line with Calce during the tournament.
"The most impressive thing is that, at 17, he plays a very mature style of hockey—he almost always makes the right decision."
Calce is also the youngest goal scorer in DEL history, having found the net for Mannheim in September 2025 at just 16 years and 100 days old.
In his statement, the centerman thanked Mannheim, which has produced a number of NHL players over the years, including Leon Draisaitl, Moritz Seider and Tim Stützle.
"The trust, support, and experiences I gained through my coaches, teammates, and everyone within the organization have played a major role in my development—both as a player and as a person."
This season, his second in the DEL, Calce has six goals and two assists in Mannheim's first 19 games.
"We believe in preparing young players to take opportunities at the highest level of the sport," Dallas Eakins, Mannheim's head coach and sporting director said.
"As much as we would have loved to continue to have him play for us, we respect and welcome his ambition."
Increased visibility ahead of NHL draft
On the surface, the notion of moving from a men's professional league to a junior league may seem like a step backwards, but Calce's move to the OHL will give Calce increased exposure to NHL scouts. The OHL is one of the top three junior leagues in Canada and according to figures released by the CHL last season, they produce more NHL players than any other developmental system.
In doing so, Calce is now following the path of Edmonton Oilers superstar Draisaitl, who left Mannheim's youth program at the age of 16 to pursue his NHL dream, joining the Western Hockey League's Prince Albert Raiders.
This, of course is not the only path to the NHL; Moritz Seider of the Detroit Red Wings and the Ottawa Senators' Tim Stützle were both first-round draft choices plucked directly from Mannheim. Calce is hoping to be taken in the first round of next summer's NHL Entry Draft.
Born to Russian parents in Mannheim, Calce changed his birth surname, Penkin, to that of his mother and stepfather last summer.

noticias.titulo: Why Indian nationals are still ending up in Russia's war on Ukraine
noticias.resumen: Whether through deception or desperation, Indians continue to be drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine. What can New Delhi do to protect its citizens from ending up fighting in Ukraine?
noticias.texto:
Why Indian nationals are still ending up in Russia's war on Ukraine
November 25, 2026
Gurpreet Singh Randhawa, a 40-year-old from Jalandhar in India's northern Punjab state, said he traveled to Russia for work after responding to a Facebook advertisement for a driving job at a garment factory.
But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces.
After escaping from his unit, he surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November. He is now being held as a prisoner of war.
In an interview with Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin, Randhawa described how, after arriving in Russia, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract and sent for training. He said they confiscated his passport and phone. His account has not been independently verified.
Randhawa's story is a familiar one in India.
He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military. Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces in October 2025. He had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release.
India's efforts to bring recruits home
The cases underline how little has changed since Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow in July 2024.
At the time, Putin assured him that Indians who were misled into joining the Russian army would be discharged. But the recruitment of Indians has continued.
In an October filing before the Supreme Court, India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said approximately 267 Indians have joined the Russian armed forces since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Of these, 139 were discharged and 51 were killed. The whereabouts of the 77 others were unknown. Russian authorities have confirmed that seven of them are missing.
The problem extends beyond Indians who travel to Russia seeking civilian employment, only to find themselves exposed to recruitment networks and the dangers of a war zone.
The MEA has also highlighted cases of Indians knowingly enlisting in the Russian military for the supposed financial benefits on offer, believing they could later secure release through government intervention.
Some had also approached Indian authorities to renounce their citizenship and obtain Russian passports. "This is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government," the ministry said.
Duped or desperate?
Former diplomat Anil Trigunayat said the growing movement of Indian workers to Russia presents both economic opportunities and new challenges for their protection.
"Inadequate oversight of recruitment networks could leave vulnerable workers exposed to exploitation," Trigunayat told DW.
He said Indian workers were often burdened by substantial recruitment fees and continued deductions from their salaries by intermediaries.
"Some of them had paid between 300,000 to 500,000 Indian rupees [$5,400 /€4,900] to Indian recruitment agents, and even while working in Russia, more than 30% of their agreed monthly salary was taken away by local and foreign agents," Trigunayat said.
The former diplomat added that some Indians who had overstayed their visas in Russia were particularly vulnerable. Military service was allegedly offered to earn substantial wages and regularize their immigration status.
Mohammad Sufiyan, from Hyderabad in the southern state of Telangana, said he was lured to Russia under false pretences and forced into active combat in Ukraine.
He had traveled abroad in search of employment and a better livelihood, but ended up in a war zone. He has since returned home to India.
"Many people are duped. Some decide it is better to seek citizenship than come back to India. It's a tough life, and people will go to any lengths to get some sort of employment," Sufiyan told DW.
Sufiyan's experience points to the economic desperation that makes such offers attractive, even when they carry the risk of being caught up in a war.
Rajan Kumar, a professor at the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of International Studies, said some Indians who traveled to Russia for work could find themselves caught up in the fighting without having joined the military.
"Some of them, they don't join the army, but they end up in the army region. They're caught in the crossfire," Kumar told DW.
He said India was negotiating with Moscow to secure the return of its citizens caught up in such situations. "Russia is very cooperative so far," he said.
Moscow prioritizes military aims over strategic diplomacy
India has been pressing Russia to take action, but the issue persists.
The recruitment efforts reflect Russia's need for more manpower for its nearly five-year war in Ukraine , and the limited influence New Delhi can exert over Moscow, despite the close political relationship between the two countries.
Mohsin Raza Khan, a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, told DW that Putin's need to sustain the war effort was taking precedence over the concerns of a strategic partner.
He points out that the Russian president was reluctant to impose another mobilization on his own population for fear of domestic unrest.
"In these circumstances, sustaining the war effort appears to take precedence over concerns raised by India. Neither Modi nor New Delhi has sufficient leverage to change that," said Khan.
Khan also said the willingness of some Indians to enlist, and even consider giving up their citizenship, is down to the lack of decent employment opportunities at home.
"For young, educated men without contacts or connections, the chances of respectable employment are so low that the risks of a high casualty war are preferable," he said.

noticias.titulo: In Afghanistan, no female doctor often means no treatment for women
noticias.resumen: Millions of women in Afghanistan, particularly pregnant women, are suffering under Taliban restrictions and are increasingly losing access to life-saving medical care.
noticias.texto:
In Afghanistan, no female doctor often means no treatment for women
November 25, 2026
In many parts of Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, male doctors are no longer allowed to treat women. The consequences have been highlighted in a recent United Nations report, which offers disturbing insight into the harsh reality many women face.
In one case, a woman from Kunar province described how she suffered several miscarriages without being able to access medical care.
Her case highlights the increasing number of pregnant women who urgently need medical assistance and are unable to receive it because of restrictions imposed by the Taliban.
And overall, women in Afghanistan are increasingly losing access to essential healthcare. This is due both to the Taliban's restrictions and to cuts in international aid funding.
Taliban remove women from public life in Afghanistan
"If a pregnant woman dies because male doctors are not allowed to treat her, her husband can marry another, younger woman. That is how the Taliban think," said 28-year-old Tamana Zaryab Paryani.
Paryani is an Afghan women's rights activist and one of the best-known voices of resistance against the Taliban.
A trained lawyer, she worked as a newspaper journalist before the Taliban returned to power. Following their takeover in August 2021, she took part in protests against restrictions on the rights of women and girls. In January 2022, she was detained by the Taliban in Kabul alongside her sisters. After her release, she managed to reach Europe.
Since then, she has continued to advocate internationally for the rights of Afghan women. At the end of October, she addressed the UN Security Council, describing the repression of women in Afghanistan and urging the international community not to normalise their systematic disenfranchisement.
"This is gender apartheid. We expect the international community to recognise it and stand with the women of Afghanistan," Paryani told DW.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees severely restricting the lives of women and girls. Girls are barred from secondary education, while women are denied access to universities. Women's opportunities to work outside the home are also severely restricted.
The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), which monitors and regularly documents the human rights situation in the country, reported in September 2025 that inspectors from the Taliban's Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice were further restricting women's access to healthcare through the enforcement of regulations and decrees.
According to the UN, around 2.6 million girls are excluded from secondary education. This is likely to lead to more girls being married off at an early age and to an increase in maternal mortality, UN Women warns.
Afghanistan has a population of around 45 million. With a median age of approximately 17, it has one of the youngest populations in the world. Around 42% of its population is under the age of 15.
The world's 'worst women's rights crisis'
"What is happening in Afghanistan goes beyond gender-based persecution, as already defined under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court," Haroon Mutasem, professor of International Criminal Law at the American University of Afghanistan and research fellow at Berlin's Humboldt University, told DW.
The Afghan legal scholar examines how the systematic oppression of women in Afghanistan can be classified and prosecuted under international law.
"This is not just about individual acts of persecution, but about an institutionalised system of oppression and domination of one gender group by another. They have established a system that considers women as secondary and defines a life for them as raising kids, working at home, and also actually satisfying the sexual desires of their men."
Mutasem argues that failure to respond to the systematic oppression of Afghan women could undermine the universal validity of human and women's rights. He warns that other authoritarian regimes and extremist movements could adopt similar practices.
According to UN estimates, in 2027 more than 4 million children under the age of five, as well as around 1.27 million pregnant and breastfeeding women, will require treatment for acute malnutrition.
Susan Ferguson, the UN's Special Representative in Afghanistan, described the situation in her latest report as "the world's worst women's rights crisis." Afghan women, she said, are now "fighting for their very survival."
Cuts in aid funding have forced humanitarian organisations to make "impossible decisions about which women and girls can receive support and which have to be turned away," Ferguson said.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Spain: Catalan separatist Puigdemont sets date for return
noticias.resumen: Former Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont plans to return to Barcelona on December 12 after nearly a decade in exile. Spain's Supreme Court has dropped the criminal case against him, clearing the way for his return.
noticias.texto:
Spain: Catalan separatist Puigdemont sets date for return
November 25, 2026
Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont said he would return to Spain on December 12, nearly a decade after fleeing the country following a failed independence bid.
The announcement comes just days after Spain's Supreme Court closed criminal proceedings against him under a controversial amnesty law, removing the last legal obstacle to his return.
Speaking at a televised news conference in Brussels, Puigdemont said he would return to the Catalan parliament in Barcelona.
"I left as President of the Government of Catalonia, and I will return to the place where Catalan democracy elects or dismisses its presidents: the Parliament of Catalonia. I will do so on Saturday, 12 December, at midday, and that very night I will be able to sleep at home, with my family," he said.
Puigdemont also announced plans to present a proposal for a renewed push for independence of Catalonia on December 17.
Who is Carles Puigdemont?
Puigdemont is a former president of Catalonia, a wealthy region in northeastern Spain with its own language, culture and a strong independence movement.
He led Catalonia's regional government in October 2017 when it organized a referendum on independence from Spain that Spanish courts had declared illegal.
The vote and the subsequent failed attempt to break away from Spain triggered the country's worst political crisis in decades, deepening tensions between the central government in Madrid and Catalan separatists.
Puigdemont fled to Belgium that same month to avoid arrest and has lived in self-imposed exile ever since.
His "Junts per Catalunya" party remains an important force in Spanish politics and played a key role in securing the parliamentary support needed for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to remain in power in 2023.
Why has Puigdemont now been cleared to return to Spain?
Spain's Supreme Court on Monday shelved the criminal case against Puigdemont after applying an amnesty law passed by parliament in 2024.
In a ruling dated November 20, the court determined that the amnesty had extinguished any potential criminal liability for Puigdemont and two other separatist figures.
The decision followed a Constitutional Court ruling in October that extended the amnesty to cover embezzlement allegations linked to Catalonia's independence bid.
The Supreme Court had initially ruled that the law did not apply to those investigated for embezzlement, including Puigdemont.
Following the Constitutional Court's intervention, the Supreme Court lifted the arrest warrant against him. Monday's decision to close the criminal proceedings completed the legal process, allowing him to return without facing detention over the 2017 case.
Why is Spain's Catalan amnesty law controversial?
The amnesty was a key concession by Sanchez to Catalan separatist parties, including Puigdemont's Junts, in exchange for their support following Spain's inconclusive 2023 general election.
The agreement allowed Sanchez to secure another term as prime minister but sparked strong opposition from conservative parties and critics who accused him of putting his political survival ahead of Spain's interests.
The conservative Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox opposed the legislation and unsuccessfully challenged it in parliament and the courts.
The controversy intensified after Puigdemont said in a recent interview with Spanish newspaper El Mundo that his party had exploited Sanchez's ambition to secure concessions for Catalonia.
"We had to test how far we could go," Puigdemont said, calling Sanchez "an amoral person with an excessive thirst for power".
"We have exploited this excessive ambition for power to inflict certain defeats on Spain that we would otherwise not have been able to bring about."
His remarks became a flashpoint in the campaign ahead of Spain's snap general election on November 29.
Polls suggest the Popular Party is likely to win the most seats but fall short of an outright majority, potentially leaving it dependent on Vox to form a government.

noticias.titulo: North Korea expels Swiss envoy over sanctions on camp accused of indoctrinating Ukrainian children
noticias.resumen: North Korea has ordered Switzerland to close its newly reopened diplomatic office. The dispute centers on Swiss sanctions against a camp accused of indoctrinating Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territories.
noticias.texto:
North Korea expels Swiss diplomat over Ukraine sanctions
November 25, 2026
North Korea has declared Switzerland's top diplomatic representative in Pyongyang persona non grata and ordered him to leave the country within 48 hours, state media reported on Wednesday.
The North Korean Foreign Ministry also called for the closure of Switzerland's diplomatic office in the capital, less than a month after it reopened following a lengthy shutdown during the COVID-19 pandemic.
According to the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), Pak Hyon Su, director general of the ministry's European Department, summoned Swiss diplomat Sylvain Astier and handed him a memorandum demanding the office's closure.
Pyongyang said the decision was in response to Switzerland's sanctions against a North Korean children's camp, describing the move as an openly hostile act.
"Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us," KCNA reported, using the acronym for North Korea's official name.
Why did Switzerland impose sanctions on North Korea?
Switzerland placed the Songdowon International Children's Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan under sanctions on November 4.
Swiss authorities accused the camp, which also hosts Chinese and Russian students, of participating in the "transfer of Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine" to North Korea.
They also said the facility contributed to "efforts aimed at the ideological conditioning and russification of Ukrainian children".
On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned the sanctions arguing that the measures violated North Korea's sovereignty by interfering with its responsibility to provide children with cultural and recreational opportunities.
How has Switzerland responded to North Korea's decision?
Switzerland's Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday that reopening its diplomatic office was independent of its sanctions policy.
"The reopening of the Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang is in line with our universalist foreign policy. Its aim is to maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues," the ministry said.
It stressed that this approach applied regardless of Switzerland's participation in UN sanctions over North Korea's nuclear program or EU sanctions related to Russia's war against Ukraine.
Swiss authorities were not immediately available for further comment on Wednesday.
Switzerland has maintained diplomatic relations with North Korea since 1974 and has long served as an intermediary between Pyongyang and Western countries.
Its office in the North Korean capital closed during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis formally reopened it during a visit in October, when he discussed normalizing relations.
It was the first visit by a Swiss government minister to North Korea since 2003.
The office operates under the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, which handles diplomatic and consular relations with North Korea. Pyongyang also maintains an embassy in Bern.
Only a few European countries have diplomatic missions in North Korea, including Sweden, Poland and the Czech Republic.
What does North Korea's move mean for relations with the West?
Experts say the expulsion is intended as a warning to other Western countries, including the United States, which has been seeking to reestablish contact with Pyongyang.
"North Korea is using Switzerland as a test case to show that sanctions and dialogue are incompatible," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, told news agency Reuters.
Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told agency AFP that Pyongyang, backed by its allies China and Russia, wanted to make an example of Switzerland.
Earlier this week, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un personally received credentials from the new ambassadors of 10 countries, including Russia and Sweden, in a rare diplomatic ceremony.
Kim said Pyongyang was seeking to expand relations with countries that respected its sovereignty but would oppose attempts to restrict the rights and development of sovereign states.

noticias.titulo: Australia, Solomon Islands sign sweeping pact seen as countering China
noticias.resumen: Australia will become the Solomon Islands' primary security partner, while the archipelago will reject any foreign power trying to "interfere" on its "sensitive" infrastructure.
noticias.texto:
Australia and Solomon Islands sign security pact in setback for China
November 25, 2026
Australia and the Solomon Islands signed a security pact on Wednesday that makes Australia the archipelago's main defense partner.
This came four years after the Pacific islands country signed a similar deal with China.
The deal ‌is a win for Canberra, which is battling China for influence in the region. It also recently secured similar agreements with Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and Fiji.
With the deal, Australia will support the expansion and development of the Solomon Islands' law enforcement.
It also includes Australian funding for investment in infrastructure and education, improved visa arrangements for Solomon Islanders, and requires ‌Honiara to consult Australia on the development of critical infrastructure.
Solomon Islands' "sensitive" infrastructure will also "remain free from militarization, foreign interference and unauthorized access".
This covers airports, ports, energy and telecommunications infrastructure, sectors where China has invested through million-dollar loans since the Solomon Islands switched diplomatic ties from Taiwan to Beijing in 2019.
"Australia is proud to be the Solomon Islands' main security partner, and that's a responsibility that ‌we take seriously," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told a joint press conference in Australian capital Canberra with his Solomon Islands counterpart, Matthew Wale.
Albanese also said the Solomon Islands would also be required to consult with Australia before striking deals with non-Pacific Island Forum countries on critical infrastructure or security cooperation.
"Solomon Islands has been for a number of years a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region. Those days are done," Wale told the press conference.
Will the China deal be affected?
Wale has been rebuilding diplomatic relationships with Canberra and Washington since he was elected in May. His predecessor Manasseh Sogavare had built closer ties with China since coming to power in 2019.
Asked whether he had ended the 2022 security pact with Beijing, Wale told journalists that he could not comment due to a non-disclosure clause in the treaty with China, set to expire in April 2027. Discussions with China were "ongoing," he said.
Asked the same question on Wednesday, China's Foreign Ministry did not confirm whether the deal had been scrapped, news agency AFP reported. However, ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun warned Australia and the Solomon Islands that their cooperation "should not target any third party."
“I think this deal, coupled with indications that the Solomon Islands will allow its agreement with China to lapse, goes beyond the success of previous deals Australia has struck in the region,” Connor Graham, a research fellow in the Pacific Islands Program at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute, told Reuters news agency.
He said it was a "blow to Chinese security ambitions in the Pacific."

noticias.titulo: Fact check: Deepfakes and 'US abandons Taiwan' claims spread ahead of vote
noticias.resumen: Ahead of local elections, Taiwan is seeing a surge in AI-generated attacks on mayoral candidate Puma Shen, alongside disinformation portraying the US as abandoning the island.
noticias.texto:
Fact check: Deepfakes, 'US abandons Taiwan' claims target island vote
November 25, 2026
On November 28, Taiwan will hold local elections that could reshape power dynamics between the sovereignty-leaning Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the Beijing-friendly Kuomintang (KMT). The outcome could influence relations between Taiwan and China, as well as regional geopolitics and ties between Washington, Beijing and Taipei.
A month before the election, there was a spike in AI-generated content featuring DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen. Claims that the US is abandoning Taiwan also increased during the same period. Experts say that fake quotes and misleading clips are being used as part of a campaign to weaken trust in US security commitments.
The V-Dem Institute at the University of Gothenburg ranked Taiwan "the country most severely targeted" by foreign disinformation for eleven consecutive years – from 2014 to 2024.
The Taiwanese Ministry of the Interior has stated that foreign actors are increasingly using diverse methods to interfere in elections. That includes manipulating election betting, inviting Taiwanese citizens to China, using donations from Taiwanese business people to organize events, such as banquets, and leveraging temple and religious activities, to mobilize and win over supporters. Taiwan has functioned with de facto independence since 1949 despite Beijing's decadeslong claim to the island as a province and repeated vows to annex it.
DW Fact Check examined viral claims that have circulated online since September during the run-up to the election.
Deepfake audio, video target pro-sovereignty candidate
Claim: Puma Shen takes drug and receives kickbacks through arms purchases from the US.
DW Fact check: Fake
An audio clip posted on Facebook on October 29, claims to show Puma Shen, the DPP candidate for Taipei mayor, admitting to receiving kickbacks from US arms deals.
The recording is heavy with background noise – a method used to mask synthetic manipulation in AI-generated audio. Multiple deepfake detection platforms, including Is this AI and Undetectable, flagged the audio as likely AI-generated.
The Facebook account that posted the audio was created on October 29, 2026 – the date the audio was also published. The account's followers are mainly profiles using languages, such as English, Arabic and Thai. That points to possible bot activity.
Another Facebook account posted an image of Puma Shen taking drugs. Apart from the "AI content" label on the post, multiple AI detector tools identified this photo as likely AI-generated.
The account was created in March 2026. Since then, a lot of AI-generated content mocking Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te and his pro-sovereignty party has been posted. It is occasionally interspersed with posts praising the development of Chinese cities.
This account's profile indicates that the primary country location for people who manage this page includes China and Taiwan.
Taiwanese independent media platform Watchout investigated the account's advertising activity and found that it had previously run at least five Facebook ads. The advertisers were identified as Peng Zhiwei and Guo Yang, both based in China. The findings suggest that the account received financial support from individuals in China.
The Taipei mayoral race is a key battleground in Taiwan's upcoming local elections. As of mid-November, polls showed a neck-and-neck contest between Puma Shen and his opponent, Chiang Wan-an, who claims to be a great-grandson of Taiwanese leader Chiang Kai-shek.
Chiang Kai-shek was a leading figure of the Kuomintang and relocated with the party to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese Civil War to the Chinese Communist Party.
While the Kuomintang was historically staunchly anti-communist, critics argue that it now promotes closer ties with China. For example, they point to a senior Kuomintang figure's proposed 10-year unification framework as evidence that its stance runs counter to mainstream public opinion in Taiwan. Although the Kuomintang subsequently stated that this framework is entirely unrelated to the current party leadership, it has sparked controversy in Taiwan.
Distorted quotes and misleading clips
Claim: A TikTok video claims to show US president Donald Trump saying the US is abandoning Taiwan.
DW Fact check: Misleading
The original video was from a Fox News interview with Trump on May 16. The interviewer did not ask whether the United States would defend Taiwan, and the US president did not comment on the issue.
Trump said he did not want Taiwan to become independent or for a war to break out, adding that the status quo should be maintained to allow tensions to de-escalate. He also clearly stated that his policy toward Taiwan "has not changed." Washington has long maintained a policy of strategic ambiguity toward Taiwan– neither explicitly guaranteeing the island's defense nor ruling out the possibility of doing so.
Correction from November 25, 2026: A previous version of this article (published on November 25, 2025) included an example referring to headlines on search engines claiming that US troops were withdrawing from Taiwan. This has been removed because while they were sensational, they were not entirely wrong because they referred to a report by a thinktank. We apologize for the error.

noticias.titulo: Houthis claim attacks on Saudi refinery, financial district
noticias.resumen: Iran-backed Yemeni Houthis say they carried out fresh retaliatory attacks in Saudi Arabia. A fire was reported at Ras Tanura oil refinery and Riyadh's financial district was attacked for the second time in a week.
noticias.texto:
Houthis claim attacks on Saudi refinery, financial district
November 25, 2026
Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen say they are continuing their attacks on Saudi Arabia, claiming to have damaged a key oil refinery as well as the petromonarchy's financial district in the capital Riyadh.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on Wednesday said that "accurate and direct" attacks targeting Ras Tanura — Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery and a major export terminal for crude — had "caused fires to break out at the facility."
Saree said an attack on Saudi Arabia's financial district, located in the capital Riyadh, was "carried out in three phases, with strikes hitting their targets accurately."
Saudi capital has been repeatedly attacked by Houthis
Saudi defense officials said that air defenses in the kingdom had taken down four Houthi drones at Ras Tanura and that 11 people had been injured when a tower in the financial district was hit.
The building in question was also targeted on November 19, but no one was injured in that attack.
The Houthis and Saudis have been fighting for over a decade as part of a civil war that has become a regional conflict with increased significance as a result of the ongoing conflict in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.

noticias.titulo: Climate loss and damage fund exists, but the money doesn't
noticias.resumen: Climate-vulnerable countries fought for years to create a loss and damage fund. Four years on, demand far outstrips funding, pledges are scarce, and disaster-hit nations are still waiting for support.
noticias.texto:
Climate loss and damage fund exists, but the money doesn't
November 25, 2026
On the sandbars and river islands of Bangladesh's Brahmaputra and its branches, families have little to fall back on when the water rises.
"The floodwater swallows everything," said 16-year-old Rasel Babu, who had traveled to Antalya, Turkey, to speak to delegates at the UN climate conference.
Created after years of pressure from vulnerable nations, the loss and damage fund was designed to help countries recover from climate disasters and irreversible climate impacts. This includes extreme weather events such as floods, heat waves and wildfires as well as slow-onset impacts such as sea level rise, desertification and damage to infrastructure and crops.
But the fund is already struggling to meet demand. It received $2.8 billion (€2.56 billion) in urgent requests in a first call for funding, with only $342 million available at the time.
Even the money promised has not fully arrived. Only about half of the money currently pledged had been received by this summer.
While the European Commission signed a €25 million ($27 million) contribution agreement to the fund on the margins of COP31, formalizing an earlier pledge made at COP28, and Spain pledged an additional €15 million, other contributions to loss and damage remained scarce.
First payout will go to Nepal after glacier collapse
The fund's first emergency response is going to be paid out to Nepal. The board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage had provisionally set aside $21.6 million following the catastrophic glacier collapse that triggered flash floods in August, killing more than 1,500 people with 5,600 more missing.
But the money has not moved yet. Nepal must first submit a funding request setting out how it will be spent.
"It's asking for a country that is dealing with the climate emergency to work on a proposal," Nepali climate finance expert Bibek Raj Kandel said, adding a layer of bureaucracy inefficient to address the urgency.
Nepal is already waiting on another request, filed after floods in Kathmandu and landslides in the eastern hills. "There's already one pending proposal sitting on the table," Kandel said. Unless the fund speeds up, he warned, it's "going to disappoint many, many countries."
Pakistan which led the push for the fund in 2022 after floods affected 33 million people and killed more than 1,730, also hasn't seen any of the money yet.
"Pakistan was one of the countries which really spoke up and managed to get the loss and damage fund on the climate agenda. But it takes a long time," Pakistan's Minister of State for Climate Change, Shezra Mansab Ali Khan Kharal, told DW.
"We have still not really got anything. We haven't seen anything on the ground at all as yet," Kharal said. Pakistan has submitted two projects and was told the cap is $200 million.
Other forms of aid often come in the form of loans.
"These promises, they are hollow promises," said Abid Qaiyum Suleri, Executive Director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI) in Islamabad, adding that for a heavily indebted country, the form of the money matters as much as the amount.
"We do not want that a climate disaster in Pakistan should translate into further debt for Pakistan," Kharal said, calling for grants rather than loans.

noticias.titulo: Germany's women's football team take stand against domestic violence
noticias.resumen: Germany's women's football team are to wear UN Women badges in games against Argentina and Peru, as domestic violence hits a record high in Germany.
noticias.texto:
Germany's women's football team take stand against domestic violence
November 25, 2026
Domestic violence has reached a record high in Germany, with 16 women subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors each hour.
UN Women Germany is one of 13 UN Women national committees worldwide, each an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization committed to gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls.
Their current campaign "Orange The World" runs from the start of International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women on November 25 to December 10, International Human Rights Day. It is designed to raise awareness around violence against women in the country and worldwide. The 2026 campaign's focus is particularly on men's responsibility in ending gender-based violence.
"In these 16 days of activism, we can deliver a lot of information. Survivors of gender-based violence can find out where to get support and be reminded that they are not at fault," UN Women Germany chair, politician and long-standing campaigner for women's rights Elke Ferner told DW. "The debate helps and it's a chance to change consciousness about the topic."
Germany captain Giulia Gwinn said in a statement via the German Football Association (DFB): "Violence against women and girls affects us all and must have no place in our society. As the women's national team, we therefore want to once again use our reach to create awareness for this important issue and jointly set a visible sign against violence."
The campaign with the women's team is not new. Two years ago, the team joined the campaign, delivering a moving video that saw players reveal the truth of statements by crossing out words.
During Germany's upcoming South America tour — part of their preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil — they are to wear special UN Women Germany badges on their sleeves in their games against Argentina and Peru.
Role models pivotal for the campaign
Ferner believes the work with role models is pivotal and that the campaign is powerful, especially in a football context. A 2022 study from Warwick Business School in the UK revealed alcohol-related domestic abuse rises by nearly 50% after England's men's football team win a World Cup game, never mind lose.
Currently, there is no data on domestic abuse during Germany games, however during the 2026 World Cup last summer, Berlin police recorded a 31% increase in domestic violence compared to the week before.
Ferner is encouraged that sport has understood the importance of the issue, and that the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) and other sports clubs and organizations are helping move the conversation forward.
In sport, this is particularly important given the problematic nature of dependency relationships that so often exist in high-performance environments. But violence against women is really a societal issue that is not specific to class, origin, religion or societal space, such as sport.
"Violence against women has structural origins and to change that you need to change the structures," Ferner said. "You just need to do it. I always say, this isn't about a lack of knowledge but rather a lack of action."
Performance is an integral part of sport, but a multi-dimensional understanding of it might help shift perspective in a country that remains driven by a performance culture.
"What is performance? Higher, faster, further? Or is it managing to look after a family of three?" Ferner asked. "Why do people who repair washing machines earn more than those looking after your kids in nursery? This is about changing business culture, but also awareness around the role men play at home and in the family.
"The picture boys and young men get of girls and women in school is a problem that needs addressing. We can't wait for generational change. This is about saving lives. We need to change societal structures."
Male power structures a problem
Sports structures are also in need of reform. Non-profit organization Safe Sport provides independent support for people affected by sexual, physical and psychological violence in both amateur and professional sport in Germany.
They are the only organization with a specific focus on violence in grassroots sports in Germany, and one of only two in professional sport in the country. They also have to contend with structures, in a sporting context, that make spaces less safe for women.
"Gender roles have become more fluid in the last few years, but in associations and clubs management positions are still occupied by men, regardless of the sport," Safe Sport manager Ina Lambert told DW.
"In professional sport, there are a lot fewer women involved in training and so the space remains male dominated, and, as a result, so do the power structures.
"We have people in search of advice, men included, who see the problems and want to enforce change, and we offer them support so they are not alone," Lambert said. "But whether in a big association or a small club, perpetrators are frequently protected, incidents are ignored and so the people who want to enforce change are often prevented from doing so."
Safe Sport, which provides free psychological and legal support, has only been in action since July 2023, but in that time the number of support requests they have received continues to grow. Psychological violence in sport in Germany is the most common case they are faced with, but sexual violence is also a major problem.
"There is finally recognition of the problem and there is a seriousness about tackling it," Lambert said.
"There is a lot of good work being done in the right direction, with many good concepts for prevention, intervention and processing violence, as well as more education, holistic training and focus on women's menstrual cycles."
Comprehensive support on the way
Germany's Interior Ministry is leading the process with participants from the country's states, organized sport, affected parties and academia to create a central hub. The center for safe sport was founded in July 2026, but investigative and sanctioning work is expected to begin in the spring of 2027.
Support from leading figures clearly makes a huge difference, but it's also clear that more data is needed. Addressing the underlying issues, such as social norms and gender stereotyping, is a must.
After all, as UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous said: "No country has yet eliminated violence against women. Ending it requires transformative action — greater investment, innovation, and unwavering political will."
This article was originally published on November 28, 2024, and updated on November 25, 2026.

noticias.titulo: German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite
noticias.resumen: German auto workers profited during the industry's boom years, but are now increasingly being asked to trade past gains for future job security.
noticias.texto:
German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite
November 25, 2026
For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process. Those days appear to be gone.
A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement.
As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided.
Volkswagen wants to freeze wages for the next two years while cutting several allowances and bonuses.
Alongside Mercedes, it's demanding longer hours under the same pay, with both companies threatening to withhold investment from German factories.
Unions have responded with warning strikes and the threat of larger walkouts. Yet workers are aware of the grim outlook, with Germany's auto industry losing more than 123,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute.
"I think that the labor representatives are in a very difficult situation," said Thomas Haipeter, a labor researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen. "On the one hand, they have to make concessions in order to safeguard jobs. And despite these massive employment reductions to safeguard the rest of the jobs and locations, what is missing for them is a kind of more offensive strategy."
A hot shower a day
Labor's outsized role in German auto companies goes back decades and includes a 1945 deal at Volkswagen promising a hot shower a day.
That year marks the start of "co-determination" at the company, in which workers are represented internally by employee-led workers' councils, as well as by outside labor unions.
Berlin then anchored labor's strong say in Volkswagen in 1960, before the firm issued public shares, ensuring government officials retained extra votes in the supervisory board. Those seats, belonging to the Lower Saxony government, tend to be sympathetic to workers.
Workers' councils, meanwhile, became a fixture across the German auto industry, with representation extending across multiple production sites within the same companies.
Pay and benefits for auto workers have risen over the years. During the last German industry boom, between 2011 and 2019, pay for auto workers clearly outpaced the average German wage.
In early 2025, auto workers were earning nearly a third more per hour than the typical German worker, when bonuses and allowances are factored in, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
That same year, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume praised cooperation with the unions as one of the company's "great strengths" during the 80th anniversary of the 1945 agreement.
Cracks in the relationship
Cracks were long in the making, according to case studies by Haipeter and others. Labor was increasingly forced to protect plants and jobs as companies chased cheaper workers abroad.
Workers' councils turned their attention to saving their own production lines. They focused on business strategy and even hired business consultants in an effort to sway strategy.
When combustion engines dominated, autoworkers could argue German production was the most technologically advanced, according to Haipeter. That changed with the shift to electric vehicles.
"This line of compromise is canceled now by management," he said. "They say it doesn't matter for us where we produce. We have to produce at the locations or in countries which are best-cost countries and not in countries which have higher wages."
Slow sales of electric autos and competition from Chinese manufacturers have, meanwhile, exposed the cost difference.
In 2024, Volkswagen abruptly canceled a series of labor agreements and threatened factory closures. After tough negotiations, labor agreed to significant cuts — €1.5 billion yearly in abandoned wage hikes and the elimination of 50,000 positions through attrition — in exchange for job security for current employees through 2030.
Management returned this summer with a restructuring plan that included the closures of four German plants. It delayed that decision following negotiations, but slated another 50,000 positions for attrition.
Volkswagen declined to comment for this article.
More hours, same pay
The most sensitive issue for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay, or even receive less for less work.
The union IG Metall won the concession for a 35-hour workweek in 1984 after seven weeks of strikes. It's now standard in every labor contract in the auto industry, although it's not uncommon for worksites to deviate from the employee agreement, according to Haipeter.
Mercedes has called for employees to agree to an exception across the company. The company acknowledged that the 35-hour workweek was "hard-won" and "means a great deal" to its workers. "However, the conditions under which it was agreed upon no longer exist today," it said in a statement to DW.
Volkswagen, meanwhile, is demanding greater "flexibility" as the negotiations get underway.
"They call it flexibility in both directions," Thorsten Gröger, head of negotiations for the union, said last week. "In the end, Volkswagen wants its employees to perform unpaid work."
The 35-hour workweek is too sacred for unions to give in, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, a longtime analyst of the German car industry.
"The unions are in a difficult position," he noted. "They battled for a 35-hour workweek, and that's an incredible privilege that comes with a lot of pride. The union knows that as soon as one factory, one production hall, gives up the 35-hour workweek, then they will have a conflagration."
Dudenhöffer sees parallels in another crisis from Volkswagen's history. After a downturn in the early 1990s, the then-head of the German state of Lower Saxony, Gerhard Schröder, pushed for an agreement for workers to work less in exchange for retaining their jobs.
"We need a mediator along these lines," Dudenhöffer said.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: 'We can no longer afford everything,' Merz says
noticias.resumen: The German chancellor has warned tax revenue means a tighter budget for 2027 and beyond. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier is in Kenya for the final leg of his Africa tour. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: 'We can no longer afford everything,' Merz says
Published November 25, 2026last updated November 25, 2026
What you need to know
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz has addressed the Bundestag during a debate on the government's 2027 budget
- President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is in Kenya for the final leg of his Africa tour
- A plaque for the Holocaust survivor Margot Friedländer is being unveiled in Berlin
- Protests are planned for the visit of ex-Mossad chief David Barnea in Berlin
Keep reading for the latest news and analysis from Germany on Wednesday, November 25:
Bayern Munich say Musiala first exhibited neurological symptoms last April
Bayern Munich says it has held talks with midfielder Jamal Musiala's management amid the difficulties surrounding his neurological symptoms and after comments from club management about his lucrative 2025 contract extension prompted criticism and controversy (read the backstory from Jon Harding on our sports desk here).
"A constructive discussion took place yesterday, Tuesday, between FC Bayern Munich and Jamal Musiala's management," the club said in a statement. "For both parties, the player's health is the absolute priority. Jamal Musiala will receive full support throuhgout his recovery process."
The club also clarified when Musiala — who collapsed twice in pre-season friendlies as a result of what he has described as "absence seizures" — first started exhibiting neurological symptoms that only became widely known with the announcement of his diagnosis at the start of this season.
"In light of various rumors circulating over the past few days, FC Bayern and 11WINS — the agency representing Jamal — wish to clarify the following: Jamal Musiala was first examined for absence-like symptoms on April 22, 2025," the club said. "This examination took place in consultation with FC Bayern and the club's medical department, immediately following the onset of these neurological symptoms."
Musiala had signed a contract extension to 2030 earlier that year. Several senior Bayern officials had voiced doubts about his contractual status in recent days, saying it appeared unlikely he would be able to return to his past peak form going forward. This prompted a stern rebuke from the players' union and others.
After being sidelined with a hamstring injury in September, Musiala returned to action last week in the 1-1 draw with Cologne.
AfD in Saxony-Anhalt put forward Siegmund to head state government
The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) has formally put forward its leader in Saxony-Anhalt to head the eastern state's next regional government.
Given the stalemate after September's elections, with the AfD by far the largest party but still well short of a majority in its own right, it's anything by clear that Siegmund will receive the 42 votes he'd need to become state premier.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the Magdeburg parliament so Siegmund would need three votes from members of other parties in the secret ballot.
But what's now clear is that a vote to see if he can command a majority will go ahead, provisionally on December 8. Siegmund had said last week that he planned to take this step.
"I am working on the assumption that there will only be one vote," Siegmund said, voicing confidence in winning the required support, even though nobody outside his party has indicated an intention to vote for him.
The left-wing populist BSW, which holds five seats, has said its members intend to abstain, while 14 of 15 CDU lawmakers in the state have said they intend to leave the chamber in the first two rounds of voting.
How does the election process work in such situations where a majority vote seems unlikely?
It's not clear how the process might end as yet.
But if a candidate stands in two votes in the state parliament — which must take place within one week of each other — and cannot command a majority in either, a new vote is triggered on whether to call new elections. This must take place within two weeks. In this situation, a simple majority voting in favor would suffice to trigger another election.
If there is no majority vote for another election, then a third vote for a state government leader is triggered.
In this final round, a candidate only needs a majority of the total votes cast, not a majority of the total number of members of the chamber, in order to be elected.
In the event that even this third vote is not decisive, with a tie of votes for and against — which given the arithmetic in the parliament does seem at least to be a conceivable possibility — then Germany's written laws don't make it explicitly clear what the tie-break function would be.
Legal experts have said they believe the most likely solution would be to continue holding votes until a majority or plurality decision can be reached.
Wadephul: Reduced Foreign Ministry budget 'difficult to understand' given global tensions
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has voiced dissatisfaction with cuts to his department's 2027 funding during Wednesday's Bundestag budget debate.
He described the planned budget for his department as "responsible," albeit adding: "But to be honest, I cannot give my budget a much better evaluation than that."
Wadephul said that given the precarious geopolitical situation it was "difficult to understand" why the Foreign Ministry was not exempt from the more general savings drive.
He noted that while the Defense Ministry budget was bolstered to a large extent by the so-called "special fund" to boost defense and rearmament spending, "not a single euro cent" of that extra-budgetary financial allowance flowed to the Foreign Ministry.
The Foreign Ministry's proposed 2027 budget is smaller than this year's, but not by very much. The proposals foresee cutting it from €6.02 billion (roughly $6.58 billion) to €5.99 billion. The largest planned cut is in contributions to the UN and the international community, falling by roughly €200 million or almost a quarter of the 2026 total.
Authorities in Nuremberg defuse World War II bomb
Experts in Nuremberg have successfully defused a World War II bomb not far south of the city center.
The 225-kilo bomb was rendered inactive just before 2 p.m. local time (1300 GMT/UTC), city authorities said in a press release.
The US bomb dropped in an air raid had been unearthed a day earlier at a construction site.
A precautionary evacuation radius of 500 meters was established to deal with the explosive, with roughly 700 residents asked to leave their homes in the hours before the operation.
"All those affected by the evacuation can now return to their homes," the city wrote.
An affected bus route was also resuming normal service, and authorities said that road closures and diversions were also being lifted.
Around 250 personnel were deployed for the operation.
Discoveries of unexploded ordnance from World War II are commonplace to this day in Germany. However, Nuremberg in the north of Bavaria represents a site rather further south and inland than the most common locations, which tend to be in the north and west, in easier reach of Allied bombing raids often launched from the UK.
The heavily industrialized western Ruhr Valley region and major cities like Cologne in North Rhine-Westphalia are the most common sites for such finds.
Berlin unveils memorial to Holocaust survivor Margot Friedländer
The city of Berlin unveiled a new memorial to Holocaust survivor Margot Friedländer.
A sign explaining the history of a building in Berlin where Margot Friedländer, then still known as Margot Bendheim, was forced to live by the Nazis has now been established.
The plaque was unveiled in Berlin-Kreuzberg by Green district Mayor Clara Herrmann.
It explains how Jews, including Margot, her mother and her brother, were forced to live there. The building on Skalitzer Strasse also housed forced laborers.
Margot's family was detained and sent to Auschwitz in 1943, where they were murdered. Margot escaped but was eventually sent to the Theresienstadt concentration camp.
She survived the war, after which she moved to the United States, but returned in 2009 to her former home. Up until her death last year, she was engaged in educating people about the Holocaust.
CDU defends budget drafted in face of 'challenges'
The head of the CDU lawmakers in the Bundestag, Thorstein Frei, defended the government's 2027 budget, despite it being "full of challenges."
He said that taxation had been eased where it most benefited people and police, intelligence agencies and the military have been strengthened.
He acknowledged that the coalition "is not yet where it wants to be" and is also not blind to the fact part of the economic growth is coming from public spending, but he pointed to positive signals from the economy, such as the increasing business climate index.
Regarding the massive increase in military spending, Frei said: "We want to be strong so that, in the end, we won't have to use that strength."
SPD calls to find solutions for government income gaps
Matthias Miersch, head of the SPD in the Bundestag, called for a discussion on how to make "large fortunes" better contribute to the good of everyone, including higher taxation on inheritance, a sticking point between the SPD and their conservative coalition partners.
"We need to discuss this now," Miersch said. "For us, this issue is by no means off the table; on the contrary, we are putting it on the agenda."
"So far, we have always managed to find a solution—and we will continue to work toward that," he added, pointing to the €34 billion gap in the budget that the government managed to fill.
"On behalf of social democracy, I would like to say that we strive for compromises every single day, even within this coalition."
Left Party slams militarization and cuts in budget
Heidi Reichinnek, the head of the socialist Left Party in the Bundestag, has also commented on the government's budget, accusing the coalition of drafting a budget "at the expense of the majority."
"Militarization and unbridled arms buildup on the one hand, brutal social cutbacks and a spree of budget cuts on the other," Reichinnek said.
She accused the government of trying to protect the profits of the wealthy and big corporations while telling everyone else to "tighten the belt."
The left-wing lawmaker said a windfall tax on electricity companies would have helped people without leaving a gap in the budget, as happened with the electricity tax reduction that the coalition agreed on.
AfD calls budget an 'orgy of debt'
Timo Chrupalla, the co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), the largest opposition party in the Bundestag, has called the government's 2027 "a pure orgy of debt" after the coalition agreed to take €210 billion ($230 billion) in debt.
Merz would go down in the history books "as Germany's chancellor of insolvency," Chrupalla said.
He attacked the government's continued funding for Ukraine while electricity costs go up in Germany, and called on the opposition lawmakers in the Green and Left parties to join the AfD in filing a constitutional challenge against the budget.
Greens slam budget as not 'serious'
"This budget has nothing to do with seriousness," the head of the Greens in the Bundestag, Britta Haßelmann, said in remarks made during the budget debate.
She lamented a chaotic process that has been full of contradictions, including what she called "fooling around" with the electricity tax.
However, she also took aim at the AfD, calling the far-right party's stance on funding for Ukraine "shameful" and accused the party of spreading misinformation.
Merz defends support for Ukraine in budget
Germany has been Ukraine's biggest backer in Europe, incurring costs to help defend against the Russian invasion.
Despite falling support among German voters for this policy and increasing budget difficulties, Chancellor Merz defended the government's decision to keep funding Kyiv.
"Russia wants more than Ukraine," Merz said in response to opposition parties during the 2027 budget debate.
"Anyone who fails to grasp this does not understand this world, or is pursuing entirely different aims with regard to our country's freedom, openness and liberalism," he added.
He also pointed to incidents within Germany that have been attributed to Russia, including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig Airport in August.
'We no longer have the money' Merz says in budget debate
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken in the Bundestag as the debate opens on the government's budget plans for 2027.
"We no longer have the money for everything," Merz said in his remarks to the German parliament.
He described the tight budget, which has to be finalized this week, as an "accurate reflection" of the "difficult situation as a country — geopolitically, technologically, and demographically" that Germany finds itself in.
"We will no longer be able to afford everything with tax revenue that we have become all too accustomed to for far too long," Merz added.
The government has €560.9 billion (around $614 billion) to spend in its core budget for 2027, but both Merz's conservative CDU/CSU and the Social Democrats, who make up the coalition government, have stressed that the budget for 2028 will be even more challenging.
The extra borrowing for defense and infrastructure, that marked a break with years of debt avoidance, "is limiting our room to maneuver in the coming years to an extent that many have not yet truly come to terms with," Merz warned.
German growth revised down for 3rd quarter
German GDP only grew by 0.1% between July and September, according to updated data from the Federal Statistics Offices (Destatis).
This marked a downwards revision from the 0.2% that had previously been estimated.
"After Germany's economic performance was robust in the first six months of the year in the face of geopolitical crises, economic growth slowed in the third quarter," statistics chief Ruth Brand said .
Despite a surprisingly good performance in the first half of the year, a slump in exports, as well as summer heatwaves and record-low water levels in rivers that hindered transportation of goods along Germany's key waterways, brought a slowdown to Europe's biggest economy.
Nevertheless, overall growth for the year is expected to reach its highest level since 2022 thanks to increased public spending on defense and infrastructure.
Protests planned over appearance of ex-Mossad chief at Bundestag breakfast
The former head of Israel's spy agency Mossad, David Barnea, is scheduled to take part in a breakfast meeting with members of the German parliament, the Bundestag, where he will discuss the ongoing war in the Middle East.
By his own admission, Barnea played a role in the pager attack that targeted members of Hezbollah in Lebanon in September 2024. The attack killed at least 37 people and injured some 300 others, including civilians. It has been described as a possible war crime by UN human rights chief Volker Türk.
That's why the human rights organization European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR) has called for Barnea's arrest, saying it filed a complaint with the Federal Prosecutor's Office.
"Germany must not provide a platform for alleged war criminals. Anyone who distributes thousands of everyday objects rigged with explosives and detonates them months later — without knowing where they will be at the time of detonation — knowingly accepts that an uncontrollable number of civilians will be injured or killed," ECCHR's Alexander Schwarz said.
Criticism also came from the Green party, with Bundestag member Kassem Taher Saleh saying Barnea had "no place in the Bundestag," in comments to the taz, due to the allegations against him. However, his Green colleague Konstantin von Notz defended the invitation, pointing to the close cooperation between Mossad and Germany's own intelligence agency.
Neither the Israeli government nor Barnea have commented on the ECCHR complaint.
Steinmeier to meet with Kenyan President Ruto in Nairobi
Following stops in the Ivory Coast and Ghana, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has arrived in Kenya for the final leg of his Africa tour.
He is set to meet with Kenyan President William Ruto to discuss bilateral relations, including economic cooperation. Kenya is one of Germany's main partners on the African continent. Following Kenya's independence from Britain in 1963, Germany was the first country to officially recognize it.
During his stay in the Ghanaian capital Accra, where he took part in the opening of the German-African Business Summit, Steinmeier called on German companies to engage more deeply in African countries.
In Kenya, the German president is set to visit the special economic zone of Tatu City, where a special tax priveleges are attracting businesses.
Steinmeier last visited Kenya in 2020, but this trip is likely to be his last, with his term ending in March 2027.

noticias.titulo: Colombian security forces storm supermarket, free hostages
noticias.resumen: A failed robbery turned into a day-long hostage crisis in one of Colombia's most popular tourist destinations. The incident comes amid concerns over the deteriorating security situation in the South American country.
noticias.texto:
Colombian security forces storm supermarket, free hostages
November 25, 2026
Security forces in Colombia stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage crisis.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said all hostages had been rescued and one of the hostage-takers had been killed.
"In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued," de la Espriella said.
Around 30 people had initially been taken captive at a branch of the Exito supermarket chain in Cartagena's La Castellana neighborhood.
Ten of them, including some elderly women, had already been released on Tuesday after hours of negotiations.
No further details were immediately available about whether any of the hostages had been injured.
How did the Cartagena hostage crisis unfold?
According to authorities, the hostage crisis followed a failed attempt to rob an armored vehicle transporting cash from a shopping mall.
Police, troops and special forces were deployed to the supermarket as authorities sought to secure the release of the hostages.
Images circulating on social media appeared to show people kneeling inside the supermarket with their hands bound. The images could not be independently verified.
Supermarket employees were among those believed to have been taken hostage.
"My son is there," Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers, told news agency AFP during the standoff.
"He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him," he said.
The supermarket chain said it was following the guidance of the authorities.
"For Grupo Exito, protecting the people's lives and safety is our priority," the company said in a statement.
The incident also temporarily disrupted air traffic in Cartagena, a Caribbean port known for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise ship tourism.
Arrivals at the city's Rafael Nunez airport were suspended for around 45 minutes in connection with the security operation.
What did Colombia's president say about the hostage crisis?
De la Espriella traveled to Cartagena on Tuesday, where he met commanders from a specialist anti-kidnapping and anti-extortion unit.
The president, who appeared in military fatigues, had previously expressed confidence that the captives would be freed.
"This is going to turn out well for the hostages," he said before arriving in Cartagena. "I'm not so sure it's going to turn out so well for the criminals."
De la Espriella ruled out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups in the incident.
Local media reported that the hostage-takers had made financial demands and requested safe passage to Barranquilla, another city on Colombia's Caribbean coast. Those reports could not be independently verified.
What is the security situation in Colombia?
Security has deteriorated across much of Colombia despite the tough rhetoric of its right-wing president, who took office in August.
On Monday, a car bombing in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.
The government blamed the attack on a faction of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels that rejects a 2016 peace agreement.
De la Espriella had visited Villavicencio following the bombing before traveling to Cartagena.
According to a Defense Ministry document shared with AFP, armed groups carried out 358 drone attacks between January and November — an average of more than one attack per day.

noticias.titulo: Domestic violence soars to record high in Germany
noticias.resumen: Every three days in Germany, a man kills his wife or ex-partner. Every 10 minutes, the police record a sexual offense against a woman. "A shocking finding," according to Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig.
noticias.texto:
Domestic violence soars to record high in Germany
November 25, 2026
The German government has presented some grim statistics with regard to misogyny, rape, violence and murder, with reported cases of domestic violence at an all-time high.
At a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Family Affairs Minister Karin Prien and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig released the latest figures on crimes that specifically target women: whether within families and intimate relationships, in public or online.
'Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories'
In contrast to the statistics pertaining to crime overall, which have remained the same or increased only slightly, reports of crimes against women have increased.
"Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories, people and particularly women and girls, whose lives are severely affected by these acts of violence," said Dobrindt.
