In 2025, some 280,000 people were victims of physical abuse in their own homes, a 2.8% increase compared to the previous year. Over 70% of the victims were female. Each hour, 16 women are subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors.
The male victims included boys who had been assaulted by their fathers.
The number of misogynistic hate crimes has also risen dramatically, by almost 50%, to 819 cases.
"The figures show us what it can mean to be a woman in Germany," said Hubig. "It can mean being killed by one's partner or ex-partner. Being a woman can also mean being physically abused by one's partner or ex-partner in one's own home. Being a woman can mean that one's sexual autonomy is brutally disregarded."
Perpetrators, victims getting younger
According to the latest findings, both perpetrators and victims are getting younger. In 2025, nearly half of all female victims of sexual offenses were under the age of 18. And the number of incidents of online violence against women and girls rose by 15.7%. This includes the unauthorized sharing of videos and photos, verbal abuse, manipulation of images, threats and online blackmail, as well as cyberstalking.
Because many perpetrators and victims are still in their teens, Prien, who is also minister for education, said the government wanted to focus primarily on schools, which she explained should become places of prevention.
"Ultimately, we need to bring about a change in people's mindsets, especially those of men. That will be the deciding factor in the end," she said.
Femicides to be classified as murder, not manslaughter
Over the weekend, Justice Minister Hubig had already announced that in future all femicides, the intentional killing of girls and women because of their gender, would be classified as murders. Currently, such crimes are often classified as manslaughter, for which the penalty is less severe than for murder.
Hubig told German broadcaster ZDF that it was increasingly common that femicides be described as family tragedies or as domestic dramas revolving around jealousy and then classified as manslaughter.
Martina Link, the vice president of the Federal Criminal Police Office, was also at the press conference in Berlin. She called for everybody to pay closer attention to the issue, within their own families, neighborhoods or at work.
"Violence against women is not a private matter," she said. "Not in our immediate surroundings nor in the digital world."
She also pointed out that when it came to sexual offenses and domestic violence, only about 5-10% of cases were reported.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
noticias.resumen: The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.
noticias.texto:
How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.
"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."
The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.
Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.
That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.
The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.
A sacred day for all
Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."
Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well
"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."
When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.
"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.
Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.
"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."
The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.
"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."
Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."
(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")
"I'm thanking God"
This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.
Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."
Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.
"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

noticias.titulo: What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
noticias.resumen: 59% of U.S. shoppers plan to use AI for holiday shopping this weekend, according to the National Retail Federation
noticias.texto:
What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday.
This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation.
But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.
Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.
Treat AI searches like a conversation with a kid
Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.
Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.
After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.
"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."
Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.
"It's best if you imagine that it's a young child who will probably misinterpret your request," Pfeiffer said. "You want to be as specific and clear as possible."
AI Agents can shop for you. Be careful what you give them
Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm. They can handle shopping tasks.
If shoppers are, for example, worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox in order to track packages, even messaging a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond just suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying (with your money).
These are useful features, but require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card. One of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform Muse asks is if the user would like to connect their email and calendar.
Meta says its AI is highly secure. Everyone is assigned their own AI agent and the company promises that information shoppers share with it is kept private. Particularly sensitive information like credit card numbers, they say, are held separately and never viewed directly by the AI.
Yet Meta also has long been accused of violating user privacy, as in a 2022 case about improperly sharing user data. Meta did not admit to wrongdoing but settled for about $725 million.
Beyond Meta, there are cases of AI jumping guardrails that programmers set for it. Users have also reported their AI agents acting without their consent, such as sending their home address to a buyer from Facebook Marketplace and booking a hotel.
Philip Bruno, chief strategy and growth officer with ACI Worldwide, says he would share what he's shopping for with AI, but warns to be more careful with personal information.
"I'm cooking for a family of four. That is fine to be able to say," Bruno says. "I would be very careful about payment information."
On that note, experts caution shoppers to be careful with other people's information. It's easy to give most AIs loads of information about your father while brainstorming his gift. Know AI agents can also use this to build profiles of the shopper's friends and family. Being illusive and not specifying who you're shopping for during the brainstorming can help.
Just like for humans, it takes time for AI to find the best deals
One major selling point for using AI agents is that they can check multiple websites and compare prices, bringing them for human review all in one spot. That does not mean the first price it shows you is the best one.
"One of the biggest misconceptions about AI is that it somehow sees everything," Pfeiffer says. "That's just false. It gets you the best answer it can as quickly as possible."
AI agents still need time to hunt for deals. Many will often let shoppers watch along as they browse the web, rather than relying on preset knowledge.
This automating can also mean time savings for the user. Agents often can run in the background 24/7.
If users are in no particular holiday rush, they can leave the AI to continue shopping for weeks or even months, only sending a notice when a price drops into a budget friendly range.
Just know these agents don't always have access to every website. Amazon, for example, blocks Muse, arguing Meta did not alert Amazon of plans and that agents did not identify themselves while browsing.
Check the AI's work
For all the advances since ChatGPT's launch four years ago, AI still hallucinates and makes mistakes.
Visa recently released a report warning buyers to beware of AI shoppers. It tested different AI models and found they failed to recommend a product that met a customer's needs in 42% of test runs – more than half of those still recommended a product that didn't match.
That provides even more reason to click through and read up on whatever potential gift an AI recommends to make sure it's what shoppers want.
Otherwise people may find themselves turning back to that same AI agent for help making a return.

noticias.titulo: Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.
noticias.resumen: Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius to prepare to dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide. And, after a nearly two-year legal battle, Kilmar Abrego Garcia's has voluntarily left the U.S.
noticias.texto:
Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.
Army Explosives Detonation In Iowa, Abrego Garcia Leaves The US, Congress And Nvidia
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.
- 🎧 The U.S. Army rescheduled the detonation multiple times after the public got wind of it last week, NPR's Quil Lawrence tells Up First. Purdue University's Andrew Whelton, who has worked on disaster planning, tells Lawrence the detonation caused stress for residents, businesses and farmers. The Trump administration pushed back on the notion that this planned action was a surprise, citing town hall meetings on the topic. Lawrence says the biggest danger in the detonation is to kids and pregnant people due to the lead dust in the air or on surfaces. There are also worries about potential harm to livestock and crops, as well as the cleanup duration.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.
- 🎧 Abrego Garcia's attorney said that he will essentially spend two years waiting abroad. His case raises concerns about due process and the risks of sending individuals to countries where they could be harmed, NPR's Juliana Kim says. The Department of Homeland Security said they are delighted by his decision to leave the U.S. The agency, in a statement, said that "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocents." After being mistakenly deported, upon his return to the U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling, an allegation he has denied.
Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.
- 🎧 Some lawmakers are upset with Huang, while others criticized Nvidia and its board, NPR's Maham Javaid says. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas is calling for a congressional investigation into Huang and urging faster action on chip-control legislation. House Democratic Committee leaders sent a letter to the president after he claimed he helped with Huang's reinstatement. They asked if he prioritizes friends and allies over the nation's economic and national security interests. They demanded a response by Dec. 8 on what he knew about Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Huang will attend a closed-door hearing with House members next week, followed by testimony before a Senate committee two days later.
Today's listen
NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.
There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here.
Life advice
If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.
- 🧠 Instead of reliving the work issue, spend 15 minutes creating a plan to address the situation. Ask yourself, "How can I handle this? What outcome do I want?"
- 🧠 Adopt rituals that engage as many senses as possible to help your brain transition between tasks. For example, try changing your clothes to signal the end of the workday. The more you repeat rituals, the easier it is for your brain to shift from work to relaxation.
- 🧠 Do something that energizes you. Activities like screen time and doomscrolling may seem relaxing, but they aren't effective.
- 🧠 Ask yourself: "If my job disappeared tomorrow, what remains of me?" You might realize your worth isn't tied to your job title.
For more guidance on how to switch off your work brain, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.
3 things to know before you go
- Dancing with the Stars wrapped up Season 35 last night, crowning Paralympian Ezra Frech and his partner, Daniella Karagach, as the winners of this year's Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.
- Frailejon, a plant of Colombia's high-mountain wetlands that's vital to the country's water supply, is facing an array of threats from farmers, ranchers and climate change. Volunteers are working to save these plants, one seedling at a time.
- Doctors are combating disinformation about routine vitamin K shots for newborns, which prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. The rate of parents skipping these shots for their kids has increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to new research in JAMA.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

noticias.titulo: Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
noticias.resumen: Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts — from beating sun to freezing nights, fire and snow.
noticias.texto:
Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
As dawn broke one recent morning over camp, we got one of our first full views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, normally hidden behind clouds.
Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts. The beating sun bakes you during the day, walking so close to the equator, but the nights quickly dip below freezing. Snow remains constantly in sight from humid rainforest and alpine landscapes, freshly charred from a wildfire three weeks before. And always beckoning is the peak, within sight, but seemingly never nearer; the high altitude means hikers need to walk slowly or else risk exhaustion and altitude sickness.
A group of friends and fellow hikers and I spent days camping at altitude to acclimatize before a final summit push during our second-to-last evening on the mountain. We trudged through heavy snow under the stars, cresting a massive volcanic crater rim, and leaned against drifts of what had become a full blizzard to reach the top in the early morning hours. I stood on the peak I'd seen only from a distance for the last week but saw only whiteness: all snow and ice, the absence of life and color heightened by my low oxygen levels.
Days later, having descended and decompressed and readying myself to fly back home, I looked back at the mountain one last time. For a few minutes, in the dusk light, the clouds parted and she revealed herself before disappearing again into the darkening evening, still as elusive as ever.
For more Far-Flung Postcards, click here.

noticias.titulo: Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
noticias.resumen: Constantly buying new things can be problematic, says journalist Eric Athas, author of the new book "Saying No to New." Here's how to break the cycle and find joy in what you already have.
noticias.texto:
Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Buyer beware: Holiday shopping season is here. Is every sale calling your name? Is your virtual shopping cart overflowing?
Before you start buying everything, take note. There's a reason new things get us excited, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New: Why New Things Are Stealing Your Time, Money, and Happiness — and How to Take Back Your Life, published in September. Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.
That constant consumption of novel possessions — whether they're brand-new, digital, secondhand or even free — can be problematic. "It's hard to be grateful for what you have if you're always on the lookout for something else," he says.
To break the cycle of chasing newness, we need to shop with more intention and find joy in what we already own, Athas says. In a conversation with Life Kit, he explains how. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Why are we so drawn to seeking out new things?
Our brains are programmed to find new things interesting and old things boring.
If you think about our ancient ancestors, it was beneficial [for their survival] to explore new foods to eat and new territory and eventually explore different parts of the world.
There's also research that shows when we encounter something new, we get a little shot of dopamine. You get that feeling of excitement when you first use that new app or try that new video game or bring home a new gizmo for the kitchen.
What are some of the downsides of chasing newness?
New things can steal our happiness. Everyone can relate to the feeling of tearing open that new box or putting on that new outfit. You do feel joy and excitement from that initially.
But science says those feelings can't last. So we have to go out and get something else, and that's where we can get into this cycle of constantly chasing happiness in new things.
These days, it feels particularly hard to focus on what you have. There's so much pressure to buy new things. Why is that?
Everywhere we go, whether that's scrolling our favorite shopping app or browsing the aisle of our favorite store, there are little cues driving our [shopping] decisions. These companies have designs we don't even realize are engineering our choices.
For example, at the checkout page of a website or an app, there might be a countdown clock that says, "Save 25% if you make this purchase in three minutes." That's a tactic meant to whip up anxiety.
The other part of this is that you can buy new things faster than you've ever been able to before. It's all seamless and frictionless.
What can we do to create more friction between ourselves and the new things we want to buy?
Expand what I call "the new-thing gap." That's the time and distance between you encountering a new thing and you acquiring it.
If you've got one-click checkout with a certain company, maybe delete the app from your phone or remove your credit card information from that app.
Another easy tactic is to drop something in your cart and leave it there for 24 hours. Researchers have found that when you delay a purchase, interest in that thing will start to decline.
What happens when you use all these tactics and still feel like buying something new?
The main thing is to make intentional choices. The goal here is not to say no to all new things.
Now that I know my brain is programmed to find new things, I bring my attention to that whenever I feel drawn to something new. Is this something I want, or am I being influenced?
You can get really good at saying no to the wrong type of new things, better at saying yes to the right type of new things.
You say because we're programmed to want new things, we can be quick to set old things aside. So is it possible to get joy from old things?
Research has found that if we force ourselves to revisit old things, we may find there's untapped enjoyment in those old things.
In one study, researchers had people go through a museum exhibit. At the end, they asked participants how much they thought they would enjoy going through the exhibit again. People predicted they would get less enjoyment from the repeated experience.
But when the researchers forced them to go through it again, the participants said, "Actually, we enjoyed that just as much, if not more, the second time." They discovered details they missed the first time around or just liked seeing everything again.
How do we apply this lesson in our own life?
Reexperience old things. Books, movies, board games, your neighborhood. Go to that restaurant down the street that you love. Travel to that city that you've been to before.
What's great is you can relieve yourself of this obligation to always be spending money, time and attention on new things. You can fight against this bias that we have for novel experiences and find there's joy and excitement hiding in plain sight.

noticias.titulo: A quintessential Route 66 diner has been serving up Americana for nearly 100 years
noticias.resumen: The Ariston Cafe opened its doors in 1924 to serve travelers along Route 66 and has dished up classic American road fare ever since.
noticias.texto:
A quintessential Route 66 diner has been serving up Americana for nearly 100 years
The Ariston Cafe along Route 66 in Litchfield, Ill., has been a favorite for more than 90 years. Just past the front door, underneath the vintage neon signs that read "Ariston" and "Budweiser," is a diner staple: a glass case, full of sweet temptations. It took one of the Ariston's owners, Will Law, nearly a full minute to reel off all 12 of the day's choices.
"There's a peach crisp bread pudding with the vanilla bourbon sauce," he said. "Then, of course, a traditional cheesecake with or without cherries, and we have a chocolate delight, a lemon delight, a coconut delight."
They were all delightful to look at and the kind of classic American comfort desserts that you might crave while you're road-tripping on America's most famous highway. All of them — like everything else served at the Ariston — are still made in-house.
Litchfield isn't the most natural stop on Route 66; it's a sleepy town about an hour outside St. Louis. But the Ariston Cafe, which sits just across the road from the charming Litchfield Museum & Route 66 Welcome Center, has become an institution in its own right with its wooden chairs and cozy decor.
Travelers still flock to the Ariston, thanks to the internet and social media. The waitstaff says many visitors come in already knowing exactly what they intend to order based on what they've read and seen online.
Right by the front door there's a guest book for diners next to a basket of reading glasses to make reading and signing easier. Within just a few days, the Ariston has welcomed patrons from Australia, South Korea, Nicaragua and Germany, among other nations. And they come from all over the U.S. too.
Bob Dickson celebrated his 75th birthday with his wife, Ann, by traveling Route 66.
"I said to her, 'I would love to go out west to Los Angeles and bring Highway 66 all the way back to where we live,'" he said. "So we did that. We took 31 days, stopped every place you can imagine on and off the highway. We had a great time, an absolutely great time talking to people and just seeing the sights."
On this day's visit, they are just a couple of hours away from their home in Quincy, Ill., and they've stopped for a last celebratory lunch on their big trip. The menu offers so many choices, from patty melts to turkey clubs to pork chops and stuffed shrimp. They said this restaurant, with its throwback vibes and sprawling menu, encapsulates the spirit of their whole road trip.
"It was really adventurous and old fashioned and very joyful," Ann Dickson said.
Opinions run hot about what exactly is the oldest eatery along Route 66, but the Ariston Cafe claims to be the oldest continually operating restaurant on the highway.
Nick Adam is one of the Ariston's former owners. His father, Pete, founded it as a candy shop in 1924. Adam says his father was very young when he arrived in this country.
"He left when he was 10 to come to the United States," Adam explained. "He went back to Greece when he was 12, and then he came back to this country."
Pete Adam seems to have had big ambitions even back then: The shop's name, Ariston, means "the best" in Greek. In 1935, he moved it to its present location on Route 66. Then Nick and his wife, Demi, ran the restaurant for decades.
From first dates to engagements, Demi Adam said the Ariston Cafe has been a fundamental part of this community for decades.
"To be honest," she said, "there's nothing else like this around."
Eight years ago, when the Adams were ready to retire, they sold the restaurant to Will Law and his partners. Law said the Ariston's position as a place locals and visitors alike choose for the big moments in their lives remains unchanged.
"I can't tell you how many wedding proposals have happened in those booths," he said. "We have a couple from Iowa that will come back every year for their anniversary just to have dinner. I see a 50th anniversary at least once a week, if not 60, 65. How cool is that? And they want to share that with you."
In 2006, the Ariston Cafe was put on the National Register of Historic Places. It's another lasting reminder of what this restaurant that steps back in time can mean to visitors in the present.

noticias.titulo: In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis
noticias.resumen: Steep discounts for "Green Wednesday," one of the highest-selling days for cannabis, help customers keep costs down. But experts say retailers are feeling the pinch.
noticias.texto:
In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis
This Thanksgiving season, Americans are paying more for almost everything: travel costs have soared, and the price of food has risen. Bringing wine to the family dinner? That costs more, too.
But there's one thing consumers buy at high rates that will actually get cheaper this time of year: marijuana.
Known in the industry as "Green Week" or "Green Wednesday," the days ahead of Thanksgiving have come to rival famed stoner holiday 4/20 as the day cannabis dispensaries see the most sales — and highest foot traffic — of the year.
In most dispensaries around the country, that means steep discounts, doorbuster specials and exclusive products. It's a good deal for customers, who line up in long queues as they await their turn with the so-called budtenders behind the counter.
Cannabis in the U.S. is a $30 billion industry with legal marketplaces in 24 states and the nation's capital, according to Whitney Economics, a firm that specializes in economic research and consulting on the business of cannabis. But in recent years, the deep discounts that have drawn in customers — and kept them coming back for weeks like this one — have squeezed retailers and resulted in a revenue decline in the legal market.
As the week began at The Forest, a dispensary in Baltimore, shoppers were stocking up for the holiday week.
A pack of gummies to bring to Friendsgiving in lieu of alcohol. A sparkling THC-infused beverage for those canna-curious in-laws. Or a holiday staple: some pre-rolls to share on an evening walk.
On bright screens posted around the store, discount offers flashed: 25% off edibles, read one; 30% off for medical patients, read another. An extra $5 off for bringing in cans of food for the store's holiday drive.
Kelley Vinton, 36, is a regular at The Forest. She's a medical marijuana user and usually sticks to a strict weekly budget, she said. But on Monday, she threw in a few little extras — for the "cousin walk," Vinton said.
"You know, you take a little breaky-poo with your cousins, and we live in the country, so we just walk, usually before dinner," Vinton said. "We smoke a joint, and we get nice and high, and get some munchies and get ready for dinner."
The federal government still classifies recreational marijuana as a Schedule I drug, meaning it is considered to have "high potential for abuse," according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. But medical cannabis was reclassified this year to Schedule III, a category shared by drugs like Tylenol with codeine and anabolic steroids.
In 2025, Whitney Economics found, revenue was down across the industry thanks to an oversupply of plant product and declining prices, driven by the discount culture of cannabis retailers.
It was the first year since 2014 — when Colorado and Washington became the first states to legalize cannabis sales for recreational use — that the industry saw a dip, according to an analysis by Whitney Economics.
"It's forced a race to the bottom," said Beau Whitney, the founder and chief economist at Whitney Economics. "What this is resulting in is great prices for the consumer, they're spending less and getting the same or more, so that's good for them on an affordability perspective. But it's hurting operators."
Though the industry has seen a slight rebound this year — an increase of about 5% in sales for the same period last year, Whitney's team found — forecasts for the end of 2026 and the outlook for 2027 remain relatively modest.
The biggest reason for this, Whitney said, is customer behavior.
Through the beginning of the 2020s, Whitney said, consumers would typically come into a dispensary with a set amount to spend. Their cannabis budget. If they got a discount, Whitney said, they'd add additional products into their carts to hit their budget.
But that began to change in 2024, as inflation rose and the cost of essentials, like gas, ballooned.
"Behavior changed literally overnight," Whitney said. "What they're doing is they're taking the discounts — and there's a lot of them now — and they're using that money to buy gas and buy groceries. So they're adjusting the amount that they purchase based on what's going on in their own personal economy."
The discount model, he said, has also forced prices down. With legal retailers competing for a pool of customers that has not seen rapid growth in years, discounts help draw people into stores. But they've also created a culture where customers expect them, several cannabis store owners said.
It's why doing well on a week like this one, as customers flood in for Green Wednesday deals, is essential for shop owners like The Forest's Christina Betancourt Johnson.
On Monday, the Baltimore store was stocked — with edibles and pre-rolls and other cannabis products, but also stacks of snacks for customers waiting in longer-than-usual lines, branded giveaways and samples of gummies to try (no weed in those).
A steady flow of customers wandered in. Some for their usual supplies, others for a little holiday shopping.
Employee Thomas Bourne loaded a vape into a paper bag for one of the dispensary's regular customers. That seemed a little light for the holiday, he observed, teasingly.
"Gotta come back for your cousin walk essentials, man," Bourne said. "'Tis the week."
The customer smiled, nodding. He'd be back.

noticias.titulo: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
noticias.resumen: The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
noticias.texto:
China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.
A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.
The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.
The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.
"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."
The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.
"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."
Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.
The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.
Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

noticias.titulo: Army detonates nearly five tons of lead-based explosives in Iowa
noticias.resumen: The controlled detonation of more than 60 barrels — roughly five tons — of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa is complete.
noticias.texto:
Army detonates nearly five tons of lead-based explosives in Iowa
The controlled detonation of more than 60 barrels — roughly five tons — of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa is complete.
The U.S. Army set off the huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa on Wednesday in a bid to dispose of the lead azide, an explosive the military has used since World War I.
"Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained. Our state agencies will continue monitoring efforts," Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe posted on X.
The initial detonation was scheduled last Friday, but was changed three times since due to lawsuits by environmental groups to block the detonation.
Some residents have voluntarily evacuated. FEMA has called on residents within the 20 miles southwest of the plant to stay indoors with windows closed to avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration.
According to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, children and those pregnant face the biggest danger from the explosion as there is no safe level of lead exposure whether it is airborne or accumulates as dust on surfaces.
The Army says the lead azide, which is used to ignite munitions, had been stored for decades at the Middletown plant. The crystals formed at some point in recent years inside the containers where they were stored. This change makes lead azide acutely sensitive to movement and changes in temperature.
At a press briefing on Tuesday administration officials said the possibility of a chemical treatment was ruled out. The munitions had degraded to the point where it was too dangerous to move them, or even open their containers without risk of an accidental detonation.
Iowa Public Radio compiled maps and information released by the U.S. Army on Tuesday, showing areas in southeast Iowa and northern Missouri may be affected by the planned explosion.
The Iowa National Guard has deployed 100 soldiers to support local efforts and federal agencies with community outreach to 150 households, according to a statement issued by Iowa's Governor Kim Reynolds.
Plans to detonate the unstable chemicals have rattled Iowans who were only told about the planned explosion at the plant last week.
Professor Andew Whelton at Purdue University, who has done environmental disaster planning, including for the U.S. Army told NPR that the timing "should have been planned better.""Because that didn't happen, because the messaging was just so poor, you had anxiety, you had stress, you had businesses planning to shut down," he said. "Some farmers have said 'we cannot bring all of our cattle. We do not have the facilities for that," Whelton added.
FEMA said they were reaching out directly to homes in the area most at risk to offer evacuation help. NPR's reporters called the FEMA hotline and were eventually told it would take several hours for a callback about evacuation help.
Trump administration officials say the detonation is the only safe way to dispose of the thousands of pounds of ordinance that was moved to a bunker in Iowa 17 years ago. In March, authorities determined that the substance had gotten too unstable to move, setting the Army and other agencies in a race for time to destroy the unstable chemicals at risk of explosion.
On Tuesday, the acting Army Secretary and leaders of FEMA and the ATF pushed back on the notion that this is a surprise. They pointed out they have been holding town-hall meetings, but they admitted that the timing of the explosion has been a moving target.
At first, the U.S. military says it was trying a non-explosive way to neutralize the materiel, then working to build berms and other counter-measures all while monitoring the weather conditions and the growing risk of an uncontrolled explosion.
Tom Croci, an official with the Environmental Protection Agency said the agencies focused on setting "the right parameters with the Army to make sure that a supervised controlled detonation was happening in the most optimal environment and at the most optimal timing.""So that was some of the back and forth to make sure that we had that right," he added.
Whelton of Purdue University said he was concerned about follow-through with the toxic sampling, and the clean up and remediation that disasters like this really need.
Whelton said the government does not have a great track record with the long term effects of toxic exposure, referencing examples like the chemical spill in East Palestine and the clean-up or the Los Angeles wild fires.
Two Iowa environmental groups sued to block the blast. President Donald Trump told the Army on Monday to wait for court approval and sign-off by Iowa Democrat Governor-elect Rob Sand, who Trump said he would blame if anything went wrong. However, a federal appeals court cleared the way for the blast Monday.

noticias.titulo: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. voluntarily for Spain
noticias.resumen: Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant who became a symbol of Trump's mass deportation campaign, voluntarily left the country on Tuesday after nearly two years of legal battles.
noticias.texto:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. voluntarily for Spain
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran immigrant who became a symbol of the pitfalls of President Trump's mass deportation campaign, has voluntarily left the U.S. after a legal battle that spanned nearly two years. He landed in Spain on Wednesday morning.
Abrego Garcia, who was arrested in 2025, mistakenly deported to El Salvador, and then brought back to the U.S., left for Spain on Tuesday, according to his lawyers and Trump administration officials.
He arrived on Wednesday morning in Madrid's international airport, Adolfo Suárez Madrid – Barajas Airport. There was no indication that he entered the country under any formal agreement with Spanish authorities.
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, said he "left the United States a free man."
"The government wanted to deport him in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia. Instead, he departed on a commercial aircraft, to a country that he chose, and able to move freely around the world," Sandoval-Moshenberg told NPR.
He called the move "a temporary departure" and said that Abrego Garcia, who has a wife and a child, both of whom are U.S. citizens, has many options to return to the U.S.
"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," he added.
Sandoval-Moshenberg said Abrego Garcia will choose where "to settle in the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration."
Another lawyer for Abrego Garcia, Sean Hecker, confirmed Spain as his destination.
U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who played a leading role in championing Abrego Garcia's case, released a statement saying he "is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man, unharmed and with dignity."
Trump administration hails Abrego Garcia's "self-deportation"
Abrego Garcia's case became a flashpoint for Trump's mass deportation campaign. It raised serious questions about due process, third-country deportations and to what extent this administration is sending people to countries where they may face threats.
Before Tuesday's move, Abrego Garcia and the Trump administration had been at an impasse about where he should go.
Abrego Garcia said he'd be willing to move to Costa Rica if the government allowed it. According to his attorneys, Costa Rica offered him refugee status. But the administration did not support that plan and instead sought to deport him to Liberia. That attempt was ultimately blocked by the courts.
The Trump administration hailed Abrego Garcia's departure late Tuesday.
"We are DELIGHTED to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Markwayne Mullin, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, wrote on X. He accused Abrego Garcia of being a gang member and a human trafficker, without evidence.
The legal battle
Abrego Garcia has been living in the U.S. for over a decade. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to his home country of El Salvador, after he made the argument that he would be tortured or persecuted there.
In 2025, immigration officers arrested Abrego Garcia and sent him to a notorious Salvadoran prison, where he claimed he suffered from beatings and sleep deprivation.
Later, immigration officials said that Abrego Garcia was deported by mistake, due to an administrative error. He was brought back to the U.S. in June 2025. Upon arriving in the U.S., he was charged with human smuggling. The allegations were based on bodycam footage from 2022, which showed Tennessee police pulling over Abrego Garcia with several other men inside his SUV. Prosecutors claim that Abrego Garcia was a human trafficker, helping immigrants move from Houston to Maryland. He denies the allegations, and his lawyers argue that the government's criminal case was retaliation after his wrongful deportation received national attention. A judge in the case ultimately dismissed the charges.

noticias.titulo: Video shows massive explosion as US Army destroys entire stockpile of lead azide
noticias.resumen: The US Army detonates around five tonnes of degraded lead azide at an ammunition plant in Iowa, destroying the country's entire stockpile of the explosive.
noticias.texto:
A massive explosion sent smoke into the sky as the US Army destroyed its entire stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
Around five tonnes of the degraded explosive, used in munition detonators, were detonated in a controlled blast. The operation raised concerns over potential health and environmental effects.
Officials said barriers, ballistic gels and foams were used to contain the blast and limit the spread of lead dust. Residents nearby had been advised to prepare for possible evacuation.

noticias.titulo: Commission wants to keep monitoring Montenegro after it joins the EU
noticias.resumen: The European Commission wants to keep monitoring Montenegro after it joins the EU, extending a new anti-backsliding tool in the draft accession treaty alongside a 10-year probation period, despite some member states questioning its added value.
noticias.texto:
The European Commission wants to keep monitoring Montenegro after it joins the EU, extending a new anti-backsliding tool in the draft accession treaty alongside a 10-year probation period, despite some member states questioning its added value.
The European Commission proposed extending a new tool, designed to prevent candidates from backsliding on their commitments as they prepare to join, so that it continues to apply even after Montenegro joins the EU.
Montenegro, the candidate furthest along on the road to membership, is the testing ground for tougher safeguards meant to avoid another Viktor Orbán, the Hungarian politician whose government has repeatedly clashed with Brussels over the rule of law.
Last week, member states broadly endorsed a draft position on the new safeguards drawn up by Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the EU Council. That cleared the way to begin work on Montenegro's accession treaty.
On that basis, the Commission tabled a first draft of the relevant treaty provisions, known as Chapter 35, which national representatives discussed on Tuesday. The text contains a significant novelty: a post-accession monitoring mechanism.
Under the original safeguards proposal, the Commission would monitor a country in the gap between the end of accession talks and its actual entry into the bloc. The aim is to stop newcomers from slowing down or reversing reforms once they have secured a political deal to close negotiations but are not yet members.
The Commission would check that the country is implementing and upholding all the commitments it made during the talks, report regularly to the European Parliament and the Council, and propose corrective action where necessary. As a last resort, it could even postpone the country's entry.
During the discussions, several member states favourable to stronger safeguards, such as Germany, France and the Netherlands, suggested extending this monitoring beyond accession. The Irish presidency left the idea out of its draft position but kept the question open.
Other countries, most notably members of the Friends of the Western Balkans group, questioned the added value, as EU member states are already scrutinised through instruments such as the rule of law reports and infringement proceedings.
They asked how the monitoring would work, which areas would need extra attention after accession and how to avoid duplicating existing tools.
The Commission, by contrast, considers it natural that the new safeguards come with monitoring of how they are applied. Still, it did not put forth such a mechanism in its original proposal.
"In light of the period during which certain safeguard clauses will remain available after accession, the EU considers that a provision on post-accession monitoring should also be included in the Accession Treaty," reads the draft text, seen by Euronews.
Particularly relevant is the so-called institutional safeguard. It would place a newcomer on a sort of probation, during which violations of EU values and rules would be swiftly addressed, including through the suspension of voting rights for the most serious offences.
The Commission's draft confirms the shortening of the probation period from 15 to 10 years, extendable by five more, as Ireland proposed. But it did not follow the Irish compromise on how the measure would be decided.
The original proposal relied on reverse qualified majority voting: a Commission proposal to trigger the safeguard would pass unless a qualified majority of member states voted against it.
The Friends of the Western Balkans pushed back, arguing this gives the Commission too much power. As a compromise, Ireland proposed ordinary qualified majority voting, under which countries would have to approve the trigger rather than block it.
The Commission, however, put reverse qualified majority voting back on the table. The Irish presidency will now take over the discussion on Chapter 35 to seek a compromise.
"I am not sure the Commission draft helped the discussion much," an EU diplomat told Euronews, asking to remain anonymous. "There is a risk that the member states will form trenches, but we need to proceed with Montenegro's accession treaty."

noticias.titulo: Unfinished Beginnings: 20,000 empty baby bottles honour children affected by conflict
noticias.resumen: The Unfinished Beginnings exhibition in Doha explores how conflict affects children who survive, from hunger and displacement to disrupted education, with artworks supporting a humanitarian cause.
noticias.texto:
The Unfinished Beginnings exhibition in Doha explores how conflict affects children who survive, from hunger and displacement to disrupted education, with artworks supporting a humanitarian cause.
20,000 empty glass baby bottles fill an exhibition space in Doha, symbolising the impact of war, hunger and displacement on children around the world.
The installation, titled Unfinished Beginnings, was created by artist Bachir Mohamad and is on display at Bin Jelmood House, part of the city's Msheireb Museums.
"The messaging behind the bottle, and especially it's an empty bottle, because it needs to be filled," Mohamad told Euronews.
"It needs to be filled with love. It needs to be filled with food. It needs to be filled with education. It needs to be filled with healthcare and more."
From Gaza to children affected by conflict worldwide
The exhibition follows Mohamad's 2024 installation, Echo of Lost Innocence, which focused on children killed in Gaza.
This time, the focus is on children who survive war but continue to face its consequences, including hunger, displacement and limited access to education and healthcare.
An estimated 520 million children worldwide lived in areas affected by armed conflict in 2024, according to figures cited by the exhibition's organisers.
The UN Secretary-General's latest annual report on Children and Armed Conflict documented 38,558 verified grave violations against children in 2025, affecting more than 24,000 children.
Mohamad said the installation aims to make the scale of the crisis easier for visitors to understand.
"Statistics and news will give you numbers on papers or through your mobile, for example, or through your TV. Art can show you these numbers. And this is what we're doing over here."
A museum connecting history with the present
Bin Jelmood House explores the history of slavery and modern forms of human exploitation, providing a setting for an exhibition examining the impact of conflict on children.
For Abdulla Al Naama, General Manager of Msheireb Museums, the exhibition reflects the role cultural institutions can play in addressing contemporary issues.
"Cultural institutions should not be only places that talk about history, but also places that interact with the world today with very important role in raising awareness and educating the general public of current issues," he told Euronews.
The exhibition is part of a wider initiative organised by Msheireb Museums and Qatar Charity, with support from UNESCO and the United Nations Office of the Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict.
Messages of hope from children in Qatar
At the centre of the installation are more than 200 origami doves made by schoolchildren in Qatar.
Each carries a message to world leaders calling for peace, offering a contrast to the thousands of empty bottles surrounding them.
The programme also includes school visits, workshops and discussions.
Visitors can purchase individual bottles to support the initiative.
For Al Naama, the exhibition's central message is that "no child should inherit war."
Unfinished Beginnings runs until 10 December, International Human Rights Day. Admission is free.

noticias.titulo: EU seeks 'fuller picture' of Ireland's alumina sales to Russia as doubts remain
noticias.resumen: Amid lingering suspicion, Brussels wants to get a "fuller picture" of Irish-made alumina sales to Russia through a new reporting mechanism.
noticias.texto:
Amid lingering suspicion, Brussels wants to get a "fuller picture" of Irish-made alumina sales to Russia through a new reporting mechanism.
The European Union is seeking additional clarity on sales of Irish-made alumina to Russia, as suspicion remains about their possible link with Moscow's war machine.
Traded as a white powder, alumina is the raw material used to make aluminium, a lightweight metal often found on the battlefield in Ukraine.
Despite public pressure from Kyiv and the Baltic countries, Brussels did not include an export ban on alumina in the 22nd sanctions package, still under negotiation.
Instead, the European Commission has proposed a reporting mechanism to improve surveillance on alumina shipments bound to Russia.
"The idea of the mechanism is that we get a fuller picture of what the trade flows are," Siobhan McGarry, the Commission's sanctions spokesperson, said on Wednesday in response to a question from Euronews. "It's not clear to us."
The mechanism will compel member states to report every three months on the amount, value, transport method, date and place of loading and discharge, contract type, importer and, crucially, final destination of alumina sold to Russia.
When asked whether the Commission reserved the right to sanction these exports if the trade data raised alarm, McGarry urged caution.
"The purpose of this reporting mechanism is to identify just that: where is this alumina ending up? And then we will look at what further measures we may or may not need to take," she said.
"We're not quite there yet."
The issue came to prominence earlier this year after a media consortium published an investigation tracing the links between Aughinish Alumina, a sprawling refinery in western Ireland, and Russia's military complex.
It detailed how Irish-made alumina is being sent to Russian smelters owned by the plant's parent company, United Company Rusal, which in turn sells the metal to a trader that supplies aluminium to sanctioned defence manufacturers.
The weapons churned out by these manufacturers have been deployed to kill Ukrainian civilians and bombard civilian infrastructure, the investigation said.
Separately, Swedish authorities concluded that Rusal remained under the effective control of Oleg Deripaska, a sanctioned Russian oligarch with close ties to the Kremlin.
The revelations triggered a scandal in Ireland, just as the country was prepared to take over the EU Council's six-month presidency.
Ukraine's top leadership asked Dublin to cease alumina sales to Russia immediately. The Irish government warned that sanctions could decimate hundreds of local jobs and disrupt a strategic supply chain for Europe. As the public outcry continued, Dublin launched a probe to corroborate the media claims.
The probe ended up in a grey area: it found "no evidence" to either confirm or refute the relation between Irish-made alumina and Russian weapons. The inconclusive findings were then passed on to Brussels "for its consideration".
At the same time, Aughinish said it had taken the allegations with "the utmost seriousness" and promised to establish a new framework of "independent, third-party verification" to enhance surveillance of alumina flows into Russian smelters.
Still, doubts continued to linger.
On Wednesday, the Commission made it clear that further answers were needed.
"One thing that was clear from what we saw over the summer when it came to Aughinish is that no one had the complete picture. And so this is an opportunity for member states and for the Commission to see what's taking place here," McGarry said.
"Alumina is a critical raw material, and we do have industries in Europe that rely on alumina, so we need to see whether we have the right balance."
In a statement, Ireland's Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment said it was "aware" of the reporting mechanism but declined to comment until final adoption.
"As Presidency, we stand ready to work with the Commission and all member states to secure the adoption of an ambitious package," a spokesperson said.
Aughinish did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
On Tuesday, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner, told Euronews he was "disappointed" that an export ban on alumina had not been proposed, calling the decision a "clear example" of political interests obstructing a "rightful measure".
Brussels aims to adopt the new sanctions before the winter break.

noticias.titulo: Australia follows EU with new online safety law, putting Big Tech at risk of multibillion-dollar fines
noticias.resumen: Australia's Digital Duty of Care Act is the latest global effort to regulate technology platforms, following in the footsteps of the EU's watershed digital legislation.
noticias.texto:
Australia's Digital Duty of Care Act is the latest global effort to regulate technology platforms, following in the footsteps of the EU's watershed digital legislation.
Australia’s parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines, in line with the European Union’s landmark digital regulations.
The Digital Duty of Care Act requires Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement. The legislation became law in the House of Representatives, where the center-left Labour Party government commands a majority, by 97 votes to 43.
The law would stand as a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment,” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Australia’s parliament.
Australian online law falls in line with EU, British legislation
The legislation is similar to the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA), passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act passed a year later.
The DSA is part of a raft of European regulations, including the Digital Markets Act and the AI Act, which seek to make the online world safer, fairer and more transparent.
Earlier this month, the European Commission unveiled its proposed Digital Fairness Act, setting out new rules to tackle manipulative online practices, improve price transparency and strengthen protections for children.
Opposition leader vows to repeal ‘authoritarian’ law
Australian opposition leader Angus Taylor told the country’s parliament that he would repeal the legislation if his conservative Liberal Party wins elections in 2028, describing the law as “authoritarian.”
“This bill is a blank check for political censorship,” Taylor said. “The bill is an attack on free speech that is absolutely central to our democracy."
The government struck a deal with the minor Greens party on Tuesday to push the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.
The Australian legislation sets minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

noticias.titulo: Captain of sunken Costa Concordia hired by tourism agency in Sorrento
noticias.resumen: The former captain Francesco Schettino was sentenced to 16 years and one month in prison after the sinking of the Costa Concordia in 2012
noticias.texto:
The former captain Francesco Schettino was sentenced to 16 years and one month in prison after the sinking of the Costa Concordia in 2012
The former captain of the Costa Concordia, the cruise ship that ran aground and then sank off the coast of Italy in 2012, has a new job in the tourism industry.
Italian media report that Francesco Schettino, who's now 66, is due to work for an agency providing consultancy and management services for holiday apartments, B&Bs and other accommodation on the Sorrento peninsula. He has reportedly been given a permanent contract.
Schettino was widely labelled a "coward" in the press after leaving the ship while passengers were still being evacuated. 32 people died in the disaster.
He was sentenced to 16 years and one month in prison over the sinking, including for manslaughter and abandoning the ship.
After spending more than nine years in prison, Schettino has now been allowed to serve the remainder of his sentence outside jail under the supervision of social services. He is not yet completely free, and his sentence is due to end in July 2030.
According to Italian media reports, Schettino has returned to his home town of Meta di Sorrento.
However, his early release is tied to strict rules. In addition to his eight-hour working day at the agency, Italian media reports that Schettino must perform four hours of community service every week as a probation condition.
Schettino is reported to have told his lawyer Francesca Carnicelli: "I can hardly wait to get started."
After leaving prison Schettino initially spent a lot of time with his family. Mayor Giuseppe Tito, a long-time friend of the former captain, told the newspaper about a phone call between them: "His voice was tired. He suffers from the constant attention of the media, but he is calm."
The Costa Concordia disaster happened on 13 January 2012, when the cruise ship, carrying more than 4,200 passengers and crew, struck rocks off the island of Giglio.
Investigators found that Schettino had taken the vessel too close to the coast during a manoeuvre intended as a "salute" to people on the island. Thirty-two people were killed.

noticias.titulo: US proposes new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, the EU included
noticias.resumen: The proposed tariffs would apply to some goods from China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. Mexico and Norway were also investigated but are outside the proposal for now.
noticias.texto:
The proposed tariffs would apply to some goods from China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. Mexico and Norway were also investigated but are outside the proposal for now.
US President Donald Trump's administration has proposed new tariffs on some goods from 14 major trading partners to curb what it says is excess factory output fuelled by subsidies and other trade barriers that put US manufacturers at a disadvantage.
The proposed duties follow an eight-month Section 301 investigation by the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) targeting excess capacity in 16 trading partners. The USTR found that practices in 14 of those economies were unreasonable and harmed or restricted US commerce.
The proposal covers China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. Mexico and Norway were also investigated. The USTR has yet to issue findings on either.
The duties would also help replace revenue lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that the emergency powers law Trump had invoked did not authorise him to impose his earlier tariffs.
Public comments are due by 5 January 2027, and hearings are set to begin on 25 January. The USTR gave no date for the duties to take effect.
The White House announced plans to impose 15% tariffs on EU goods on top of existing most-favoured-nation (MFN) duties, with exemptions for some products. Its draft notice also sets out an option of up to 20% if it finds that ongoing talks and existing commitments are "unsatisfactory".
The draft notice exempts some EU goods already subject to US tariffs under Section 232, including cars and certain car parts, steel, aluminium, patented medicines and semiconductors.
European Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill said on Wednesday that the EU “takes note” of the preliminary finding of the investigation, but added: “We strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity.”
China faces the highest proposed rate
The Trump administration says low-priced imports from these trading partners undercut American companies and have contributed to the US goods trade deficit, which reached $1.24 trillion (€1.13tn) in 2025.
The proposed tariffs are based on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the US to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable or discriminatory foreign practices that burden or restrict US commerce.
A US administration official said the proposed duties would be consistent with the trade deals Trump reached last year.
The USTR proposes tariffs of up to 20% on many Chinese goods. Any tariff already charged under Section 301 over forced labour would be deducted from that rate. It proposes tariffs of up to 10% on some products and would exempt others. If talks with Beijing fail to resolve the US concerns, the USTR could consider a rate of up to 40% on all Chinese goods. The same deduction would apply.
An official said to AP that the tariffs were unlikely to undermine the US-China trade truce, which is due to expire on 10 January.
China's foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun rejected Washington's accusations of overcapacity and called for talks on Wednesday. "Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone's interest," he said.
Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China's purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.
In a separate Section 301 action, USTR said it was proposing new duties after talks with Brazil failed to make meaningful progress.
The US is proposing higher import taxes for certain out-of-quota raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on finished Brazilian aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker. USTR said the broader increase in out-of-quota sugar duties would also apply to imports from other countries.
The wider US proposal also covers Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. Investigations into Mexico and Norway are still pending, and both countries are excluded from the proposal for now.
The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

noticias.titulo: EU member states take 'egoistic approaches' regarding fossil fuel imports, says expert
noticias.resumen: Szymon Kardaś, Energy expert for the European Council of Foreign Relations, says at EU level there is no "clear targets regarding fossil fuels phase out, neither indicative nor legally binding".
noticias.texto:
Szymon Kardaś, an energy expert at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), says the EU lacks “clear targets for phasing out fossil fuels”, whether indicative or legally binding.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
He argues that stronger energy cooperation is essential if the European Union is to become fossil fuel-free, warning that member states tend to act “individually” and “egoistically” when addressing immediate challenges.
Kardaś calls for “more coordination” and a “collective approach” to accelerate the phase-out of fossil fuels across the bloc.

noticias.titulo: Russian strikes kill seven in Ukraine as Kyiv hits three refineries
noticias.resumen: Russia's drone attack killed people in six Ukrainian regions and hit a Naftogaz gas production facility, a DTEK thermal power plant and power networks in several parts of the country. Ukrainian drones struck Russian refineries in Samara and Rostov regions and an airbase in Nizhny Novgorod region.
noticias.texto:
Russia's drone attack killed people in six Ukrainian regions and hit a Naftogaz gas production facility, a DTEK thermal power plant and power networks in several parts of the country. Ukrainian drones struck Russian refineries in Samara and Rostov regions and an airbase in Nizhny Novgorod region.
Russia launched scores of drones at energy and civilian targets across Ukraine overnight on Wednesday, killing at least seven people in six regions, authorities said.
The attack involved 112 Shahed, Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, of which 88 were shot down or neutralised, Ukraine's air force said.
One person was killed in Bila Tserkva in Kyiv region, where the strike damaged critical infrastructure, an Epicentr shopping centre and a Nova Poshta postal branch, local authorities said.
One person was killed and seven injured in Kharkiv region after a strike hit a minibus on a highway, regional governor Oleh Synehubov said. Two people aged 76 and 69 were killed and another wounded in Sumy region.
Two people were killed in Odesa region on Tuesday evening — a 41-year-old and a 17-year-old — and one person was killed and three wounded in Zhytomyr region. Casualties were also reported in Chernihiv and Donetsk regions.
Russian forces struck a Naftogaz gas production facility in the Poltava region, the acting head of the company Serhiy Fedorenko said.
A fire broke out and the facility suspended operations. "This is not the first such attack and, unfortunately, not the last," Fedorenko said, adding that Russia was deliberately targeting gas production "to deprive Ukrainians of heat in winter."
Energy facilities in the Dnipropetrovsk region were also hit, triggering emergency power cuts across several districts.
A significant number of consumers lost power in Zaporizhzhia region, Zaporizhzhyaoblenergo head Andriy Stasevskyi said. More than 9,000 customers were left without electricity in Odesa region following Tuesday evening's attacks, regional governor Oleh Kiper said.
The energy company DTEK reported a large-scale strike on one of its thermal power plants, causing serious damage and forcing it to stop generating electricity. DTEK did not specify the location, noting it was the third large-scale strike on its plants in November.
Ukraine strikes Russian refineries and airbase
Ukrainian drones simultaneously struck three Russian oil refineries overnight, hitting plants in Samara and Rostov regions, according to Ukrainian monitoring sources.
Two refineries in Samara region — the Kuibyshev and Syzran plants, both part of Rosneft — were struck, with fires breaking out at both facilities.
Regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed the attack but did not name the facilities, saying one person was killed, power had been cut in several districts and a number of schools would operate on an adjusted schedule.
Regional authorities said 145 drones were shot down over the Samara region. Euronews could not independently verify these claims.
The Syzran refinery has a processing capacity of 8.5 million tonnes of oil per year and produces petrol, diesel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil and bitumen.
The Kuibyshev refinery has a primary processing capacity of 8.8 million tonnes per year. Ukraine last struck the Syzran plant on 15 September. The Kuibyshev refinery was also struck that month.
The third refinery struck overnight was the Novoshakhtinsk plant in Rostov region. Regional governor Yuri Slyusar confirmed the attack, saying a combined strike of more than 50 drones and missiles lasted six hours before the plant suspended operations.
Russian oil refining volumes have fallen by an estimated 45% since late October, according to analysts.
Ukraine's General Staff also reported overnight strikes on the Savasleyka airbase in Nizhny Novgorod region, which it described as one of Russia's key aviation facilities and the base from which aircraft carrying Kinzhal missiles launch strikes on Ukrainian cities.
According to Kyiv's military, three MiG-31 and two Su-34 aircraft were damaged and would be unable to fly "for some time".
Ukraine destroyed a span of the road section of the Crimean Bridge last week, halting car traffic, though train services have been restored.
