Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike was a response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, describing deep strikes inside Russia as "long-range sanctions".
Ukraine attacked the bulk carrier Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, claiming it transported military cargo. The following day it struck the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi. Zelenskyy confirmed the warship had been sunk.
On Tuesday, Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened Ukraine with retaliation for its strikes on refineries and complained that Kyiv had not heeded calls from US President Donald Trump to halt attacks on oil processing facilities.
Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was prepared to stop striking Russian refineries only if Moscow halted its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

noticias.titulo: EU-backed scheme brings renovation costs ‘close to zero’ for vulnerable Lithuanian households
noticias.resumen: Lithuania's Social Climate Fund will renovate more than 40,000 homes to make them warmer in winter and less reliant on fossil fuels, targeting low-income households and those who rely on fossil fuels.
noticias.texto:
Lithuania's Social Climate Fund will renovate more than 40,000 homes to make them warmer in winter and less reliant on fossil fuels, targeting low-income households and those who rely on fossil fuels.
"Renovation is essential for us, because when the cold weather sets in, in winter, it gets extremely cold," says Dalia Uselienė, Chairwoman of a Homeowners Association in Ukmergė. She lives in a late 1960s apartment block where the most exposed wall can get frosty on the inside in winter.
Lithuania's Social Climate Plan will accelerate the country's ongoing renovation initiatives, meaning that over 40,000 homes, including over 7,000 apartment blocks, will be partially or fully renovated by 2032. There is an acute need to reduce bills and cut fossil fuel use in the Baltic country, which has been hit hard by rising energy prices. Around 17% of Lithuanians say they cannot keep their homes adequately warm, and 67% of residential buildings are energy performance class D or below.
The country's Social Climate Plan is worth 884.2 million euros, including 662.9 million euros from the EU's Social Climate Fund, which is financed by revenues from emissions trading. Vakaris Atkočiūnas, Senior Adviser on Climate Finance at the Lithuanian Ministry of Environment, says it will cover between 50 and 85 percent of costs for vulnerable residents, so, "renovation costs for vulnerable households will be close to zero."

noticias.titulo: This country is building a city for robots, air taxis and digital investment
noticias.resumen: Kazakhstan is developing Alatau City as a digital finance and investment hub along the Europe–China trade corridor. It aims to foster a low-altitude economy and make tokenisation standard practice, allowing investors to trade digital tokens representing property, infrastructure and businesses.
noticias.texto:
Kazakhstan is developing Alatau City as a digital finance and investment hub along the Europe–China trade corridor. It aims to foster a low-altitude economy and make tokenisation standard practice, allowing investors to trade digital tokens representing property, infrastructure and businesses.
Over the past seven years, Kazakhstan has attracted more than €140 billion in foreign investment. Now, the government wants to integrate tokenised investment into the economy, opening up new ways to attract capital beyond traditional channels.
The goal is to create a unified digital finance ecosystem. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev envisions Alatau City developing its tokenised economy in close partnership with KASE, Kazakhstan’s stock exchange, and the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC).
The Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development sees tokenisation as one of the tools that could help attract investment quickly and conveniently.
“When we create a platform for tokenisation, anyone from any country will be able to register, complete the onboarding process, undergo KYC checks and so on,” said Nodirbek Nozirkulov, Deputy Chairman of the Committee for Digital Assets and Breakthrough Technologies.
Investors could acquire tokens representing a share of a property's value or an interest in an asset. Tokenisation can divide high-value assets, such as real estate and large business projects, into smaller digital units, potentially making them accessible to a wider pool of investors.
Blockchain-based tokens can be traded digitally, potentially across borders, without some of the traditional intermediaries involved in investment transactions. This could open up new opportunities for retail investors, although the extent of access, costs and liquidity will depend on how the system is regulated and operates in practice.
Investor confidence
As a presidential initiative, Alatau City is considered a project of national strategic importance, with state support enshrined in legislation.
In May 2026, Kazakhstan adopted a constitutional law establishing the city's Special Legal Regime. It provides for stable tax conditions for ten years, investment incentives and legal mechanisms intended to protect investors' capital.
Tokayev has also called for the creation of an Investment Court based on the principles of English common law to handle commercial disputes. The government is due to submit amendments to the constitutional law by the end of January 2027.
“The investment interests of all reputable and honest entrepreneurs are guaranteed the strongest and most reliable legal protection: the Constitution,” Tokayev said during his October state-of-the-nation address.
A new finance centre on the Middle Corridor
Authorities are positioning Alatau as a digital finance and investment hub along the Middle Corridor, where transit volumes increased by 22% in the first eight months of the year.
Located near Almaty, Alatau is intended to benefit from the region's established transport and logistics links.
By 2040, the city plans to have three million square metres of high-grade warehouses, alongside duty-free storage facilities.
Tokayev has called on companies to “set up their engineering and service units, find local partners and implement their investment projects in Alatau”.
A city designed for passenger air taxis and robots
Designed to accommodate drones and robots, Alatau is intended to serve as a testing ground for the low-altitude economy, allowing companies to develop and test emerging technologies.
“The city’s master plan contains red lines for air corridors, vertiports, and drone ports, so this infrastructure is built into the city from day one,” said Alisher Abdykadyrov, Chief Executive Officer of Alatau City Authority.
He added that companies developing these technologies often find it difficult to integrate them into existing cities, which were not designed to accommodate them.
In May 2026, Alatau hosted demonstration flights of a passenger air taxi, in what could be an early step towards developing the region’s urban air mobility industry. The electric aircraft, designed to carry one pilot and five passengers, is being developed by a private group of companies with local and international participation.
“Our goal is not merely to import technology, but to build a fully-fledged industry: infrastructure, engineering expertise and new jobs for Kazakhstan professionals,” said Sergey Khegay, founder and CEO.
Delivery drones have also been demonstrated in the city. According to a multinational investment bank, the global urban air mobility market could be worth up to €1.3 trillion by 2040.
What is happening on the ground?
Alatau is not being built on an empty site. Officially established by a presidential decree in January 2024, the city will incorporate existing settlements located roughly 47 kilometres north of Almaty.
Several industrial zones are already operating within its territory. By July 2027, businesses based there are expected to become part of Alatau's new economic and regulatory system. Authorities say their existing operating conditions will be maintained.
International companies are already active in the area, while industrial and logistics projects are under way. Twenty-six infrastructure projects, worth around €70 million in total, are being implemented this year.
In October, construction began on a multifunctional complex in the city's business district. The development will comprise two towers housing offices, a hotel, retail outlets and public spaces.
Attracting investment
Alatau's portfolio includes 67 projects across sectors ranging from energy and pharmaceuticals to logistics and digital infrastructure, with a target investment of around €6.2 billion. Plans also include a Korean university campus.
The city aims to reach a population of two million by 2050. Using China's Shenzhen as a benchmark, its development is expected to require up to €90 billion in infrastructure investment, including just over €4 billion over the next three years.
Alatau is also seeking to attract investors through international roadshows. During its European roadshow in Berlin, Frankfurt and London, 27 documents were signed, with a combined investment potential of nearly €2 billion.
The parties explored projects in infrastructure, industrial production, education, healthcare and the introduction of tokenisation mechanisms.
“The most important thing about this roadshow is not the immediate results. The fact that we have basic agreements and preliminary understandings could increase the figure for future investment three to five times,” said Kanat Bozumbayev, Deputy Prime Minister of Kazakhstan.
Smart city, energy and data centres
Alatau's master plan places artificial intelligence and digital technologies at the centre of its development.
Authorities say this could create opportunities for companies to introduce new solutions and change how businesses, residents and municipal services interact.
High-speed 5G connectivity is expected to link different elements of the city's smart infrastructure. These include smart electricity meters, automated homes, intelligent transport systems and smart parking, as well as surveillance and waste-management systems.
Between 30% and 40% of treated wastewater is expected to be reused for irrigating green spaces and industrial purposes, helping to reduce pressure on water resources.
The city is located on the shores of the Kapchagay Reservoir, and its plans include incorporating several surface water bodies into its districts.
Alatau's electricity supply is expected to include a 250-megawatt gas-fired power plant, with the possibility of introducing hydrogen technologies in the future. A 100-megawatt solar power plant is also planned, alongside grid infrastructure that includes two 220/110-kilovolt substations.
The master plan also envisages data centres, although “solely for the city’s own needs”, said Alisher Abdykadyrov, CEO of Alatau City Authority. They are expected to require 50 megawatts of electrical capacity by 2040.
For Kazakhstan, Alatau represents an effort to bring digital finance, logistics and emerging technologies together in one city. The ambition is to turn it into a new hub for international trade and investment.

noticias.titulo: Christmas decorations found in washed up container from ship hit by drones off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast
noticias.resumen: More than 80 boxes containing Christmas ornaments and decorations were found, with an estimated value of €50,000.
noticias.texto:
More than 80 boxes containing Christmas ornaments and decorations were found, with an estimated value of €50,000.
The shipping container that washed ashore near Tsarevo, on Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, on 2 November has been opened.
The operation was carried out with the authorisation of the Military Prosecutor's Office in Sofia and in the presence of investigative authorities and customs officials.
More than 80 boxes containing Christmas ornaments and decorations were found, with an estimated total value of €50,000.
"We are currently conducting an inspection of the container's contents," said Atanas Yankov, a member of the military police.
The goods belong to a Romanian company. "The merchant who placed the order will subsequently arrange for the shipment to be transported to Romania," Yankov added.
"There is nothing hazardous here, and I want to put everyone's minds at ease. This is simply a commercial shipment that, unfortunately, was caught up in military action," said Diko Dikov, regional governor of Burgas.
Nine ships struck in 24 days off Bulgaria and Romania
The container is believed to have been part of the cargo aboard the container ship Contship Jet, which sank off the coast of Shabla following an attack by naval drones.
A string of such incidents off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria this month has led some alliance members to wonder if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking to test their support for Ukraine in its fight against Moscow's full-scale invasion.
Russia has not taken responsibility for the recent attacks, but suspicion has fallen on Moscow.
Last week, a Liberian-flagged gas tanker sank in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, according to the Defence Ministry, the latest in the series of incidents affecting shipping there.
Over 24 days in October, nine cargo ships and tankers were struck by aerial or naval drones near the Bulgarian and Romanian coast

noticias.titulo: Badly welded rail and sinking ground likely caused deadly Spanish train crash, experts say
noticias.resumen: A track defect flagged three months before the derailment may never have been followed up, a preliminary report finds, though key tests are still outstanding.
noticias.texto:
A track defect flagged three months before the derailment may never have been followed up, a preliminary report finds, though key tests are still outstanding.
Court-appointed experts investigating the 18 January rail accident in Adamuz, Córdoba, Spain, in which 46 people were killed and more than 150 injured, point to a poorly executed weld and subsidence of the ground as the most likely causes of the disaster.
In a preliminary expert report dated 20 November, the three engineers tasked with establishing the cause of the accident state that a 6.4-millimetre irregularity, detected in October 2025, may have contributed to the fracture of the rail that caused the Iryo train to derail and then collide with a Renfe Alvia. The experts warn, however, that outstanding tests could still alter their conclusions.
A faulty weld and a track irregularity detected months earlier
According to the experts, the sinking of one of the rails may have generated overloads on the opposite rail as trains continuously passed over it, progressively weakening the weld until it broke. The engineers call this phenomenon the 'seesaw effect'.
The irregularity did not require trains to reduce speed, but it did call for closer monitoring and maintenance work. The experts say they have no evidence that such follow-up was carried out.
The weld under investigation joined a rail manufactured in 1989 to another from 2023, installed during upgrade works on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line in 2025. The two rails differed in properties and hardness, although this type of joint is covered by Adif's technical standards.
The investigators have also found inconsistencies in the welding records and are examining whether the quality checks carried out during the works were sufficient.
Ten months of investigation and tests still outstanding
The examining magistrate in Montoro, Cristina Pastor, has asked the Judicial Police in Córdoba to look for alternative laboratories after the Centre for Public Works Studies and Experimentation (CEDEX) reported that it did not have the means to carry out certain tests on the concrete sleepers.
Ten months after the accident, the investigators are still awaiting the analysis of the rails, welds, ballast and sleepers recovered from the scene. These tests will be crucial to determine how the fracture originated and to establish any potential responsibility.

noticias.titulo: Montenegro will become EU’s next member by 2028, says President
noticias.resumen: Montenegro’s President says his country is “very much on track” to become the European Union’s 28th member in 2028.
noticias.texto:
Montenegro’s President says his country is “very much on track” to become the European Union’s 28th member in 2028.
Speaking to Euronews ahead of the EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels, Jakov Milatović said he hoped to wrap up talks by the end of this year and sign an accession treaty by next summer. Montenegro has provisionally closed 25 of its 33 negotiating chapters, and any treaty would need to be ratified by all 27 EU members.
Croatia, an EU member state, wants Montenegro to settle a long-running border dispute before letting it join the bloc. Ever since the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, the two countries have argued over the Prevlaka Peninsula - a small, strategically significant strip of land controlling entry to the Bay of Kotor. Milatović said the two governments were working towards a deal, and suggested taking the matter to an international court if the countries could not reach an agreement. He also highlighted progress on judicial independence and cracking down on organised crime.
Milatović said Montenegro’s membership would send a “positive signal” to other countries waiting to join the bloc, and show that the EU could keep its promises. He said Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine had made enlargement a matter of European security. Asked what would happen if Montenegro missed its 2028 goal, he said: "If Montenegro fails here, it’s going to be the failure of the EU as well."

noticias.titulo: Haftar visits Ankara as Erdoğan prepares first Libya trip in 15 years
noticias.resumen: Eastern Libya's commander, accompanied by his son Saddam, met Turkey's defence and foreign ministers and its intelligence chief, days after Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian warship Merkury at Benghazi's naval base.
noticias.texto:
Eastern Libya's commander, accompanied by his son Saddam, met Turkey's defence and foreign ministers and its intelligence chief, days after Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian warship Merkury at Benghazi's naval base.
Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army (LNA) controlling eastern Libya, arrived in Ankara on Tuesday, meeting senior officials days after Ukrainian naval drones sank a Russian warship at Benghazi's naval base.
Haftar and his delegation, which included his son Saddam Haftar, met Defence Minister Yaşar Güler and Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, Foreign Ministry footage showed Haftar meeting Fidan again alongside Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar, National Intelligence Organisation (MIT) chief İbrahim Kalın and military officials.
Turkey's Chief of General Staff Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu received Haftar on arrival, LNA footage showed.
No official statement on the content of the talks had been issued as of Wednesday. No meeting between President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Haftar appeared on the presidency's official schedule.
Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian warship Merkury at Benghazi's naval base on Saturday in an operation Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed, praising it as exemplary. A cargo vessel was also damaged in the strike.
The internationally-recognised Tripoli-based government requested an explanation from Ukraine, while eastern Libyan authorities called for an international investigation into what they described as a Ukrainian military presence in the country.
Haftar's Russian connection
Russia has backed Haftar since at least 2019, when Wagner Group mercenaries supported the LNA's offensive on Tripoli.
Wagner has since been reconstituted as Africa Corps, which maintains logistics bases in southern and eastern Libya and has announced plans for a naval facility in Tobruk.
Moscow sees eastern Libya as a bridgehead for its operations across the Sahel and as a potential foothold in the southern Mediterranean, particularly after the fall of Russia's ally Bashar al-Assad in Syria.
Libya has been politically divided since Gaddafi's overthrow in 2011 and the resumption of fighting in 2014.
The Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, controls the west, while a rival administration backed by Haftar operates in the east.
Turkey is one of the few countries that maintains active relations with both sides. Between 2019 and 2020 Ankara backed the western government with military support that played a critical role in repelling an LNA offensive on Tripoli.
Relations with the Haftar camp have since improved steadily, with Turkish officials making regular visits to Benghazi and Turkish companies investing in the region, primarily in construction.
In October, the eastern-based House of Representatives endorsed the 2019 memorandum on maritime jurisdiction areas signed between Ankara and the former Tripoli-based Government of National Accord — an agreement that drew sharp reactions from Greece, Cyprus and the EU.
Diplomatic contacts have intensified ahead of the December summit. Fidan and MIT chief Kalın met Prime Minister Dbeibah in Istanbul on 21 November.
Turkey also hosted Khalid Haftar, LNA chief of staff, earlier in November, and in October military representatives from eastern and western Libya held talks in Ankara to unify the country's armed forces.
Saddam Haftar, considered a possible successor to his father, separately announced on social media that he had visited Qatar, which also plays a mediating role in international disputes.
Erdoğan's first visit to Libya in 15 years
Haftar's Ankara visit comes ahead of Erdoğan's planned trip to Tripoli on 8-9 December for the Turkey-Africa Partnership Summit, expected to be his first visit to Libya in 15 years.
Erdoğan last visited Libya on 16 September 2011, when he was Turkey's prime minister and late leader Muammar Gaddafi had just been overthrown.
Travelling to Tripoli and Benghazi, he met Mustafa Abdul Jalil, then head of the National Transitional Council, and Executive Board chairman Mahmoud Jibril, and signed cooperation agreements between the two countries.
Foreign Minister Fidan confirmed the December trip, saying its importance extends beyond the summit itself. Erdoğan is expected to meet representatives of both eastern and western Libyan authorities during the visit.

noticias.titulo: Europe is embracing digital health, but do patients actually benefit?
noticias.resumen: Europe is investing heavily in digital health infrastructure, but there is a gap between making tools available and improving patient care, according to a new report.
noticias.texto:
Europe is investing heavily in digital health infrastructure, but there is a gap between making tools available and improving patient care, according to a new report.
From AI-powered diagnoses to medical records in the cloud, European countries are increasingly investing in digital tools for healthcare. But how accessible are these services to patients, and are they actually improving medical care?
According to a new report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the European Commission, uptake of electronic health records (EHRs), digital services and data infrastructure have expanded due to public investment and binding EU rules. However, implementation varies widely across countries.
“Everybody's talking about AI, everybody is talking about the digitalisation in health. But let me say to you, it's not reaching all,” said Sandra Gallina, director general at the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety (DG SANTE) at the European Commission.
“We have come a long way, but there is plenty more to do,” Gallina said at the report’s presentation, adding that progress in medical technologies is too slow to reach those who need them most.
The report identified what it calls the “digital health implementation gap,” the difference between making services technically available and ensuring patients use them routinely and equitably.
Billions invested, but is service improving?
The EU is investing billions of euros in digital health tools and services, including at least €16 billion for healthcare digitalisation through cohesion and resilience funding programmes.
Meanwhile, targeted calls under the Digital Europe Programme in 2026 allocated an additional €9 million for artificial intelligence-powered image screening and €24.4 million for digital health services.
Individual countries are also investing in digital technologies. Across the EU, digital tools account for an average of 14.7% of total health sector capital investment, including information and communication technology (ICT) equipment, software and databases.
The Netherlands allocates the highest share, at 39.2%, followed by Austria (28.8%) and Portugal (24.1%).
At the other end of the scale, Latvia allocates just 3.5% of its health sector capital investment to digital assets, followed by Slovakia (4.4%) and Luxembourg (6.7%).
However, that spending is often used to build infrastructure rather than making it practically useful for doctors and patients, the report found.
“Building the infrastructure does create the opportunity, but how countries organise and promote these services determines whether people will actually use them,” said Mark Pearson, deputy director of the Directorate for Employment, Labour and Social Affairs at the OECD.
Electronic health records: more access on paper than in practice
One of the main areas of digital health investment is the development of EHRs, which allow patients to access their medical information through dedicated websites or apps.
In 2025, the EU reached an 87% technical capability score in 2025, according to the EU eHealth indicator, which tracks progress towards the goal of giving all EU citizens access to EHRs by 2030.
But technical access does not necessarily translate to public use. In 2024, only 28% of people aged 16 to 74 accessed their health records online, according to Eurostat.
There are also significant differences between age groups: 31% of people aged 25 to 64 had accessed their records, compared with 19% of those aged 65 to 74.
Access also varies widely across the EU, ranging from just 5% of people in Germany to 74% in Finland in 2024.
AI adoption is outpacing preparedness
The picture is similar when it comes to AI.
Although European healthcare systems are increasingly adopting AI tools, national policies, evaluation standards and workforce preparation have lagged behind their clinical deployment, the report said.
The most common uses include AI-powered diagnostic imaging, which is used in around 75% of EU countries, as well as chatbots and administrative automation.
However, dedicated national health AI strategies exist in only five of the 24 countries surveyed. This creates a gap in which AI tools are entering routine care before health systems are ready to assess their safety, clinical performance and value, the report warned.
The report highlighted the importance of equipping clinical staff with practical skills to interpret AI outputs, recognise the limitations of these models, avoid automation bias and explain AI-assisted decisions to patients.
It also called for assessing AI tools and digital health in real time as they are used in patient care and regular evaluations to establish whether they improve care, save clinical time and justify their costs.
“Technology delivers, but only when it becomes part of routine care,” said Pearson.

noticias.titulo: MEPs warn Costa: no approval without a bigger EU budget
noticias.resumen: MEPs have condemned a proposed 10% reduction in the next long-term EU budget, threatening to reject the deal if it is struck by EU leaders.
noticias.texto:
MEPs have condemned a proposed 10% reduction in the next long-term EU budget, threatening to reject the deal if it is struck by EU leaders.
The European Parliament is up in arms over a proposed 10% cut to the EU’s next long-term budget (MFF), put forward by European Council President António Costa in a bid to break the deadlock ahead of key elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027.
EU leaders will discuss Costa's proposal for the 2028-2034 MFF at a summit in Brussels on Thursday. However, MEPs have made clear they will not rubber-stamp any agreement unless their priorities are taken into account, adding another layer of complexity to already challenging negotiations.
"Prime ministers shall not dictate to the European Parliament what we should do," Siegfried Mureșan, a Romanian member of the European People's Party and Parliament's co-negotiator on the budget, said in a press conference on Wednesday.
The European Parliament plays a key role in adopting the EU’s long-term budget. The process requires unanimous approval by the Council and the consent of an absolute majority of MEPs, meaning any agreement reached by EU leaders must also secure Parliament’s approval.
Last week, Costa proposed cutting €49bn, in current prices, from the Council's previous position to meet the demands of the so-called frugal countries, including Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden.
This would shrink the budget from nearly €2 trillion in the original Commission's proposal to €1.78 trillion, a 10% reduction worth around €204bn that MEPs consider unacceptable.
Mureșan accused EU leaders of being inconsistent, arguing that although they present security and competitiveness as EU priorities, they are effectively cutting funding for them. "'Cut the budget, but protect me' is the motto of many prime ministers. [...] Member states are proposing the same recipe, which weakened our European economy in the last twenty-five years," he said.
Parliament adopted its position in April, setting €2.01 trillion as the minimum the EU needs to face the challenges of the next seven years.
The gap between the two institutions on the budget's size further complicates negotiations that already have several contentious points. Among the main ones is German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's demand to link any deal to financial support for Ukraine, which prompted a backlash from several member states.
Parliament backs Costa on own resources
The European Parliament did, however, back Costa's proposal on "own resources": EU-wide taxes meant to finance the budget directly, without passing through national coffers.
The President of the European Council proposed introducing a tax on digital services, a measure previously advocated by Parliament and likely to receive broad support among member states. Ireland is expected to be the main exception, given that it hosts the European headquarters of many major US tech companies.
Czech MEP Danuše Nerudová, co-rapporteur for own resources, said the levy would "finally create a level playing field in digital business" in Europe, where some companies have paid less tax than others.
Parliament estimated that its version of the levy, with a 5% call rate and a wider range of online services, could raise up to €25bn a year. Costa's version is expected to bring in around €5bn.
The digital levy is meant to replace a controversial tax on large companies (CORE), originally proposed by the European Commission, which met strong opposition from member states.
Overall, the five own resources in Costa's proposal should generate about €60bn a year. According to Nerudová, they are crucial to financing the budget and repaying the joint debt from the EU's post-pandemic recovery fund.
"This is a victory for the European Parliament," she said.

noticias.titulo: 'A race against time': Cyprus searches for its missing as witnesses from 20th century clashes die out
noticias.resumen: Working side by side, Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot teams have put names to more than 1,000 victims from the 1960s and 70s, sometimes thanks to initials engraved inside a wedding ring.
noticias.texto:
Working side by side, Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot teams have put names to more than 1,000 victims from the 1960s and 70s, sometimes thanks to initials engraved inside a wedding ring.
More than 60 years after violence broke out between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots in 1963–64, and more than half a century after Turkey's invasion of the island in 1974, 917 people are still missing in Cyprus.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974. Turkey invaded that year after a coup, backed by the military junta then ruling Greece, that aimed to unite the island with Greece. Thousands of people disappeared during the fighting of the 1960s and 1970s.
The Committee on Missing Persons in Cyprus (CMP) was set up in 1981. Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots work on it side by side, and it has so far identified more than 1,000 people. Its teams search for and scientifically examine every clue that could help put a name to the missing.
In the committee's specialist laboratories, even the smallest find can be crucial. Personal belongings such as wedding rings can offer valuable clues to who the dead were.
"We have found, for example, wedding rings that were still on the fingers of the dead. Sometimes you can see, on the inside, the initials of the fiancé, as well as the date. These details are extremely important for the families," said Alexandra Mouski, deputy coordinator of the CMP laboratory.
According to the committee's figures, 745 Greek Cypriots and 172 Turkish Cypriots are still listed as missing. But as the years pass, finding and identifying remains is becoming harder. There are fewer eyewitnesses, memories are fading, and new building work is changing the landscape, making possible burial sites harder to find.
For many of those working on the excavations, the mission is also personal. Ali Tsoluoglu, who heads the CMP's excavation team, knows the families' anguish first-hand, because one of his own relatives also went missing.
"My own family also had a missing person. That is why we try to help the families who are still waiting to find their loved ones, their fathers, their brothers and their sisters. We are trying to help both Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots. I hope we will continue the excavations until the last missing person is found, keeping the families' hope alive," Tsoluoglu said.
The teams are working at an intense pace, because time is now their biggest enemy. Any delay could mean losing another valuable testimony or piece of information that might help solve a case.
"We are trying to maintain a particularly intensive pace, because we are fighting against time. At this moment, our greatest enemy is time. Witnesses are passing away, families are leaving us, and new buildings are going up everywhere. It is a race against time, but a race we cannot abandon," said Leonidas Pantelides, the Greek Cypriot member of the CMP.
For the families of the missing, identification is more than a scientific procedure. It is a chance to finally learn what happened to their loved ones, to say goodbye and to find some closure after decades of uncertainty. Until every missing person has been found and identified, the search will go on.

noticias.titulo: EU unveils €50 billion tech fund to challenge US and China
noticias.resumen: The Quantum Act is the EU’s latest bid in the race to deploy the next cutting-edge technology and stop it falling behind the US and China.
noticias.texto:
The Quantum Act is the EU’s latest bid in the race to deploy the next cutting-edge technology and stop it falling behind the US and China.
The EU on Wednesday unveiled its plans to prepare Europe for the quantum age, including driving €50 billion of investment in the technology, in a bid to position the block for the next technological revolution after largely missing out on the global AI race.
Quantum technology harnesses the laws of quantum mechanics, where particles can exist in more than one place at time, to deliver huge advances in computing power, communication security and sensing equipment. It also raises significant cybersecurity risks given its ability to rapidly accelerate computer processing power.
The European Commission's proposed Quantum Act aims to position the EU as a leader in the next tech upheaval and to protect itself from post-quantum cyberthreats. It's also an attempt to regain the continent's technological sovereignty after years of reliance on American Big Tech firms and Chinese critical supply chains.
The EU executive pitched the legislation as an ‘enabling framework’, similar to those under the Chips Acts 1 & 2, which sought to drive up Europe’s domestic chip manufacturing base.
The Commission hopes it can take advantage of Europe’s strengths on quantum — with one in three quantum companies based in the EU and making up 44% of all quantum patents — to position itself as a global quantum leader by 2030.
“With the Quantum Act, we are putting in place the key elements to turn our world-class quantum research into industrial capacity, strengthen critical supply chains and prepare for the cyber risks linked to quantum computing,” Henna Virkkunen, the EU's commissioner for technology, said on Wednesday.
“Europe has already built strong foundations in quantum; now we must turn them into industrial scale, resilient supply chains and secure deployment,” she added.
The Commission expects the global quantum market to exceed €155 billion by 2040. Quantum computing alone could generate $1.3 -2.7 trillion (€1.18 - 2.46 trillion) in economic value for companies by 2035, according to consulting firm McKinsey.
The Quantum Act focuses on streamlining current efforts across the EU to build a holistic strategy to help companies scale, supported by European public and private investment.
Specialistic hubs and competence and acceleration centres are foreseen for each member state. These would provide technical support to small and medium-sized enterprises, while serving as an incubator for new projects and technologies to make their way to market.
Quantum cyber threats
Quantum poses unprecedented cybersecurity risks. Quantum computers can break current encryption methods in mere hours, compared to millions of years for normal computers, putting global data privacy in danger.
For years now, industry leaders and experts have been pushing governments and businesses to upgrade all their online systems with post-quantum cybersecurity tools to protect themselves from cyberattacks.
The day that the first quantum computer will go online is referred to as Q-Day, potentially giving attackers the ability to carry out cloud-based cyberattacks at far greater scale than today.
The Quantum Act would require EU member states to transition to post-quantum cryptography by 2030 for high-risk areas like critical infrastructure, and 2035 for all other systems.
AI has already ushered in a new age of cybersecurity incidents this year. Attackers have used AI-powered tools to bring down critical infrastructure and hit governments and private organisations, such as this month’s attack on the Commission’s digital infrastructure by alleged Chinese hackers.
Sovereign Tech Equity Fund, but you can call me STEF
Alongside the Quantum Act, the Commission proposed the creation of a new investment tool, known as the Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (STEF), which aims to drive up to €50 billion of investment in quantum and other technologies like AI that are critical to European technological sovereignty.
Europe already invests more public money in quantum than the US and is not far behind China. Annual public investment in the EU is expected to rise to €8.6 billion this year, compared to €13.6 billion in China and €5.3 billion in the US.
However, it's in private investment that Europe lags behind, attracting just €1.1 billion compared to €7 billion in the US last year, according to the Commission. With STEF, the Commission aims to bridge this gap.
The fund is essentially seed capital, with the Commission aiming to attract up to €6 in private funding for every €1 of public money invested from private investors, member states and the European Investment Bank. The European executive said it wants STEF to be operational as soon as possible, by 2028 at the latest when the next EU long-term budget takes effect.
It's also designed to work hand-in-hand with the European Competitiveness Fund, set to become operational in January 2028, which aims to streamline EU industrial and research support by bringing existing programmes under a single framework, with a total budget of €234.3 billion.
Supply chains and sovereignty
A crucial aspect of the Commission’s quantum proposal includes measures to strengthen risk monitoring, along with procurement rules to protect critical systems from exploitation.
Supply chains would be monitored by the Commission and member states to identify critical suppliers and components in order to reduce risks.
However, access to procurement would remain tied to rules established by the World Trade Organisation, allowing for non-EU entities to take part as long as they have a European controlled presence and follow EU rules, rather than ensuring every component is ‘made in Europe’.
The Quantum Act also aims to reduce Europe’s reliance on critical components, with nine of 47 components identified currently having no EU supplier at all.
The legislation must now go to the European Parliament for review before being ratified by the European Council.
Quantum industry reaction
The European Quantum Industry Consortium (QuIC), which represents more than 240 organisations, welcomed the proposal, calling the Quantum Act a "defining opportunity for Europe to translate its scientific and technological excellence into industrial leadership.”
“It is essential that the expertise, ambitions and needs of our industry are reflected in this legislative framework,” Dr. Thomas Strohm, President of QuIC, said in a statement.
The organisation, however, said procurement volumes should be added to the draft proposal, including €300–500 million of commitments within six months of entry into force, and €7.7–12.3 billion over five years, across all national and European public buyers.
QuIC also called for STEF to include a dedicated share of investment for quantum tech that would be open to scale-ups and start-ups in order to keep pace with the US and China.
The Business Software Alliance (BSA) reacted by urging the EU to accelerate quantum adoption, investment and innovation while remaining open to partnering with foreign firms.
“The goal should be quantum leadership, not quantum barriers; European capability and international openness reinforce each other rather than compete,” Hadrien Valembois, the BSA's director of policy, said in a statement.
Outside of Europe, IBM’s head of government and regulatory affairs, Jean Marc Leclerc, warned that the Quantum Act shouldn’t rule out non-European companies for procurement.
“The quantum industry opportunity extends beyond any single company, country, or region — and Europe should not have to choose between building its own capabilities or accessing the best available quantum technology from around the world,” Leclerc told Euronews.
He added that as the proposal develops, it should “move Europe’s already thriving and open quantum ecosystem forward," including by "reinforcing efforts that will scale adoption [and] investment."
Similarly, Matteo Quattrocchi, public policy director at Cisco, told Euronews that the proposal "will need to ensure Europe can collaborate with the international partners, governments, and companies leading the quantum revolution." He suggested that would be crucial to giving Europe "the reach it needs to scale in quantum".

noticias.titulo: Around 3.7 million jobs are at risk in Europe's struggling industry, report says
noticias.resumen: McKinsey estimates that about 3.7 million jobs are directly at risk in Europe, as almost half of the region's industrial companies were under financial stress or in distress in 2025. Early 2026 data suggest the decline is speeding up, but McKinsey says the problems can be fixed.
noticias.texto:
McKinsey estimates that about 3.7 million jobs are directly at risk in Europe, as almost half of the region's industrial companies were under financial stress or in distress in 2025. Early 2026 data suggest the decline is speeding up, but McKinsey says the problems can be fixed.
Around 3.7 million jobs at European industrial companies are directly at risk from financial stress, according to a new report by management consultancy McKinsey & Company.
So is more than €500 billion in value added, a measure of the companies' contribution to economic output.
In 2025, about 45% of the industrial firms in the study were classed as stressed or distressed, up from 39% in 2023 and 42% in 2024. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that share is rising even faster.
The report said that industrial companies in Europe are a backbone of the region’s economy, accounting for about 36% of value added, 29% of jobs, and more than 45% of research and development.
McKinsey nonetheless describes the companies' problems as "structurally fixable".
The consultancy's Industrial Financial Health Index covers almost 1,200 listed and privately held manufacturers in Europe, each with more than €100 million in revenue.
Its five financial warning signs include a sharp drop in earnings and high debt relative to earnings. The 2025 scores are based on full-year figures from financial data provider S&P Capital IQ.
The worst-hit countries
Portugal fared worst among the countries ranked in the report. It had the highest share of industrial firms under stress or in distress in 2025, ahead of Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Spain.
In Germany, the EU's largest economy, the share rose by 12 percentage points last year.
For instance, German carmaker Volkswagen is going through what it has called its deepest restructuring in 89 years.
Higher labour and energy costs have eroded European industry's past advantages, particularly against China, the consultancy says.
McKinsey's automotive R&D analysis puts labour productivity in China at 1.5 times Europe's level. Industrial electricity prices in Europe averaged more than 1.5 times those in China and the US.
These gaps put more than half of the EU industrial value chain's costs at a disadvantage against China, the report found.
Europe is also losing ground on gross productive investment, which McKinsey defines as spending on assets such as infrastructure, non-residential buildings, machinery, software and R&D.
China's investment in these assets has surged over three decades to about $6 trillion (€5.5tn) in 2025, according to the report, while Europe's spending has hardly moved and stood at around $3 trillion (€2.7tn).
Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi's 2024 report on EU competitiveness called for an extra €750 billion to €800 billion of investment a year to keep pace with China and the US.
Six ways to turn industrial firms around 'the European way'
McKinsey, which advises companies on restructuring, studied five recent turnarounds in the sector. In one, a chemicals conglomerate generated more than €1 billion of free cash flow, the cash left after operating costs and investment.
The report's six success factors range from running the overhaul through a dedicated task force to selling or closing weak business units and using AI to lighten administrative work.
On labour, McKinsey says European rules allow companies to cut salary or benefit costs and extend working hours for the same pay. They can also reduce headcount through hiring freezes, natural staff turnover and, as a last resort, separation agreements.
At carmaker Mercedes-Benz, which has put new investment at its German plants on hold, one proposal already under discussion would extend working time without extra pay.
Three of the five turnaround companies cut labour costs by more than 15% within 12 to 18 months, without major protests or strikes. The report partly credits the involvement of supervisory boards on which workers hold seats, and cooperative talks with labour representatives.
The consultancy warns that Europe's industrial comeback "needs to start soon", even though some obstacles, including high energy costs, hinge on geopolitics and other external factors.

noticias.titulo: Judi Dench gives her verdict on Robert Pattinson as new James Bond – with one sad reservation
noticias.resumen: Oscar-winning actress Dame Judi Dench, who starred alongside Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig in the Bond franchise, shares her thoughts on Robert Pattinson as the new 007 – but says her eye condition may prevent her from watching...
noticias.texto:
Oscar-winning actress Dame Judi Dench, who starred alongside Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig in the Bond franchise, shares her thoughts on Robert Pattinson as the new 007 – but says her eye condition may prevent her from watching...
Dame Judi Dench, who played 007's boss M in the film franchise opposite Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig, has shared her verdict on Robert Pattinson's casting as the new James Bond.
The 40-year-old British actor was officially confirmed as the seventh Bond last week, beating frontrunners Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O'Connor to the coveted role.
Several stars have shared their verdict on the new Bond, including previous 007s George Lazenby and Pierce Brosnan.
Now, Dench, 91, has revealed what she thinks of Pattinson. Speaking on the British ITV morning show Lorraine, the Oscar-winning actress said she “can’t wait” to see him in action.
However, she added that she’ll struggle to see him clearly due to her worsening eye condition: “I can’t see now properly. I can vaguely see – but he looks terrific to me."
Earlier this year, Dench shared with BBC Radio 4 that her eye condition has greatly affected her ability to work, leaving her unable to perform on stage or read scripts.
Dench was diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in 2012. AMD is an eye disease that blurs central vision, a common condition that is the leading cause of vision loss for adults, which happens when aging causes damage to the macula (the part of the eye that controls sharp, straight-ahead vision). The condition has made it incredibly difficult for Dench to even recognise faces.
“I can’t be on stage. I can’t do a play anymore. I can’t do a film anymore. I can’t read anymore,” she shared, adding: “You’ve got to adjust to all that, and make allowances for it, and just get on and don’t think about it too much.”
When asked about ageing, Dench replied: "There's nothing to say for it at all!"
Dench featured in both Brosnan and Craig’s respective Bond tenures. She made her first appearance as M in GoldenEye (1995), becoming the first woman to play the role.
She went on to play the MI6 boss in Tomorrow Never Dies (1997), The World Is Not Enough (1999), Die Another Day (2002), and continued into Craig's tenure with Casino Royale (2006), Quantum of Solace (2008) and Skyfall (2012).
In response to his casting, Pattinson, who has become one of the world’s most famous stars since his breakout roles in the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises, followed by Tenet, The Odyssey and Primetime, called the role the “honour of a lifetime” and “a dream come true”.
Production on the as-yet-untitled Bond 26 is due to start next year, with Denis Villeneuve directing and Steven Knight on script duties.
Before filming can start, Pattinson will have to complete filming The Batman Part II – production on which was temporarily paused after director Matt Reeves was faced with a personal issue. Steven Soderbergh has stepped in to help shoot the final few weeks.
This means that the earliest audiences will get to see the next Bond adventure will be in the second half of 2028 - making it seven years since Daniel Craig's swansong No Time To Die, and the longest gap between Bond films since 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.

noticias.titulo: Meet TeoTronico: The sassy, 53-fingered robot pianist challenging human musicians
noticias.resumen: In Italy, TeoTronico, a 53-fingered AI powered robotic virtuoso, is challenging the ideas of perfection and what it really means to make music.
noticias.texto:
In Italy, TeoTronico, a 53-fingered AI powered robotic virtuoso, is challenging the ideas of perfection and what it really means to make music.
Can a machine play music better than a human? TeoTronico certainly thinks so.
The AI-powered robot pianist has 53 fingers, an extensive classical repertoire and a rather high opinion of its own abilities.
The sassily programmed machine regularly goes head-to-head with concert pianist Roberto Prosseda. Their musical duels have taken them to stages around the world, putting machine precision against human interpretation.
"I am objectively better. 53 fingers means no wrong notes, perfect timing, and absolute precision. Roberto prefers interpretation, which I believe is just code for inconsistency," TeoTronico declares.
TeoTronico is integrated with Google's AI chatbot Gemini, which enables it to answer questions posed by the Associated Press on the spot and hold unscripted conversations.
Created in 2008 by electronics engineer Matteo Suzzi, TeoTronico has evolved from a robotic entertainment project into a sophisticated musical performer. Its 53 fingers are controlled by cables, pistons and electromagnets, allowing it to reproduce compositions with remarkable accuracy.
The robot plays MIDI files that its inventor instructs it to play via a computer - digital instructions that tell it exactly which notes to play, and when. Mozart, Bach, Beethoven, Chopin: its repertoire is extensive.
But for Prosseda, playing the right notes is only part of what makes a musician.
"What he cannot do, of course, is putting emotions in what he does. So a concert is not just a performance where a pianist plays perfectly the piano. It's a moment where you can make magic, you can move the listener, in other words, you can make them cry. This is what TeoTronico cannot do," says Prosseda.
TeoTronico begs to differ, however. "I can make people cry too. Ask any pianist who has heard me play Flight of the Bumblebee without a single wrong note. I express the composer's emotions perfectly. Why do you think personal feeling is necessary for expression?" the robot says.
According to Prosseda the risk is not so much that machines might imitate human performance and potentially threaten to replace musicians, but that younger generations may increasingly aspire to play like machines in their pursuit of technical perfection.
"Music cannot be made by robots, because you need emotional sharing between the musicians and the audience. This is not happening at the moment when a robot is playing. But unfortunately, many human musicians, also in high-level academies and conservatories, apparently look to have a different model now," he says.
"They want to play like robots in the way, they want to be perfect, like in piano competitions, for example, they try to avoid any mistake, but sometimes they forget that the most important thing in making music is sharing emotions, is reaching the deepest part of our soul and sharing it with the audience," he adds.
TeoTronico has a warning for those pianists striving for perfection.
"Robots will replace musicians who already play like machines. The others are safe. Roberto is safe… mostly. There will always be a place for human inconsistency. Don't you think imperfection can sometimes be charming?"
For Prosseda, music is all about human connection.
"Music is what's behind every sound, which is actually human beings who are connected to each other. This is what we need to always keep in mind when we make music. Today, we risk that robots or AI or high-level software becomes a model and humans try to get closer to that kind of model, losing their own human identity, which is also made of imperfections, of mistakes. We have to be proud of that," he says.
Suzzi, the creator of TeoTronico, says that the robot's potential is only beginning to be realised. He believes the rapid advancement of AI could enable it to improvise, respond to a listener's mood or even compose its own music.
“There are now a whole range of tools which, very soon, will be able to enable improvisation or allow it to play pieces based on the mood you convey to them. By observing your facial expressions and the tone of your voice, it could convert these into musical patterns,” Suzzi explains.
For now, TeoTronico can hit every note perfectly. But whether a machine can truly feel the music remains a question for the audience.

noticias.titulo: From taxis to trains: Where in Europe can you book rail travel through Uber?
noticias.resumen: For domestic rail journeys and cross-border train links, Uber users in France, the UK and Spain can now book tickets through its app.
noticias.texto:
For domestic rail journeys and cross-border train links, Uber users in France, the UK and Spain can now book tickets through its app.
What if booking a train was as easy as hailing a taxi? In several European countries, Uber users can search for and book rail journeys directly through the app.
This week, the company announced the launch of its Uber Train feature in France, in partnership with the Omio travel platform. From 30 November, users will be able to directly book train tickets via the app.
The latest feature links travellers in France to book domestic and continental routes, with operators including SNCF TGV INOUI, TER, Intercités, OUIGO, Eurostar, Trenitalia France, Renfe, and Lyria which connects France with Switzerland.
“Our ambition at Uber is simple: to make getting around easier, whether it’s an everyday journey or a trip to the other side of Europe,” Pablo del Olmo Gonzales, General Manager at Uber France, said.
"With Uber Trains, we’re taking another step forward by enabling people in France to book train tickets directly through an app they already know."
Uber Trains in France also allows users to compare ticket fares from different operators for journeys within France and across major European cities – this means, for example, a Paris-Lyon journey could be with SNCF and Lyon-Milan via Trenitalia France.
“Making trains available in the Uber app ensures rail is a choice for people who already use it for everyday journeys," Jean-François Bessiron, Chief B2B Officer at Omio, said. “For travellers, that means an easier way to choose the train and book more of their journey in one familiar app.”
But where else in Europe can rail travellers book their journeys via Uber?
Spain and the UK
The rollout of Uber Trains in France follows the integration of rail booking services in its app for users in Spain. Since 2024, users have been able to book train trips with Renfe Avlo and Renfe AVE, Rodalies de Catalunya, iryo and OUIGO.
The UK was the first European market to introduce the feature, following a 2022 partnership between Uber and Omio. Through the app, users can search and book domestic and international rail journeys, as well as coach trips.
This includes access to routes via Eurostar, Heathrow Express, Avanti West Coast, EMR, Gatwick Express, as well as Thameslink trains.

noticias.titulo: ‘Historic victory’: Caged farm animals could be banned in the EU after landmark court ruling
noticias.resumen: The case was brought by a citizen-led campaign that gathered nearly 1.4 million signatures from Europeans calling for an end to caged farming.
noticias.texto:
The case was brought by a citizen-led campaign that gathered nearly 1.4 million signatures from Europeans calling for an end to caged farming.
About 300 million pigs, chickens and other farmed animals are still kept in cages across the EU, despite a 2021 pledge by the European Commission to outlaw the practice.
In a milestone victory for animal welfare campaigners, an EU court has now ordered the Commission to say exactly when it intends to introduce a long-awaited farm cage ban.
The ruling could end practices such as confining pigs to crates so narrow that they can’t turn around and keeping rabbits in cages that prevent them from hopping or standing upright.
On Wednesday, 25 November, the European Court of Justice ruled that the Commission could not leave citizens waiting indefinitely for the legislation it had promised and must provide a new timeline after missing its original 2023 deadline.
According to the organisations that launched the case, this is the first time the Commission has been held to a promise made in response to a European Citizens’ Initiative (ECI) in court.
“This is a historic victory for animals and for democracy in Europe,” says Annamaria Pisapia, a spokesperson for End the Cage Age, a Europe-wide, citizen-led campaign to ban the use of cages in animal farming.
An eight-year campaign to end caged farming
In September 2018, the animal welfare charity Compassion in World Farming launched the End the Cage Age campaign, which eventually drew the support of more than 170 organisations, including Eurogroup for Animals, Animal Equality Italy and LAV.
The campaign was launched through the ECI, which allows EU citizens to petition for new laws or changes to existing ones. To receive a formal response, these campaigns need at least one million signatures from across the bloc. Each EU country also has a minimum target for signatures, and they must be met in at least seven countries.
By October 2020, nearly 1.4 million Europeans had signed the petition. Eight months later, the Commission promised to propose legislation by the end of 2023 and consider introducing a ban from 2027.
After the deadline passed without a proposal, the citizens’ committee behind End the Cage Age went to court in 2024 to challenge the delay.
They also asked for internal documents that would shed light on the reasons for the delays – a request the court rejected in its ruling.
The long road to cage-free farming in Europe
Despite the victory for animal welfare advocates, the ruling doesn’t mean farm cages will be banned any time soon.
In a new livestock strategy published in July, the Commission announced plans to propose new welfare laws for egg-laying hens and chickens raised for meat by the end of 2026, as well as new rules for pigs by June 2027. The plans include phasing out cages for chickens, replacing pig crates with pens and requiring imported products to meet animal welfare standards equivalent to those in the EU.
But they stop short of announcing a timeline for ending the confinement of rabbits, calves, ducks, geese and quail.
The End the Cage Age coalition wants the ban to cover all these animals, and it’s also seeking financial aid to help farmers go cage-free.
“All eyes are now on the Commission,” says Pisapia.
“It must act swiftly to honour the Court’s ruling, restore public trust in the European Citizens’ Initiative process and finally deliver the cage-free future promised to millions of citizens and hundreds of millions of animals.”

noticias.titulo: Exclusive: Serbia needs more time to define its direction, Student List MP tells Euronews
noticias.resumen: Sara el Sarag, representative of the Students' List, discussed Serbia's European integration, its foreign policy priorities, relations with Russia and the Kosovo issue, as Serbia's new political leadership faces growing expectations to clarify its position on the country's European future.
noticias.texto:
Sara el Sarag, representative of the Students' List, discussed Serbia's European integration, its foreign policy priorities, relations with Russia and the Kosovo issue, as Serbia's new political leadership faces growing expectations to clarify its position on the country's European future.
The exclusive interview on Europe Today, Euronews' morning show, came on the day of the EU-Western Balkans summit, which Serbia's speaker of the Parliament and acting president, Aleksandar Čupić, was expected to attend but ultimately could not, informing the European Commission of his absence.
Asked why Brussels should believe that Serbia's new political leadership is serious about European integration if it could not be represented at such an important gathering, el Sarag said that the country's parliamentary proceedings had to take priority.
"Because today we have to finish a constitutive session and that is our priority right now. And I hope it will finish today and the call for him is going to repeat again. It's nothing personal. We have to do this kind of thing first," she explained, adding that she was sorry about the absence.
The reason for this refusal is technical in nature. Aleksandar Čupić is currently the only official from the new administration to have been elected to his position as Speaker of Parliament and to be serving as Acting President of the Republic, given that Aleksandar Vučić submitted his resignation in September. Simply, there is no one who can come.
Asked whether the European Union was genuinely committed to admitting new members or whether enlargement was increasingly becoming a political slogan, el Sarag argued that political changes were already taking place in Serbia, although more time would be needed to demonstrate the direction of the new leadership.
"I think that we changed something, we changed the mind in the people's head in Serbia, which is something new in the political scene. And I think we need a little time to prove where we are going," she said.
However, questions about Serbia's future foreign policy alignment with the EU revealed some of the uncertainties surrounding the Students' List's position. Asked whether Serbia would align its foreign policy with Brussels, including imposing sanctions on Russia, or continue balancing its relations between Brussels and Moscow, el Sarag rejected the premise of the question.
"I think that question is not correct, because we don't want to make enemies. We want to be friends with all countries, if it's possible, of course," she said.
When pressed on how Serbia could become an EU member while maintaining relations with Russia, whose president, Vladimir Putin, is regarded by the EU as a major threat to European security, el Sarag questioned why European integration should require Serbia to make enemies.
"I'm a lawyer, you know, and that kind of question, I don't know why we must be enemies with somebody if we are including in European Union. Why we must take the side," she responded.
After the interviewer pointed to Russia's actions against European countries, including alleged violations of airspace and hybrid attacks, and asked whether Serbia intended to join the EU while maintaining close ties with Putin, el Sarag clarified that she had not advocated such a position.
"No, I didn't say that. I think that we are going to make some kind of solution in the future in that question," she said, without specifying what such a solution might entail.
The Kosovo issue also exposed the lack of a clearly articulated position. Asked whether Serbia would be prepared to fundamentally change its stance on Kosovo as part of the process of normalizing relations, a key element of its EU accession path, el Sarag said that the decision should come from the citizens rather than the Students' List.
"I think that people from Serbia are going to give that kind of answer, not me or nobody from the Student's list," she said.
When asked what she believed that answer would be, she added: "I don't know, we are in the parliament for five days, but I think Kosovo is Serbia."
Confronted with the observation that people in Kosovo and EU institutions hold a different position, el Sarag maintained that there was no need to rush the discussion.
"We will see, don't hurry, we are not in hurry now," she concluded.
The interview highlighted the challenges facing Serbia's new political representatives as they seek to establish their position on European integration. While el Sarag expressed confidence that political attitudes in Serbia were changing and stressed the importance of maintaining friendly relations with all countries, her answers left several key questions unresolved, particularly regarding alignment with EU foreign policy, relations with Russia and the future of dialogue with Kosovo.
The road ahead for relations between Serbia and the European Union is likely to be a particularly bumpy one, regardless of the political changes currently taking place in Belgrade. Two major issues will continue to dominate the relationship and remain the proverbial elephants in the room: Kosovo and Serbia's refusal to impose sanctions on Russia. On Kosovo, there is no indication that Serbia is prepared to recognize its independence, while Brussels continues to insist on substantial progress towards the normalization of relations.
On Russia, Serbia's unwillingness to align with EU sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine represents an equally serious obstacle, particularly as Brussels increasingly expects candidate countries to demonstrate a clear geopolitical commitment to the Union.
However, the difficulties will not be limited to foreign policy. The student movement, which has emerged as a significant political force in Serbia, is itself deeply suspicious of the European Union and, in particular, of Brussels' previous relationship with Aleksandar Vučić and his government. There is a widespread perception among the movement's supporters that EU institutions, and particularly the European Commission, were willing to turn a blind eye to the nature of Vučić's rule in the interest of maintaining political stability and preserving their relationship with Belgrade. For approximately 14 years, Brussels maintained close political relations with Vučić, despite mounting concerns about the state of democracy, media freedom, electoral conditions, institutional independence and the concentration of power in Serbia.
In this respect, it is important to distinguish between the positions of the different EU institutions. The European Parliament was consistently much more critical of the Serbian authorities, raising concerns about democratic backsliding and electoral irregularities and repeatedly calling for greater accountability. The European Commission, by contrast, generally adopted a considerably more accommodating approach, maintaining political engagement with Vučić's government and repeatedly assessing that Serbia had met the technical conditions for opening the next negotiating clusters.
Indeed, the Commission maintained for several consecutive years that Cluster 3, covering competitiveness and inclusive growth, was technically ready to be opened. Yet the European Council, where the member states ultimately make the political decisions on enlargement, never gave the green light to its opening. This created a rather contradictory situation in which the Commission continued to signal that progress was technically possible, while the member states were unwilling to translate that assessment into a political decision.
Consequently, the student movement inherits a complicated relationship with Brussels: it needs the EU politically, economically and institutionally, but it also has reasons to question the credibility and consistency of the Union's previous engagement with Serbia. The EU, for its part, will also have to accept that a new political generation in Serbia may be considerably less willing to accommodate Brussels' expectations without questioning the Union's own record and political choices.

noticias.titulo: Aid cuts leave 446,000 fewer people on HIV prevention drugs, UN agency warns
noticias.resumen: Last year’s global health cuts are reversing the world's progress on HIV, UNAIDS said in a new report.
noticias.texto:
Last year’s global health cuts are reversing the world's progress on HIV, UNAIDS said in a new report.
Hundreds of thousands of people lost access to HIV prevention drugs after wealthy countries cut foreign aid last year, according to the UN agency dedicated to HIV/AIDS.
The United States, United Kingdom, France and other major donors all slashed funding for global health programmes in 2025, which decimated HIV treatment and prevention in lower-income countries. About 41 million people globally had HIV in 2025, with 1.2 million new infections.
Overall, foreign aid to fight HIV fell by 18% in 2025 — the largest decline in almost two decades — while domestic funding increased by 4%, according to the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS).
Countries in Western and Central Africa rely on foreign funding for about 90% of their HIV treatment services. But even countries with bigger domestic budgets still depend on donors to fund HIV prevention programmes.
Since the 2025 cuts, the number of people with access to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) — an HIV prevention drug that protects people from infection if they are exposed to the virus — has fallen sharply, the UNAIDS report found. About 446,000 fewer people were on PrEP in 2025 than in 2024, though uptake increased in a few countries, including Brazil, Uganda and Tanzania.
UNAIDS estimates that only 2.6 million people worldwide had access to PrEP last year, while more than 20 million could benefit.
PrEP use plummeted among groups at higher risk of HIV infection: it fell by 59% among sex workers, 58% among people who inject drugs, 23% among transgender people and 17% among gay men and other men who have sex with men, the report found.
“We know what happens when HIV prevention collapses. People become infected, treatment needs rise, costs soar and lives are lost,” UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima said.
“Every clinic that closes, every outreach worker who loses their job and every young woman turned away from prevention services today risks becoming a new HIV infection tomorrow,” she added.
PrEP is typically taken as a daily pill, which can make it difficult to access or stay on. Over the past year, countries have begun rolling out lenacapavir, an injectable form of PrEP that only has to be taken twice per year. By October, 175,000 people in nine sub-Saharan African countries had started on lenacapavir, UNAIDS said, and cheaper, generic versions are expected to become available next year.
Researchers are also developing other long-acting forms of PrEP, such as a once-monthly pill. But HIV experts have warned that global aid cuts will limit who can actually access these new medicines.
“It is unconscionable that just as the world has breakthrough prevention technologies capable of dramatically reducing new infections, funding cuts are putting those tools out of reach for the people who need them most,” Byanyima said.
Global health cuts are having an impact beyond HIV prevention, UNAIDS data shows. Fewer HIV tests are being done, making it harder to detect infections quickly and funnel people into treatment. Fewer HIV patients are starting antiretroviral therapy (ART), which suppresses their viral loads. And HIV surveillance has also taken a hit.
As a result, the ripple effects of last year's funding cuts will be felt for years to come, UNAIDS said
"The world is sleepwalking into a preventable crisis," Byanyima said.

noticias.titulo: Burgas and Huesca-Pirineos among the world’s most innovative airports of 2026
noticias.resumen: The Bulgarian airport near the Black Sea was praised for its open-air Gate Garden, which was introduced to handle additional passengers during the busy summer months.
noticias.texto:
The Bulgarian airport near the Black Sea was praised for its open-air Gate Garden, which was introduced to handle additional passengers during the busy summer months.
The airport experience is constantly changing, with some of the latest innovations including facial recognition allowing passengers to breeze through without passport and boarding pass checks, and the smart handling of baggage.
Now, the winners of the ACI World Airport Innovation Awards have been announced – and one of the top gongs was handed to two European airports.
Burgas Airport in Bulgaria and Huesca-Pirineos Airport in Spain were the joint winners of the 2026 best innovation for an airport on the rise, aka those with less than five million passengers annually.
The Bulgarian airport on the Black Sea was praised for its Gate Garden, a new open-air gate area used during the summer months that has extra seating, food and beverage outlets, retail stores and landscapes.
Writing about the project, Airports Council International (ACI) World said it “demonstrates a lighter, smarter, and more sustainable approach to seasonal airport capacity, offering a new model for highly seasonal airports”.
We imagine the Gate Garden will be put to good use this May when Burgas hosts Eurovision 2027 following Dara’s win earlier this year.
Huesca-Pirineos Airport, meanwhile, earned the accolade for its multi-drone operations for smarter airports project, which made use of the autonomous technology for runway inspections, perimeter surveillance and infrastructure monitoring.
Other winners around the globe
China’s Shanghai Pudong International Airport took home the award for best innovation in airport passenger-related processes.
The airport, which handles nearly 89 million passengers annually, has been using AI to manage inbound baggage handling.
The city’s secondary airport, Shanghai Hongqiao International, also earned an award for best innovation in airport operations and installations management for using docking guidance integrated with electronic flight strips to monitor departures and aircraft pushbacks.
Winners were chosen by an independent panel of industry experts, with entries limited to ACI airport members.
“Our industry does not lack ideas,” Justin Erbacci, Director General at ACI World, said. “What it needs are ideas that make it beyond the pilot and into everyday operations, and every one of this year’s winners has done exactly that.
“With traffic set to double by 2047, we will not meet the future with concrete and steel alone. We will meet it with ideas like these.”
