noticias.titulo: US tells citizens to leave Iran, warns hostilities could escalate fast
noticias.resumen: The US Virtual Embassy in Iran said Tehran, Yemen's Houthis and other aligned groups may target US interests and citizens in the region, including companies and institutions. The alert followed Iranian attacks on US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait and a Houthi strike on Riyadh that injured 11 people.
noticias.texto:
The US Virtual Embassy in Iran said Tehran, Yemen's Houthis and other aligned groups may target US interests and citizens in the region, including companies and institutions. The alert followed Iranian attacks on US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait and a Houthi strike on Riyadh that injured 11 people.
Washington warned citizens across the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance after Iran attacked US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait and Yemen's Houthi forces struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district, wounding 11 people.
The US Virtual Embassy in Iran issued a security alert on Wednesday citing the attacks and warning that hostilities could escalate rapidly.
It said Iran, the Houthis and other groups aligned with Tehran may target US interests and citizens in the region, including companies and institutions.
"Do not travel to Iran for any reason. United States citizens should leave Iran immediately," the alert said.
A Houthi attack on Tuesday struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district, wounding 11 people, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence said.
Bahrain's Interior Ministry said Tehran's attacks on Saturday wounded two people and caused a fire at a civilian industrial facility.
US citizens in the region were urged to monitor airline and airport operations and prepare for possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.
The alert also warned that rules for crossing Iran's land borders and entry conditions in destination countries may change at short notice.
Citizens were advised to avoid demonstrations, large gatherings and areas with a heavy police presence, and to stay alert in places associated with the US.
In the event of air attacks, the alert said citizens should keep away from doors, windows and debris, keep their mobile phones charged and follow instructions from local authorities.
It directed citizens to register with the US State Department's information system to receive security updates.
The US and Iran have had no diplomatic relations since 1980. Switzerland acts as the protecting power for US interests in Tehran, and the alert named the US interests section at the Swiss embassy there as a point of contact for citizens needing assistance.

noticias.titulo: 13 restaurants topped LaListe’s ranking for 2027 – including seven in Europe
noticias.resumen: L’Assiette Champenoise in Tinqueux, France, earned a 99.5 score, reserved for the best restaurants in the world, for the first time this year.
noticias.texto:
L’Assiette Champenoise in Tinqueux, France, earned a 99.5 score, reserved for the best restaurants in the world, for the first time this year.
LaListe’s Top 1,000 World’s Best Restaurants 2027 list is out now – and more than half of the spots earning the very highest rating are in Europe.
Created by pulling together reviews from food critics, restaurant guides, other media sources and bloggers, each one is rated with a score out of 100, which is then weighted based on its reliability and reach. These are brought together, along with online reviews from guests, to create an overall score.
Only 13 restaurants received the highest rating – 99.5 – this year, with seven of these places found in Europe, including two in France, and one each in Switzerland, Italy, Sweden, Spain and Germany.
“L’Assiette Champenoise and Sushi Saito are new at the top, and Frantzén is back,” LaListe founder and CEO Philippe Faure said. “But great gastronomy is not defined by the size of the bill: with our new European selections, we show that it is possible to eat remarkably well at reasonable prices.”
Outside of the continent, the US and Japan had two restaurants apiece, with the final two coming from Macao and Hong Kong.
The very best restaurants in Europe, according to LaListe
L’Assiette Champenoise, the new addition to LaListe’s top step, is in Tinqueux, a suburb just outside of Reims.
Owned by chef Arnaud Lallement, the restaurant has had three Michelin stars since 2014. Signature dishes include the blue lobster, created in homage to his father, who passed the restaurant down to him, and the caviar with smoked haddock and potato.
Cheval Blanc by Peter Knogl in Basel, Switzerland, also has three Michelin stars, as well as 19 Gault&Millau points. There, you can expect “French haute cuisine meets Mediterranean and Asian influences”.
In Brusaporto outside of Bergamo, the family-run Da Vittorio (also three Michelin stars) offers several tasting menus, with one centred around truffles, another around seafood, and one that gives free rein to the chefs.
The first Swedish restaurant to earn three Michelin stars, you’ll find Frantzén in Stockholm. Owned by Björn Frantzén, he is the only chef in the world to have three restaurants with the top accolade – the other two being Zén in Singapore and FZN in Dubai.
In Paris, Guy Savoy has been among the best restaurants in the world since its opening in 1980, earning two Michelin stars in 1985 before going up to three in 2002 (although it has since been demoted as of 2023).
Martín Berasategui, whose various restaurants have a total of 11 Michelin stars, making him the most decorated Spanish chef, has his eponymous restaurant in Lasarte. It has held three Michelin stars since 2001, and serves Basque cuisine.
Last, but not least, Schwarzwaldstube in Baiersbronn has held its three Michelin star rating since 1993. Offering views of the Tonbach Valley, guests can enjoy French cuisine with a modern twist.
All the restaurants with the highest 99.5 LaListe rating for 2027
- 1. Cheval Blanc by Peter Knogl at Hôtel Les Trois Rois in Basel, Switzerland
- 2. Da Vittorio in Brusaporto, Italy
- 3. Frantzén in Stockholm, Sweden
- 4. Guy Savoy in Paris, France
- 5. L’Assiette Champenoise in Tinqueux, France
- 6. Le Bernardin in New York, US
- 7. Martín Berasategui in Lasarte, Spain
- 8. Schwarzwaldstube in Baiersbronn, Germany
- 9. SingleThread in Healdsburg, California, US
- 10. Robuchon au Dôme in Macao
- 11. Matsukawa in Tokyo, Japan
- 12. Sushi Saito in Tokyo, Japan
- 13. Lung King Heen in Hong Kong

noticias.titulo: Stunning Supermoon photos: The best shots of last night's Beaver moon lighting up the night sky
noticias.resumen: From Germany to Dubai, catch up on the best photos of last night's Supermoon.
noticias.texto:
From Germany to Dubai, catch up on the best photos of last night's Supermoon.
It is a stargazer and photographer's dream: a rare Supermoon lit up the sky across the world on Tuesday.
A Supermoon, which is more of a popular term than a scientific one, is used to describe when a full moon is at its closest point to the Earth. The phenomenon usually occurs only three or four times a year.
Because the moon inches a little closer than usual, it appears to be larger and brighter.
If you didn't get a glimpse of last night's Supermoon, do not worry - there are three more coming up soon.
A forest near Frankfurt, Germany
Why is it called the Beaver Moon?
November’s full Moon is traditionally known as the 'Beaver Moon', a nickname linked to the time of year when beavers prepare for winter by building dams and gathering food.
Dubai, UAE
The technical name for a Supermoon is a perigee full Moon, and it can appear up to 14 per cent larger and 30 per cent brighter than a full Moon at apogee.
Lighting festival, Myanmar
Hadera, Israel
Manhattan, New York
When is the next Supermoon?
When Supermoons happen, they happen in groups - we get four or five Super Full Moons in a row (or four or five Super New Moons in a row).
The last Supermoon of 2026 could be particularly magical, as it will rise on 24th December, celebrated as Christmas Eve in many European countries.
The next two Supermoons after that will be on 22nd January 2027 and 20th February 2027.

noticias.titulo: EU rejects Trump’s case for new tariffs
noticias.resumen: Brussels disputes Washington’s finding that Europe is fueling global industrial overcapacity as the U.S. proposes a 15% levy.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The European Commission on Wednesday rejected Washington’s claim that Europe is fueling global industrial overcapacity, after the Trump administration proposed a 15% tariff on the 27-country bloc. “We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Olof Gill, the Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson, said in a statement. “The EU and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” he added. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, led by Jamieson Greer, found that 14 trading partners, including the European Union, China and Japan, had artificially deflated prices by flooding markets with manufactured goods. The decision follows a trade investigation launched in March. Greer on Wednesday proposed a 15% tariff on the European Union, in line with the ceiling agreed in the transatlantic trade truce struck in July 2025 between U.S. President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Greer, who is expected to dial in next Monday to a meeting of European trade ministers, can expect pushback on the excess capacity probe. EU ministers are also expected to bring up the lack of progress on lowering tariffs on EU products containing steel — some of which still face U.S. duties of as high as 50%. The overcapacity investigation, launched under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, is the second of two trade probes initiated in the spring as part of the Trump administration’s mission to rebuild its tariff wall. After the “reciprocal” duties Trump imposed in 2025 were invalidated earlier this year by the U.S. Supreme Court, the administration imposed a 10% tariff on the European Union, citing concerns that Brussels had failed to ban the import of goods made using forced labor. The higher of the two tariff rates will apply, rather than the two being added together, a senior U.S. official said . The official added that the proposed duties would likely take effect in January at the earliest, after USTR holds hearings and receives public comments. The chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, Bernd Lange, lambasted the conclusions of the USTR report as “absurd.” “Anyone who expected calmer waters after the midterm elections was mistaken. Few seriously expected that in the first place,” Lange said in a statement, referring to a Nov. 3 vote that returned firm majorities for the Democrats in the Senate and the House of Representatives. “Neither the Supreme Court ruling nor the verdict of the voters has swayed Donald Trump. When a court strikes down the legal basis for his tariffs, he looks for another. His aim remains the same. He uses tariffs to put pressure on trading partners and wring ever more concessions out of them.”

noticias.titulo: EU Parliament’s socialists and liberals halt talks with EPP
noticias.resumen: The three centrist groups were negotiating over deal that could have involved Roberta Metsola getting third term as president.
noticias.texto: STRASBOURG ― The Socialists & Democrats and liberal Renew Europe groups in the European Parliament have suspended talks on a centrist coalition deal with the center-right European People’s Party after it teamed up with the far right on a package of green legislation, according to two people familiar with the matter. The three political families were negotiating a written midterm coalition agreement ― with the S&D and Renew seeking to lock the EPP into working with the center parties after it repeatedly voted through key migration and climate legislation with the far right since the last EU election in 2024. As part of that deal, the EPP wanted the other two centrist groups to support incumbent Parliament President Roberta Metsola for a third term. This is a developing story.

Während Maximilian Krah vor einem Radikalismus warnt, der ein Parteiverbot provozieren könnte, und sich von Martin Sellner distanziert, bringt Tino Chrupalla millionenfache Abschiebungen ins Spiel. Die aktuellen Artikel zur AfD von Frederik Schindler bei WELT gibt’s hier . „Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands? Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch. Fragen und Feedback gern an insideafd@politico.eu . noticias.titulo: Parliament clears 7 EU budget files for negotiations
noticias.resumen: The vote headed off a possible challenge from the far right.
noticias.texto: The European Parliament voted by large majorities to send seven proposals for the EU’s next long-term budget straight into negotiations with the Council, heading off a possible challenge from the far right . The lawmakers were voting on the proposals for Global Europe , the European Social Fund , Horizon Europe , the Connecting Europe Facility , the European Competitiveness Fund , the asylum and migration program and AgoraEU . These proposals are now moving to negotiations with the Council of the European Union based on reports adopted by the committees responsible for each file.

noticias.titulo: Sánchez to skip EU summit before Spanish election
noticias.resumen: Spain's prime minister has picked French President Emmanuel Macron as his proxy.
noticias.texto: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will delegate his voting powers to French President Emmanuel Macron as he won’t be able to attend the European Council summit on Thursday and Friday, according to an EU diplomat. Spain heads to the polls on Sunday, with Sánchez at risk of losing his parliamentary majority. On Thursday evening, he will face conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, far-right leader Santiago Abascal and left-wing alliance chief Ada Colau in the final debate of the campaign. Wielding Spain’s vote as well as his own, Macron will have extra leverage at a summit dominated by bilateral negotiations between leaders. The extraordinary summit will kick off Thursday with a discussion among all leaders on the EU budget and a €45 billion loan to Ukraine, followed by several hours of restricted meetings, two EU diplomats said. Leaders will reconvene Friday morning to advance negotiations. Leaders will also sign off on the appointment of Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next European Central Bank chief on Friday morning, with Macron casting Spain’s vote as well. Sánchez has opted for a liberal leader from another big country, rather than delegating to fellow center-left figures such as Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen or Malta’s Robert Abela. Sánchez and Frederiksen have clashed over migration policy since the Danish leader teamed up with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to demand tougher border controls following the crisis in Spain’s enclave of Ceuta on the Moroccan border. Europe’s Social Democrats are set to formally discuss Frederiksen’s hard line on migration, particularly her backing for deportation hubs in Rwanda. This article was updated.

noticias.titulo: He’s coming home: Catalan leader Puigdemont plans return to Spain
noticias.resumen: The former Catalan president hinted he's prepared to lead the independence movement once again.
noticias.texto: Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont will return to Barcelona on Dec. 12, ending nearly a decade of self-imposed exile in Belgium. “I will return to Catalonia without asking for permission and without asking for forgiveness,” Puigdemont said at a press conference in Brussels on Wednesday. The former Catalan president initially fled to Belgium in October 2017 to avoid prosecution over his role in the region’s 2017 unauthorized independence referendum . Spanish authorities spent years trying to extradite the separatist leader but Belgian judges repeatedly thwarted their efforts. In 2024, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez opened the door to his return by securing the passage of a sweeping amnesty for those involved in the independence movement in exchange for crucial support from Puigdemont’s center-right Junts party. Spanish courts refused to apply the amnesty to Puigdemont, but after the EU’s top court ruled that he should benefit from the measure, Spain’s Constitutional Court this week lifted the remaining charges. In a 2024 interview with POLITICO, Puigdemont said he yearned to return to his hometown of Girona and “ become anonymous once again .” On Wednesday, however, he hinted at a renewed leading role in the separatist movement. “We need to update the strategy because we have learned from our mistakes,” he said, adding that he remained “committed to the independence of Catalonia.” His return could set the stage for a fresh confrontation with Madrid if the center-right People’s Party and far-right Vox emerge as the winners from Sunday’s snap election. Among other measures, both parties want to dissolve political forces that promote independence.

noticias.titulo: EPP votes with right-wing majority to relax EU nature laws, opening new rift in Parliament
noticias.resumen: The vote shows Europe’s lawmakers are still divided over how to balance environmental protection and industrial growth.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The center-right European People’s Party sided with the Parliament’s right-wing majority on Wednesday to push through a plan to speed up environmental assessments for industrial projects, after conservatives failed to reach an agreement with center-left lawmakers. The right-wing deal comes after Parliament’s centrist groups spent the last 24 hours scrambling to salvage a delicate political deal that ultimately broke down over a disagreement about the future of EU nature laws. It reflects a deepening chasm between the center-right European People’s Party and the center-left Socialists and Democrats — the two largest political groups in Parliament — over the bloc’s green agenda. “The political games that I have witnessed during this process leading up to this vote is a shame for this house and I am deeply disappointed with the working methods of the EPP,” said Renew MEP Emma Ytterell, who led the negotiations on the file. Renew and S&D lawmakers subsequently suspended broader talks on a centrist coalition deal with the EPP, in a move which has implications for the EU presidency . MEPs voted on a proposal that aims to accelerate environmental assessment processes for businesses to make it easier for them to launch industrial projects. It’s part of a so-called omnibus package put forward by the European Commission to simplify several EU environmental laws. Voted in with 367 lawmakers in favor, 268 against and 25 abstentions, Parliament’s adopted position calls on the European Commission to review two core EU nature conservation laws, the Birds and Habitats Directives, that protect threatened plant and animal species. The vote was supposed to take place on Tuesday, but was delayed after an agreement between the centrist Renew group, the center-right European People’s Party and the center-left Socialists and Democrats fell through over a disagreement about reopening these two EU nature laws. The deal collapsed when the EPP decided to support an amendment put forward by the right-wing European Conservatives & Reformists group, which called on the Commission to propose a legislative review of the Birds and Habitats Directives. That prompted the S&D to reject the deal altogether. “We reached out across political groups and put workable solutions on the table,” said Radan Kanev, a Bulgarian MEP who led the talks on behalf of the EPP group. “Unfortunately, an amendment out of the scope of the actual legislation became a dividing line, which prevented a broad majority for the final vote.” Negotiations between the centrist forces continued until late on Tuesday but the groups were unable to find a compromise. The ECR amendment made it into the final deal. Parliament’s final position also includes amendments from the far-right Patriots for Europe group that would exempt some types of forestry management activities from having to go through environmental assessments. The Patriots for Europe celebrated the deal, pointing to “another alternative majority” in Parliament in a post on the social media platform X. The group added that the proposal would lead to less red tape for “families, farmers and industry.” The MEPs still have to negotiate a final deal with EU governments in the Council of the EU before the law can come into force. This article has been updated.

noticias.titulo: Von der Leyen: Energy ceasefire would show Putin is serious about peace talks
noticias.resumen: “A strong European team will participate in the next round of talks” on Ukraine, the European Commission chief tells lawmakers.
noticias.texto: STRASBOURG — Vladimir Putin’s agreement to a winter energy ceasefire and a Black Sea truce to allow Ukrainian food exports “would show that Russia is serious about negotiations,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday morning. “As discussed at last week’s coalition of the willing meeting, Russia should agree to a winter ceasefire on energy infrastructure, and a truce to ensure the safe passage of food exports through the Black Sea,” she told European lawmakers at a Parliament debate in Strasbourg. Von der Leyen met with the coalition to discuss the European position on Ukraine-Russia peace talks brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump. She added the Commission was helping strengthen Kyiv’s hand at the negotiations by stepping up sanctions and providing cash so as to put pressure on Russia, which persistently bombards cities across Ukraine in an unrelenting military assault. The Commission on Monday proposed its 22nd sanctions package , which includes transaction bans on more Russian banks, restrictions on European companies helping Russia develop or maintain its energy infrastructure, an EU visa ban on current and former members of Russia’s armed forces, and a ban on Europeans sitting on the governing bodies of Russian companies. Sanctions “erode the foundations of Russia’s war, and we have many indicators pointing to a worsening outlook of the Russian economy,” she said. The strategy is twofold, she said: “First, maximum support for Ukraine, combined with maximum pressure on Russia. And second, full European engagement in negotiations for lasting peace.” She added that Europe’s financial support was a key part of the peace talks, and outlined the new loan structure to cover Ukraine’s 2027 needs, including €45 billion provided by the EU. “A strong European team will participate in the next round of talks,” she vowed. “We will judge progress based on Russia’s actions, not simply on its words.”

noticias.titulo: Ukraine’s raid in Libya damaged more than a Russian warship
noticias.resumen: Legal experts say the attack likely broke international law, undermining the rules that keep conflicts from spreading.
noticias.texto: Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO. Ukraine’s attack on a Russian warship in a Libyan port was a striking military success. It may also have broken international law. “An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war” was how Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauded Sunday’s sinking of the Merkury, one of Russia’s most advanced corvettes, docked at the time in Benghazi. Ukraine’s leader proudly announced on his Telegram channel that the operation, involving seven Ukrainian-made sea drones, had also disabled a Russian cargo ship suspected of transporting weapons. From a military perspective the operation was indeed another one of Ukraine’s audacious commando missions. It was reminiscent of the derring-do spirit of Winston Churchill’s “Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare,” better known as the Special Operations Executive, which mounted commando raids along the French coast, causing havoc and raising British wartime morale during WWII . In fact, the day before, while visiting Kyiv, Britain’s defense secretary Wes Streeting had coincidentally compared Zelenskyy to Britain’s iconic wartime leader. The comparison was ironic given the circumstances. Despite Churchill’s impatience and determination to take the fight to the enemy, the wartime prime minister was careful to avoid breaching the laws of armed conflict at sea. He didn’t, for example, order British warships to sink the German cruiser Admiral Graf Spee when it was cornered in Montevideo after the Battle of the River Plate. The trapped warship’s captain ultimately decided to scuttle the ship. But Zelenskyy wasn’t so restrained this week. According to international legal scholars, the attack likely violated international law as well as Libya’s sovereignty. The country’s eastern administration, based in Benghazi, has called on the U.N. to investigate the sinking as well as “reports regarding the presence of Ukrainian personnel, experts or military units” in western Libya. The Libyans would have a good case if they lodged a complaint with the International Court of Justice, said David Letts, a retired Australian naval officer and now director of the military law program at the Australian National University in Canberra. “Unless you’re wanting to mount an argument that Libya is somehow involved in the conflict between Ukraine and Russia and neutrality doesn’t apply, I’m struggling to see how this sinking sits within the law,” Letts said. Letts is one of the authors of the Newport Manual on the Law of Naval Warfare, a compilation of legislation published and updated by the U.S. Naval War College. He says Ukraine’s Benghazi attack is “quite different when compared to their strikes against Russian vessels in the Black Sea and in Black Sea ports” in disputed and not neutral waters. The laws of neutrality are largely based on the 1907 Hague Convention, which codified the rights and duties of non-belligerent states during armed conflicts. Under it, countries at war are prohibited from conducting attacks, blockades or mine-laying within neutral waters. In return, neutral states shouldn’t let belligerent warships turn their ports into military bases. Stays are generally limited to 24 hours, with exceptions for damage, repairs or poor weather. “The attack was a violation of Libya’s neutrality,” said James Kraska of the U.S. Naval War College and professor of international maritime law in the Stockton Center for International Law. “An attack is lawful if it’s beyond 12 nautical miles from the coastline, but, of course, inside it’s a violation.” “Now on the Ukrainian side, what their argument might be is that a belligerent warship ought only to stay 24 hours in a foreign neutral port. If it goes beyond 24 hours, then the warship is at risk, and Libya might not be in compliance,” Kraska, a retired U.S. Navy commander, told POLITICO. “If there’s inclement weather, or repairs are needed to make it seaworthy, then the time can be extended,” he added. Some scholars, he added, would argue that Ukraine would need to contact the Libyan authorities to find out the status. In terms of its boldness and reach, Monday’s attack wasn’t entirely unprecedented. In March, Libyan authorities reported damage to the Russian gas tanker Arctic Metagaz while it was en route to Egypt. Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the tanker with naval drones likely launched from Western Libya. Kyiv neither confirmed nor denied its involvement. The governments of Sudan, Mali and Niger have also accused Ukrainian special forces of mounting operations in their countries, where Russian mercenary soldiers are present. Kyiv has denied those allegations. This time, though, Kyiv has proudly admitted sinking the Merkury in a neutral port. Why? And does the breach of law on neutrality actually matter? Zelenskyy’s office didn’t respond to questions from POLITICO on the sinking, including as to whether it had sought counsel from senior government law officers before approving the attack, and whether it had notified Libyan authorities beforehand to request the ship leave Benghazi. In the past, when questions of neutrality have arisen or Ukraine has been accused of breaching the laws of warfare, Kyiv has said this is no time for niceties as it is the aggrieved nation. When a U.N. monitoring mission in 2023 alleged abuse of Russian POWs, for example, the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry thanked the mission for documenting Russia’s violations but pushed back on the claims against Kyiv, arguing: “We consider it unacceptable to place responsibility on the victim of aggression.” Former U.K. diplomat Tim Willasey-Wilsey, now a fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a defense think tank in London with close ties to Ukraine’s defense ministry, says that when it comes to the sinking of the Merkury, he doesn’t believe the legal issues are important. “Who gives a stuff, really, you know? To be honest, I don’t think the legality particularly matters.” He said the biggest political risk for Kyiv is diminishing the “remarkable degree of Western support for Ukraine,” and so was reassured when Wes Streeting came out so quickly in support. The attack, he said, reflected desperation in Ukraine, where ballistic missile attacks are devastating civilian infrastructure, itself a violation by Russia of international law. “The war is clearly getting more and more visceral, and I think the timing of the Benghazi attack is testimony to the sense of desperation that there is now in Kyiv.” But turning a blind eye to the Benghazi attack only adds to the erosion of international legal norms and the undermining of the post-1945 “rules-based international order,” which Moscow and Beijing have little time for. It makes the seas more dangerous. Letts stressed how important it is for countries like Ukraine to stick to what’s legal. “I wonder what the attitude would be if this vessel had been docked in Genoa or Southampton, say, rather than Benghazi,” he added. “I think there’s an element here of ‘It was only over there, so it doesn’t really matter.’” “Having built up a body of law that tries to protect victims of armed conflict, tries to limit the scope of armed conflicts, are we willing to wave goodbye to all of that?” he asked. “Are we willing just to have total warfare with all the rules gone and to say, ‘The last 100 years or so are a waste of time. Do whatever you want.’ I don’t think we are.”

noticias.titulo: Violence against women in the digital age: When the internet becomes a weapon

noticias.titulo: Slovakia’s Fico snubbed Poland and Europe, insulted Ukraine veterans (again), and callously lied about Putin’s war (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,734)
noticias.resumen: As Slovak PM Robert Fico shrugs off war in Lviv and snubs both Warsaw and Brussels, thousands of grieving families, maimed soldiers and fresh Russian strikes in western Ukraine expose just how far his rhetoric has drifted from the front’s brutal reality.
noticias.texto: An attempt to explain to Slovakia’s prime minister that there is a war in Lviv. The situation in Kupiansk is worsening. New details about the disastrous Ukrainian attack on Toretsk last spring, and a comparison with the current situation. Maps of the day – Kupiansk and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi; Toretsk in May 2025; Toretsk and Kostiantynivka in November 2026 . Videos of the day – Ukrainians received their first Lynx fighting vehicles and shared interesting details about them; the Russians captured Popasna on 7 May 2022, and today it is 40 km from the front line and a ghost town; a pickup truck is missing a wheel, so soldiers replaced it with a tree stump. An attempt to explain to Slovakia’s prime minister that there is a war in Lviv. “There is simply not even a hint of any war in Lviv. The war there is concentrated primarily on the front line,” Robert Fico said on Wednesday (25 November) morning at the Slovak parliament’s European affairs committee, following his recent visit to Lviv, in Western Ukraine. He also reiterated to MPs that Slovakia would not support the €45bn loan for Ukraine. He described the European Commission’s effort to split it into two parts, with €25bn going to military aid and €20bn to civilian aid, as “a trick by the Commission”. Fico made these remarks just two days after Polish prime minister Donald Tusk called on him to show solidarity with Poland , whose territory was hit by Russian cruise missiles. “I do not know whether this appeal will touch your soul, but I am certain that this issue will determine Europe’s future,” Tusk said about aid to Ukraine. This is not the first time the Slovak prime minister has cast doubt on Ukraine’s suffering. While he himself has not yet dared to travel to Kyiv, on 23 January 2024 he nonetheless arrogantly declared : “Do you seriously think there is a war in Kyiv? Surely you cannot be serious. Life there is completely normal.” By then, the Ukrainian capital had already been targeted by air raids for two years. It cannot be assumed that Fico lacks the means to verify the real situation in Lviv, so the most likely explanation is that he is knowingly lying. Another possibility is that, under the influence of Russian propaganda, he has completely lost touch with reality. The following lines are an attempt to explain to the Slovak prime minister what city and what country he repeatedly insults with his remarks. noticias.titulo: EU commission proposes €50bn tech fund to buy into AI, quantum and other strategic companies
noticias.resumen: The EU Commission has presented plans to launch a €50bn tech sovereignty fund to take stakes in strategic companies to prevent them leaving to the US or China.
noticias.texto: The European Commission on Wednesday (25 November) revealed the first details of a future fund with a target size of €50bn designed to take direct stakes in strategic companies so that they remain in Europe. “We are now creating the legal basis so that we can set up such a fund,” said Henna Virkkunen, the EU’s tech sovereignty chief. She called the fund’s size a “target” and a “sufficient starting point” which is meant to “leverage” further investments worth €400-500bn, she said. Some member states already have smaller sovereign funds of their own. But investment needs in critical technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum computing or other ‘deep tech’ sectors, “often need investments of hundreds of millions of euros,” she said. “We have to really pool our resources in Europe,” she said, adding that the EU does not have that kind of equity fund at European level. noticias.titulo: EU court rules commission failed to act on citizens’ initiative calling for ban on animal cages
noticias.resumen: In the first ruling of its kind, the European Court of Justice decided that insufficient action was taken by the EU Commission after 1.4 million people signed an European Citizens’ Initiative petition to ban cages for farmed animals. The Brussels executive is expected to propose a cage phase-out plan in December.
noticias.texto: By delaying its response to requests for a ban on cages for farmed animals, the EU Commission failed to meet its legal obligations, the EU court has found. In the first ruling of its kind, the European Court of Justice decided on Wednesday (25 November) that insufficient action was taken after 1.4 million people signed a European Citizens’ Initiative petition to ban cages for farmed animals. In its judgment, the General Court in Luxembourg upheld the action of a citizens’ committee seeking a declaration that the commission failed to act. The commission is legally obliged to respond to petitions once they reach 1m or more signatures. In 2021, it responded positively to ‘ End the Cage Age ’ after MEPs also voted to endorse the initiative. But the Brussels executive is yet to propose the animal rights legislation that the petition requested. Read more Poll shows public revulsion on caged hens ahead of EU-ban deadline ‘Historic victory for animals’ The court decision was “a historic victory for animals and for democracy in Europe”, said Annamaria Pisapia, a spokesperson for the petitioners. noticias.titulo: A Russian plan to federalise Moldova could give it a window to control access to EU membership
noticias.resumen: A reported Russian plan to federalise Moldova would hand the Kremlin a lever over who joins the EU. Europe should rule it out before it reaches the table.
noticias.texto: Moscow’s strategy in its negotiations with Ukraine is no secret. The war’s resolution is no longer the sole subject of bilateral talks, but rather one item in a long list of maximalist demands. Russia now demands a new “security architecture” for all of Europe, with the war’s end a secondary priority. It is not hard to compare this stance with Russia’s December 2021 ultimatum, demanding that Nato members commit to no further enlargement of the alliance and a ban on Nato activity in Eastern Europe. Moldova, yet again, finds itself directly at the centre of Russia’s confrontation with the West. In late November 2003, Vladimir Putin was preparing to fly to Chișinău to witness the signing of the Kozak Memorandum, a Russian plan to turn Moldova into an asymmetric federation in which the breakaway region of Transnistria would hold a blocking vote over national decisions. The plan collapsed the night before. Under heavy Western pressure, Moldova’s leadership withdrew its consent, and Putin never boarded the plane. Twenty-three years later, the same idea appears to be back. This time, the idea is subsumed within the negotiations over Ukraine. Europe risks watching from the corridor. Read more War of propaganda: Russia calls Ukraine a ‘burden’ and uses Moldova as a ‘testing ground’ to sabotage EU enlargement Russian outlet Eho, citing sources close to the talks , reported this week that Moscow is seeking to restructure Moldova as a federation of Moldova, Transnistria and Gagauzia, with independence referendums in the two regions should Moldova join the European Union. The proposal would reportedly also include the withdrawal of Russian troops from Transnistria in exchange for a Moldovan commitment not to join any military alliance. The report is unconfirmed. But its logic fits Russian policy so closely that European capitals cannot afford to dismiss it. Read more [Interview] Moldova races for EU membership by 2030: ‘We owe this chance to Ukrainians’, minister says A veto over enlargement The most dangerous element is the referendum clause, because it targets the EU itself. Moldova’s 1994 law on Gagauzia already grants the region a right to external self-determination, if Moldova’s status as an independent state changes. The reported proposal would attach an explicit secession trigger to EU membership. If incorporated into a settlement, this provision would attach the threat of territorial fragmentation to Moldova’s European integration. The referendum need never take place for that threat to shape accession. Any Moldovan government would have to pursue membership knowing that it could trigger a new secession crisis. Moscow would gain a means of obstructing accession through Moldova’s internal politics. Russia’s economic leverage in Transnistria has weakened, with Gazprom’s direct supplies stopping in January 2025, while the EU accounted for 76.9 per cent of the region’s exports in the first half of 2026. A settlement of the kind reported would offer Moscow a means of converting that weakening material leverage into a lasting role in Moldova’s constitutional order. Read more [Interview] ‘Whenever we take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies’. Moldova energy minister Dorin Junghietu on why Chișinău is betting on diversification Moscow has responded with escalating threats. Russia’s deputy foreign minister Mikhail Galuzin warned that Moscow would treat any attempt to force reunification as an act of war against Russia. More recently, Russia’s envoy to the OSCE claimed that Chișinău’s fiscal policy toward the region could provoke a new military confrontation. Moscow is treating the extension of Moldova’s fiscal rules as grounds for escalation. Gagauzia has no frozen conflict, no separatist army and no line of contact, despite latent tensions. Its inclusion extends the proposal beyond settling the Transnistrian conflict and into restructuring Moldova’s national decision-making. A federal settlement granting Moscow-aligned regional leaderships blocking powers over national decisions could extend Russian influence into Moldova’s central institutions. Read more EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe What Europe should do This is where Europe’s responsibility begins. Washington is in a hurry to close a deal, and a small candidate country on Europe’s periphery can look like a cheap concession from across the Atlantic. It is not cheap for the EU. The EU has opened accession negotiations with Moldova, committed €1.9bn through its Growth Plan and is now funding its air defences. All of that would be hollowed out by a settlement that hands Moscow a lever over Moldova’s constitution. Europe does not need a new policy, only to use the leverage it already has. First, the EU and its member states should state publicly that Moldova’s constitutional order and its accession path are not negotiable in any format without Moldova. Second, the mandate of Europe’s negotiator should include the full withdrawal of Russian troops and munitions as an unfulfilled Russian obligation. In May, the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas argued that Russian withdrawal from Transnistria should be one of the EU’s demands in negotiations with Moscow. That demand should be explicit in any European negotiating mandate. That promise should now be written down. Third, Europe should refuse any sanctions relief or return of Russian gas while Russian troops remain on the territory of an EU candidate. Chișinău should turn its existing reintegration measures into a clearer political offer, with explicit guarantees for residents of the left bank, and Brussels should be ready to support it. It should put forward its own reintegration offer, with clear guarantees for residents of Transnistria within a unitary state, and Brussels should be ready to fund it. If there is no plan from Chișinău and Brussels on the table, it will consider one from Moscow.

noticias.titulo: ‘No woman is immune’ – AI ‘nudifiers’ that strip clothes from photos are thriving in Italian Telegram groups, report finds
noticias.resumen: Italian authorities, like Brussels, have been slow in combating anonymous online abuse targeting women through intimate photos. New research reveals just how quickly these groups reproduce.
noticias.texto: Social media groups sharing non-consensual images of women, mostly from men known to them, are popping up as fast as one is shut down in Italy – dominated by automated nudity. Paris-based NGO AI Forensics tracked four Italian Telegram communities circulating image-based sexual abuse material between September and November 2026, and found that these groups were quickly being replaced by others after they were found out. Invitation links for backup groups would remain pinned on the communities’ websites, which administrators prepared in case of a ban. In a report released on Wednesday (25 November), AI Forensics revealed that a third of the four groups’ messages engaged in seeking, offering, trading or selling intimate material depicting a real woman that is most likely known to the perpetrator. Partners represented 12 percent of the groups’ targets, while five percent were acquaintances, 3.5 percent ex-partners, and 3.8 percent family members. Read more Women MEPs targeted by AI ‘nudifier’ apps push EU leaders to enforce December ban The revelations hit particularly hard following the ‘Mia moglie’ scandal , after an Italian Facebook group whose name translates to ‘my wife’ was found to be circulating images of 32.000 members’ partners and acquaintances in a swimsuit or nude without their knowledge. The subsequent response by authorities revealed a slow process that was easy to subvert by quickly disappearing and replacing groups. noticias.titulo: Listen: Can the United States actually dismantle the International Criminal Court?
noticias.resumen: Tajikistan has officially announced that it wants to leave the International Criminal Court. This comes as Donald Trump steps up his campaign against the court, with Washington threatening sanctions and putting diplomatic pressure on its allies. So, how serious is the threat to the ICC?
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : Tajikistan has officially announced that it wants to leave the International Criminal Court (ICC). This comes as Donald Trump steps up his campaign against the court, with Washington threatening sanctions and putting diplomatic pressure on its allies. So, how serious is the threat to the ICC? Tajikistan was until now the only country in Central Asia to have ratified the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC. And it’s not the only country withdrawing. No fewer than six other countries have notified the UN of their intention to withdraw this year: Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Venezuela, Chad and Nauru. Another blow to the court came last week, when Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping issued a joint declaration warning the court not to abuse its jurisdiction. Here’s a quick reminder of what the ICC is, and what it isn’t. The ICC was established in 2002. Its job is to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of four of the most serious international crimes: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. The ICC is a court of last resort. It is supposed to step in only when national authorities are unwilling or genuinely unable to investigate and prosecute these crimes themselves. Read more The clock is ticking: Europe is running out of time to save the International Criminal Court That’s how it came to issue an arrest warrant against Russian president Vladimir Putin in March 2023 over the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia. In November 2024, the court issued arrest warrants against Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant. They are accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, including using starvation as a method of warfare. Those warrants were made possible by the fact that the ICC can investigate crimes committed on the territory of a member state, even when the alleged perpetrators come from a country that has never accepted its authority. It can also exercise jurisdiction when the accused is a national of a member state, or when the UN Security Council refers a situation to it. Now, Washington wants to challenge that principle and, more broadly, dismantle the ICC. The US is seeking to prevent the ICC from exercising jurisdiction over individuals from countries that are not members of the court, even when the alleged crimes were committed on the territory of a member state. Such a change would fundamentally alter the court’s reach. On top of that, the Trump administration is also putting pressure on the ICC and its member states. According to Politico , US diplomats have been urging NATO allies to withdraw from the Rome Statute and immediately stop providing material support to the court. Read more International Criminal Court wins EU’s top human rights prize in defiance of Trump’s sanctions We cannot say whether the seven countries that have notified their withdrawal this year have done so because of US pressure. But the timing is noteworthy, particularly in the cases of Venezuela, Chad, Nauru and Tajikistan. And then, there are the sanctions. Over the past months, Washington has sanctioned several judges and prosecutors, including the court’s president, Tomoko Akane . In October this year, the United States went a step further and sanctioned the ICC as an institution. These sanctions have concrete consequences: restrictions on financial transactions, frozen assets, and bans on entering the United States, among other things. According to MEP Chloé Ridel, these sanctions are already affecting the ICC’s work: the prosecutor’s activities have slowed down, and some people have been sidelined from certain cases. But can the US actually dismantle the ICC? If fewer countries cooperate, the court becomes increasingly difficult to operate. The court still has 125 member states, and the withdrawal process takes time. But its ability to function depends heavily on international cooperation, financial resources and political support. The combination of American sanctions, diplomatic pressure and growing opposition from major powers is, however, sending a very negative signal about respect for international law. That’s why many actors are calling on the EU to activate its Blocking Statute, in order to neutralise the effects of US sanctions in Europe, at least. This would not be a game changer, but it could make the ICC’s work slightly easier if fewer companies were reluctant to work with the court because of the risk of US sanctions. So far, however, the commission has not proposed activating it.

noticias.titulo: Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit
noticias.resumen: EU leaders are heading for a clash over the bloc’s next long-term budget, with deep divisions over its size, new revenue sources and funding for Ukraine. German chancellor Friedrich Merz is demanding that all 27 member states contribute to Kyiv’s needs, while several countries are seeking opt-outs.
noticias.texto: EU leaders are expected to clash on Thursday and Friday (26 and 27 November) over the latest proposal for the next EU budget, presented by EU Council president António Costa. Ukraine financing for 2027 is also set to be divisive – after German chancellor Friedrich Merz threatened to block the whole budget unless all 27 member states help pay for Kyiv’s needs. Costa’s revised “negotiating box,” unveiled last Saturday, cuts the overall size of the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028-2034 by €204bn in current prices, compared with the European Commission’s initial proposal of July 2025. It is also a further €40bn cut to the previous plan presented by the Irish presidency in early October. “On the MFF, the time has come to reach an agreement,” Costa said in his invitation letter to EU leaders on Tuesday (24 November), which also referred to the need to meet “Ukraine’s financing needs for 2027 … and beyond”. Costa said the EU has a collective “responsibility” to deliver a budget that could help the bloc deal with the challenges ahead, while keeping national contributions “reasonable”. To square that circle, he is relying heavily on new revenue sources, known in Brussels jargon as “own resources”, which he said could generate about €60bn a year. The main novelty is a digital tax, an old French idea backed by the European Parliament. Read more EU lawmakers target US Big Tech with budget-financing levy Other revenues would come from the Emissions Trading System (ETS) , the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) , a levy on electronic waste and tobacco excise duties. On top of that, taxing crypto assets and earning revenue from radio spectrum auctions are also on the table. The problem with own resources is that they are a hard sell, because they are extra taxes that need unanimous backing from all EU member states. Costa’s proposal has already received criticism from the so-called frugal countries, including Austria, Denmark, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden, which believe it is still too high, and from the so-called cohesion friends, who say it is too low. Read more Costa’s EU budget plan for 10 percent cuts pits ‘frugals’ against ‘cohesion’ group ahead of crunch summit Sweden’s EU affairs minister, Jessica Rosencrantz, for example, said on Saturday that the budget remained too large and that Sweden’s contribution would rise far too much under the plan. Poland, for its part, leads the opposition to new EU own resources based on ETS, alongside Finland and the Czech Republic, and despite Costa’s proposal for a gradual phase-in from zero percent in 2028 to 30 percent by 2034. On Monday, the Visegrád Four (Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia) leaders, together with Austria, rejected Costa’s offer as “unacceptable” after a meeting in Bratislava. noticias.titulo: [Interview] Cutting funds for Erasmus+ student scheme would be ‘giving up’ on Europe’s future, says lead MEP Zdrojewski
noticias.resumen: Students need not fear deep cuts to the Erasmus+ exchange scheme in the next EU budget, despite the frugal winds blowing from member states, says Bogdan Zdrojewski, a Polish MEP who is the EU Parliament's lead negotiator on the programme.
noticias.texto: As EU leaders gather in Brussels on Thursday and Friday (26 and 27 November) to discuss budget cuts for 2028 to 2034, even darling projects, such as the student-exchange programme, Erasmus+, risk losing out. The student scheme, which turns 40 this year, has helped over 17 million people to study and live outside their home country. Some 78 percent of participants say they improved their language skills and more than a quarter met their long-term partner during the exchange. But Polish centre-right MEP Bogdan Zdrojewski, who is in charge of negotiating Erasmus+ funding on behalf of the European Parliament, told EUobserver he remained optimistic despite the prevailingly frugal atmosphere. In your report of 22 October you outlined what Erasmus + should look like in the next financing cycle. Compared to what the European Commission proposed, you asked for an additional €7bn. How realistic do you consider this ask? We have to remember that we were starting with €26bn, which is the amount allocated for the current budget. It was important for us to increase that to account for inflation, including rising cost of living for students staying in different European cities. The most common demand was that we should take a more realistic approach to the differences in the cost of living between individual cities. We tried to demonstrate to the European Commission just how substantial the changes needed to be. We wanted to move away from a one-size-fits-all nominal amount and introduce greater flexibility. We also wanted that the situation would be monitored every year, possibly introducing adjustments. Another point is the overall budget. I was particularly keen to bring it up to around €50bn. NGOs and organisations working with young people suggested that it would be an appropriate response to the current needs. Read more Costa’s EU budget plan for 10 percent cuts pits ‘frugals’ against ‘cohesion’ group ahead of crunch summit The parliament backed your report by 454 votes against only 93 – an overwhelming majority. What makes Erasmus+ so popular with MEPs? It has become popular only now. I was responsible for the Erasmus+ programme during the 2014–2019 period, and I remember one MEP who argued that it should be discontinued because it had already fulfilled its purpose. We had overcome the barrier symbolised by the Berlin Wall, students could now travel freely, and there was no longer any need for an Erasmus+ programme, he said. He even used a rather striking metaphor to justify his position: He claimed that young people were now doing nothing but having fun, and that the only outcome of this fun was not learning, but children being born as a result of Erasmus. But he was unlucky: Just two or three weeks later, at the very same committee meeting, he accused the European Commission of having no programme to address demographic challenges. I replied that there was such a programme, and it was called Erasmus+: there are already 1 million children born to couples who met during the exchange. That was a time [2014-2019 term] when Erasmus+ had many opponents. This time, however, that was not the case. I did not hear a single voice calling for Erasmus+ to be discontinued. “If the programme were cut by, say, 30 percent, I would be absolutely devastated and would conclude that Europe was giving up on its future” What has changed since then to persuade even the eurosceptics? noticias.titulo: Oil and gas firms join Big Tech push for faster EU data centre permits and weaker green rules
noticias.resumen: Eni, ExxonMobil and EDF are among the fossil-fuel firms that lobbied the European Commission to fast-track data centres, new research by Corporate Europe Observatory shows.
noticias.texto: Fossil-fuel companies and associated lobby groups held at least 54 meetings with the EU Commission on data centres and AI infrastructure between December 2024 and the end of October 2026. This is according to findings published on Wednesday (25 November) by the Brussels-based lobby watchdog Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO). The lobbying is aimed at EU plans to triple its data centre capacity within five to seven years, as spelled out in a commission proposal circulated in June. Companies and their interest groups accounted for nearly 94 percent of all lobby meetings on the file, CEO found. Read more Loophole in new EU labelling will let fossil-fuelled data-centres pass as ‘green’ Italian oil major Eni was the most active fossil-fuel firm and had at least six meetings with senior officials on AI and data centres between December 2024 and October 2026. In its submission , Eni asked that the commission’s data centre approach “be grounded in the principle of technological neutrality” and that power from gas combined with “carbon management strategies” be put on an “equal footing” with renewables. In Italy, Eni already markets this as so-called ‘blue power’. The lobby watchdog however describes carbon capture “a get-out-of-jail-free card” that has failed to deliver on its promises of avoiding global warming. EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra also criticised the central role given to the technology at the UN climate talks in Antalya, which failed over the weekend, telling reporters that carbon capture “falls from the sky as if it is the solution to the whole problem.” Read more Carbon capture doesn’t work — yet the EU is going for it ExxonMobil, French energy giant EDF, Finnish utility Fortum and big business lobbies with oil and gas firms on their boards, such as BusinessEurope, and the German and Dutch business associations, also lobbied the commission on its data centre plans. They wanted quicker permits and fewer environmental rules, much like Big Tech did, as CEO and Dutch research group SOMO documented earlier this month. Google for its part tried to push the commission to limit the right to object to data centre projects to “immediate neighbours and only during the zoning process” meaning that in practice a complaint would more often come too late. Google also pointed to Austria, where only people living within 50 metres of a project can challenge a permit, and urged the commission to introduce the system in all EU member states. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. Visit account.euobserver.com/membership

noticias.titulo: Sánchez admite que Ábalos le ha hecho "mucho daño" y critica que PP y Vox pongan en cuestión la limpieza del proceso electoral
noticias.texto:
Sánchez admite que Ábalos le ha hecho "mucho daño" y critica que PP y Vox pongan en cuestión la limpieza del proceso electoral
La Hora de la 1
- El candidato socialista apuesta por "regular" e "intervenir" el mercado de la vivienda si logra una "mayoría progresista"
- "El sistema de pensiones goza de una extraordinaria salud", defiende Sánchez
El presidente del Gobierno y candidato socialista a la reelección, Pedro Sánchez, ha admitido en una entrevista en La Hora de la 1 que el caso de corrupción que ha llevado a prisión al exministro José Luis Ábalos le ha hecho "mucho daño" y ha defendido que su Gobierno es "íntegro" y que sus ministros han dedican "muchas horas al servicio público".
"Yo elijo a mucha gente, durante mis años de Gobierno he nombrado a entre 54 y 56 ministros de mi país", ha sostenido, para insistir en la "integridad" de su Ejecutivo. "La corrupción cero no existe, pero la tolerancia cero sí existe, hemos sido contundentes", ha afirmado.
Sánchez, asimismo, ha defendido que tras la dimisión de Santos Cerdán el PSOE ha reforzado y cumple con las recomendaciones del Consejo de Transparencia y sostiene que son "el partido más transparente, a diferencia de PP y de Vox".
Critica que PP y Vox pongan en cuestión la limpieza del proceso electoral
Sánchez también ha criticado que PP y Vox pongan en cuestión la limpieza del proceso electoral y les pide que acepten los resultados del 29 de noviembre. "Estamos viendo que el PP y Vox están de los nervios con la movilización. Que lo haga Vox... ¿pero que lo haga el PP? Están poniendo en duda la limpieza del sistema electoral", ha alertado.
"Les inquietan las urnas de cartón de los consulados ante la participación que está habiendo", ha dicho Sánchez, en referencia a algunos comentarios de miembros del PP.
"Me parece preocupante, no es la primera ni la segunda vez que el PP no reconoce los resultados y Vox ha dicho que reconocerá los resultados si no se hace trampa", ha remarcado.
Sánchez apuesta por "regular" e "intervenir" el mercado de la vivienda
El candidato socialista a la reelección ha respondido también sobre la problemática de la vivienda. Según él, es necesario "regular" e "intervenir" el mercado de la vivienda para garantizar el derecho a una vivienda digna y evitar una nueva "burbuja inmobiliaria". En este sentido, ha acusado al PP, Vox y Junts per Catalunya de ejercer de "tapón" a estas políticas.
Por ello, ha pedido una "mayoría reforzada progresista" en las próximas elecciones generales para poder actuar con "más fuerza" en materias como la vivienda a lo largo de los próximos cuatro años.
Sobre medidas concretas, Sánchez ha apuntado a dar capacidad a las comunidades de vecinos para decidir sobre la apertura de apartamentos turísticos, aplicarles el IVA turístico o crear bonificaciones fiscales para pequeños propietarios e inquilinos.
Garantiza la viabilidad del sistema público de pensiones
Sánchez no ha dejado ninguna duda sobre la viabilidad del sitema público de pensiones. "El sistema de pensiones goza de una extraordinaria salud", ha dicho el presidente del Gobierno.
Para mantener vigente este sistema, el candidato socialista ha dicho que es necesario que la seguridad social ingrese más recursos a través de la subida de los salarios y también con más personas cotizando. En este sentido, ha apuntado a la regularización de personas migrantes como una vía para que España cuente con más trabajadores que aporten a la caja común.
"Salarios, más gente trabajando y la productividad sostendrán el sistema de pensiones", ha zanjado.
Sostiene que "no hay elementos ciertos" para hacer responsable a Marruecos de la crisis de Ceuta
Pedro Sánchez, sobre la crisis migratoria en Ceuta, sostiene que "no hay elementos ciertos para decir con rotundidad" que la entrada masiva de migrantes a finales de julio pasado "provenga del régimen marroquí". Es más,m ha dicho que su experiencia constata "que la cooperación con el régimen de Marruecos" ayudó en el control fronterizo, "pues exigió una cooperación muy intensa durante esas horas y esos días y continúa siéndolo".
También se ha referido a la crisis migratoria que vive Canarias, con una constante llegada de cayucos a la isla de El Hierro. "Hablamos con autoridades de Senegal y Gambia, esperemos que se puede reducir la llegada de cayucos los próximos días", ha dicho. Asimismo, ha garantizado que España tiene una capacidad de acogida que permite "atender con dignidad a estos seres humanos que llegan a Canarias".
Sánchez reprocha al CGPJ que guarde silencio con el PP
También en la entrevista en La Hora de la 1, Sánchez se ha quejado de que el Consejo General del Poder Judicial (CGPJ), "en su vertiente conservadora" se ha expresado "con excesivo celo" cuando él ha manifestado su opinión contraria a alguna decisión judicial, pero no hacen lo mismo con "dirigentes de la derecha".
Además, considera "sorprendentes" algunas decisiones judiciales como suspender el derecho al voto de nacionalizados por la 'ley de nietos' y considera que se está "cercenando" un derecho fundamental. Asimismo, y aunque ha dicho que debe ser "contenido" en sus expresiones, sostiene que hay decisiones judiciales "francamente sorprendentes" y piensa que es una opinión compartida con un gran número de ciudadanos.

noticias.titulo: El PP considera un "asalto institucional" que el Gobierno use los reales decretos como "herramienta electoral"
noticias.texto:
El PP considera un "asalto institucional" que el Gobierno use los reales decretos como "herramienta electoral"
Las Mañanas de RNE
- Asegura que para el PP la lucha contra la violencia de género es "sagrada"
- También cuestiona el voto por correo y el voto en "urna de cartón"
El vicesecretario de Cultura y portavoz del PP, Borja Sémper, ha considerado este miércoles "bochornoso" y un "asalto institucional insoportable" que el Gobierno utilice los reales decretos como "herramienta electoral".
En una entrevista electoral en Las Mañanas de RNE, el también número 3 por Madrid del PP al Congreso ha lamentado que se haya "naturalizado cosas que no deberíamos haber naturalizado", en referencia a la aprobación de decretos leyes en los últimos Consejos de Ministros con medidas sociales, como la ampliación de los permisos laborales por maternidad y paternidad. "Me parece una vergüenza", ha insistido.
Sémper ha apuntado que "ahora deprisa y corriendo" el Gobierno de coalición están aprobando "cosas que no se han hecho en ocho años" e incluso, volviendo a aprobar medidas como los decretos de vivienda que fueron tumbados por el Congreso, usando así "el Consejo de Ministros para hacer política electoral".
Para el dirigente 'popular', no solo es censurable hacer campaña electoral desde el Consejo de Ministros, sino que también estén "comprometiendo decenas de miles de euros sin tener presupuestos y condicionando al futuro Gobierno".
Por otro lado, ha anunciado que "lo primero" que hará el PP si llega el Gobierno es "un plan de vivienda, una nueva ley del suelo, ley antiokupación, y medidas fiscales para acceder a la vivienda a los jóvenes".
También cuestiona el voto por correo
Al igual que hiciera este martes, el líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, Sémper también ha cuestionado el voto por correo y en especial ha sembrado dudas sobre las urnas de cartón en algunos países. "Puede no parecer propio de una democracia consolidada y es una imagen a erradicar porque no proyecta seguridad", ha señalado. Aunque ha asegurado que en el PP confían "en nuestros cónsules y en el procedimiento".
En cuanto a la posibilidad de cuestionar el resultado si los 'populares' no ganan, como dijo el presidente del Gobierno y candidato del PSOE a la reelección, Pedro Sánchez, Sémper ha garantizado que "como ha hecho siempre el PP, se va a respetar cualquier resultado electoral".
Y preguntado por las palabras de Feijóo asegurando que los informativos de RTVE parecían "norcoreanos", el portavoz del PP ha incidido en que "la televisión española ha experimentado un retroceso en su función social preocupante, en materia social, cultural y ha incrementado en la escaleta el contenido político". Por ello, ha defendido que hay que "revertirlo". "Una televisión que habla más de política no es la televisión pública que merece España", ha zanjado.
Asegura que el PP no admitirá "retrocesos" en la lucha contra la violencia de género
Con motivo del Día Internacional de la Eliminación de la Violencia hacia la Mujer, Sémper ha asegurado que el PP no admitirá "ningún retroceso" en la lucha contra la violencia de género, si bien ha admitido que también quieren incorporar la lucha contra otras violencias.
"Para el PP es sagrada la lucha contra la violencia contra la mujer. Es incuestionable. Pero además, hay otras violencias que tienen un impacto social desgarrador", ha defendido tras ser cuestionado por si posible Gobierno pactado con Vox podría afectar a la lucha contra la violencia de género, ya que este partido prefiere hablar de violencia intrafamiliar en lugar de violencia de género.
Y ha insistido: "La violencia contra la mujer es tan obvia que no hay que diluirla. Pero hay que incorporar también otras violencias, como la que ocurre en el entorno familiar", ha sostenido.
No obstante, ha querido dejar claro que los posibles pactos con los de Santiago Abascal "no van a desdibujar los avances que ha experimentado la sociedad española estos años" y se ha referido en concreto también a "las políticas de igualdad u orientación sexual". "Esas líneas son infranqueables", ha asegurado. Además, ha pedido dejar de usar este tema "de manera partidista".
Sémper ha señalado que "la violencia de género nos interpela a todos" y que la cifra de "47 mujeres asesinadas este año es insoportable". Por ello, ha abogado por incorporar medidas al Plan Nacional contra la Violencia de Género, como "mejorar el sistema de reacción y protección a las mujeres, reforzar la capacidad de la Policía Nacional y Guardia Civil en la persecución del delito, ampliar la prisión permanente revisable para los agresores sexuales y asesinos y reforzar el sistema Viogen e incorporarlo al Ministerio del Interior".
La política migratoria y la política exterior
Preguntado por la crisis migratoria y cómo habría actuado el PP si hubiera estado en el Gobierno, el portavoz 'popular' ha admitido que "no hay una varita mágica para solucionarlo", pero ha abogado por "aplicar una política de inmigración realista".
Entre sus medidas, ha señalado que no se puede "permitir que Argelia, Marruecos, Senegal o Mauritania miren para otro lado o utilicen la inmigración para presionar a Europa o España". También ha advertido de que "España no puede acoger más inmigración irregular porque los servicios públicos están tensionados".
Así, ha defendido que hay que "vincular" la inmigración a un puesto de trabajo. "Quien venga a nuestro país, tiene que venir con un contrato de trabajo o a con la pobilidad de trabajar". Además, ha sostenido que hay que "evitar que lleguen" y si vienen "garantizar que vuelvan" a sus países, y para ello, ha asegurado que es "fundamental" la política diplomática y trabajar en origen.
Sobre política exterior, Sémper ha considerado que la llevada a cabo por el Gobierno estos años ha sido "equivocada" y que siempre se ha actuado en "términos partidistas". "Se ha convertido en algo habitual que lo que ocurre en el mundo se convierte en debate nacional", ha criticado. Además, ha defendido que "independientemente de quien gobierne en EE.UU., las relaciones deben ser óptimas".

noticias.titulo: Mejoras en el sistema Viogén y más formación en violencia de género: ¿qué proponen las expertas y los partidos este 29N?
noticias.texto:
Mejoras en el sistema Viogén y más formación en violencia de género: ¿qué proponen las expertas y los partidos este 29N?
- RTVE habla con expertas que ponen el foco en la mejora de los sistemas de protección, la prevención y la especialización judicial
- El 016 es el teléfono de atención a víctimas, gratuito y no deja huella en la factura; el correo es 016-online@igualdad.gob.es
Elena tenía 37 años y es la última mujer asesinada por violencia de género en España. Con ella, ya son 47 las mujeres muertas a manos de sus parejas y exparejas en este 2026, que suma la mayor cifra de asesinatos machistas desde 2023. Una veintena de niños y niñas han quedado huérfanos solo en lo que va de año. No son datos que inviten al optimismo.
Durante el año pasado, una mujer fue asesinada a manos de su pareja o expareja cada 7,4 días y la cifra de muertas por esta lacra se eleva a 1.385 desde el año 2003, cuando empezaron a contabilizarse oficialmente.
Esta legislatura que acaba ha estado marcada por la aprobación en febrero de 2025 en el Congreso de los Diputados del nuevo Pacto de Estado contra la violencia de género, constituido en 2017 para unificar y reforzar las políticas de prevención, protección y asistencia a las víctimas incluidas en la histórica Ley de Medidas de Protección Integral contra la Violencia de Género de 2004. La renovación de ese pacto de Estado contó con el único voto en contra de Vox.
En los últimos años, asuntos relacionados con el feminismo y la lucha contra la violencia de género han ocupado parte importante del discurso político, a veces no precisamente para mostrar consenso, y se han convertido en campo de batalla en las campañas electorales. La de las elecciones generales del 29N no está siendo excepción.
La violencia de género entra también como punto a tratar en todos los programas electorales con propuestas que van desde la aprobación de una nueva Estrategia Estatal para combatir las Violencias Machistas por parte del PSOE a garantizar la fiabilidad de los dispositivos que vigilan las órdenes de alejamiento por parte del PP, que ha dicho que suprimirá el Ministerio de Igualdad, si gobierna.
Vox, por su parte, promete en su programa electoral derogar las leyes que han "criminalizado a los hombres y desprotegido a las mujeres" y Frente Amplio quiere ampliar un 10% la partida presupuestaria contra las violencias machistas.
[Consulta aquí el comparador de programas de RTVE]
En RTVE Noticias analizamos con expertas y asociaciones que trabajan con mujeres maltratadas qué queda por hacer en materia de violencia de género.
¿Se sienten las mujeres maltratadas protegidas por el sistema?
Cada vez que se conoce un nuevo caso de asesinato machista, aparece un patrón que se repite en la mayoría de los feminicidios: no había denuncia previa.
Según datos de este año del Observatorio contra la Violencia Doméstica y del Género del Consejo General del Poder Judicial y la Memoria de la Fiscalía General del Estado, solo el 22% de las víctimas mortales había presentado una denuncia contra su pareja o expareja. Y este es uno de los principales agujeros.
"Aunque la horquilla oscila levemente, por norma general de cada diez mujeres asesinadas que hay en el cementerio, solo dos habían denunciado. Esto es muy grave porque es indicativo de que la mujer no se siente protegida por el sistema y es dramático porque cuando una mujer se decide a denunciar ya lleva muchos años sufriendo muchos tipos de violencias, normalmente simultáneas: física, psicológica, sexual o económica", afirma a RTVE Noticias la catedrática de la Universidad Carlos III y experta en igualdad y violencia de género, Rosa San Segundo, que habla de una clara desconfianza en el sistema judicial y el pánico a un proceso a veces eterno que supone una revictimización.
"Es un proceso larguísimo en el que se reactiva la violencia del agresor y en el que las medidas de protección son lentas. A veces todo se complica tanto que algunas mujeres quitan las denuncias porque el vía crucis puede ser infinito", explica Carmen Benito, presidenta de la asociación Mujeres Unidas por el Maltrato.
Durante el segundo trimestre de este 2026, los Tribunales de Instancia de toda España recibieron un total de 55.712 denuncias, un 9,81% más que en el mismo periodo del año anterior, según datos aportados por el Consejo General del Poder Judicial. El número de sentencias dictadas fue de 16.553, de las que el 82,62% fueron condenatorias.
Carencias en la formación de jueces
Las expertas ponen el foco en una necesidad clave: una mayor formación y especialización de los profesionales que tratan a las víctimas, junto con el tiempo y los recursos que tienen para analizar cada caso, especialmente en el área judicial.
María Eugenia Prendes es fiscal de sala de Violencia contra la Mujer y explica a Objetivo Igualdad de TVE que las mujeres deben "armar bien la denuncia" antes de presentarla porque a veces son ellas mismas las que minimizan la situación en el relato que hacen, lo que achaca al estado psicológico en la que se encuentran: "Hablan desde el trauma y el sufrimiento, eso les hace tener saltos y fallos en la memoria".
Incide en que "hay que saber cómo tomarles declaración, poniéndolas en el centro", para añadir que es necesario que en los juzgados existan unidades de valoración de forenses integrales y especializadas, de las que formen parte psicólogos y trabajadores sociales.
"La ley de violencia de género preveía que se creasen en el plazo de dos años y aún no se ha creado en muchos sitios", se queja Prendes, que pone en valor el abordaje integral "de lo civil y penal" en el mismo juzgado, pero insiste en esa falta de formación especializada a la hora de establecer los indicadores de riesgo y las medidas cautelares. Apunta a que existe cierta brecha entre lo que dice la ley y la realidad práctica en los juzgados.
La experta en igualdad y violencia de género Rosa San Segundo coincide en este problema de base, que califica de "grave". Cree que los jueces conocen las leyes, pero tienen muy poca formación "específica y profunda" sobre lo que rodea la violencia de género y la complejidad que esta entraña. "No saben cómo se comportan la víctima y el agresor, cómo interactúan, cuáles son los ciclos de la violencia y las dobles caras de unas conductas que a veces chirrían en los juzgados por puro desconocimiento".
Coinciden en que es necesario, por tanto, que los profesionales conozcan los mecanismos de dependencia emocional y la magnitud en la manipulación y la anulación de la víctima para entender por ejemplo por qué en un momento dado vuelve con su agresor o retira una denuncia y que eso no sea usado en un juicio en su contra.
Todo esto, alerta, puede llevar a la denegación de las medidas de protección y órdenes de alejamiento que derive en situaciones de peligro extremo. Apuesta, además, por medidas judiciales y policiales de protección más severas.
Mejoras en el sistema Viogén
Viogén es el sistema de seguimiento integral en los casos de violencia de género que depende del Ministerio del Interior y por el que se evalúa el riesgo para cada víctima- bajo, medio, alto y extremo- centralizando en el mismo la información policial, judicial y de servicios sociales sobre el caso. Más de 110.000 mujeres en España están activas en este sistema, con datos de este pasado mes de octubre.
Las expertas coinciden aquí en la necesidad de mejorar la coordinación entre los juzgados de familia, las fuerzas de seguridad y los servicios sociales para actuar "con rapidez y eficacia", explica la presidenta de la asociación Mujeres Unidas por el Maltrato.
